title: [RFC]: [RL - WIP] Checkpoint -> Kernel Format transition graph
author: S1ro1
body:
# Motivation.

### Why?

With growing size of models, inference becoming faster, one thing is stagnating. Weight transfer in RL workloads is usually done with a single NCCL broadcast where every rank loads the full model weights through an iterator and does the whole post-processing logic itself. This is wasteful and also can become a bottleneck. This requires creating a global process group, requires a lot of synchronization and utilizes at most 1 NIC (50GB/s). A lot of work has been done on using RDMA-like transport for weight reloading. This process is (almost) synchronization free and utilizes direct memory writes/reads from remote GPU memory, through IB/EFA/etc. This can significantly speedup the transfer, as there is no synchronization involved, trainers exchange metadata with inference and then either trainers push, or inference engines pull the required weights from its corresponding memory addresses. The issue here becomes the knowledge of how the weights are laid out in inference/trainer memory.

### Checkpoint x Kernel format

Currently, weights get loaded from disk from a `HF`-like checkpoint, go through processing and end up in a so-called `kernel format`. This format is how the weights exist during the engine life-time. Some notable examples being

- quantized into FP8, scales rearranged into TMA friendly format
- `qkv`/`gate_up` fusion
- `ColumnLinear` for TP

This itself seems okay, but the issue is deeper - this format depends on the runtime configuration. Let's say you want to inference GLM5 FP8. Depending on if you end up using `DeepGemm` FP8 MoE or `Cutlass` FP8 MoE, your gate-up projection might end up like `w1w3` or `w3w1` - and this is just a single example, there is way more of them that I'm not familiar with. You might see the issue here, trainer needs to know the layout of the inference weights, if they were quantized, if they were padded, etc (endless options here) to be able to either directly load them or directly write them to the inference engine. Having this information is non-trivial in most cases


# Proposed Change.

## Example use-case
I have done some exploration into how would such transfer engine look like, the results are quite amazing honestly, cutting transfer of 800B model from ~40-50sec to 1sec.

## Approach
The approach can be split into 2 different paths, depending if the main use-case would be with `PUSH` or `PULL`. As for implementation details, we have ended up using [nixl](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl?tab=readme-ov-file) to do the memory writes/reads

## 1. `PUSH` - this diagram is taken from our design that we have done in [prime-rl](https://github.com/PrimeIntellect-ai/prime-rl/pull/2326)
```
trainer rank 0           orchestrator              inference (all ranks)
     │                         │                         │
     ├── touch STABLE ─────────▶                         │
     │                         ├── /pause ───────────────▶
     │                         │◀── ack all ─────────────┤
     │                         ├── touch NIXL_READY      │
     │◀── see NIXL_READY ──────┤                         │
     │                                                   │
     ├───────── dist.barrier() across all trainer ranks ─│
     │                                                   │
     ├─────────── RDMA WRITEs (every rank) ─────────────▶│
     │                                                   │
     ├──────── spg.barrier() across trainer+inference ───│
     │                                                   │
     │                         │◀── /resume ─────────────┤
     │                         ├── resume ──────────────▶│
```

This is a preliminary design, focused on correctness, not performance (viz the extensive synchronization), but still cuts the transfer to 1.5sec across ~200+ GPUs

This approach depends on pre-exchanged metadata between trainer and inference. This metadata includes but is not limited to addresses and lengths of the remote pointers. Trainer also needs to be aware of the conversion format itself, that brings us to the first proposition 

### Proposition 1
Document the whole translation between `checkpoint -> kernel` formats. This can look as such (obviously extended to all the possible uses in processing) - open to discussion.

```python
    ConversionSpec(
        "mlp.gate_up_proj.weight",
        ("mlp.gate_proj.weight", "mlp.up_proj.weight"),
        quantization=QuantizationSpec(torch.float8_e4m3fn, ".weight_scale_inv"),
    ),
    ConversionSpec(
        "mlp.down_proj.weight",
        ("mlp.down_proj.weight",),
        quantization=QuantizationSpec(torch.float8_e4m3fn, ".weight_scale_inv"),
    ),
```

### Disadvantages

- This would require extensive changes to the whole model processing logic in VLLM, where every operation above the tensors loaded from the checkpoint format would have to be recorded and added into a graph composed of operations as such. RL frameworks would then have to replay this graph to construct their weights matching the VLLM format

### Advantages

- This is fairly framework agnostic, RL frameworks would extend VLLM workers to initialize what they need in their RDMA framework/lib of choice, then when ready submit a write to pre-exchanged tensor pointers and would be done with things.


## 2. `PULL`
This proposition approaches the problem from the other side. If we had Workers pull from the trainer itself. I haven't thought of this approach that much as it doesn't suit our proposal that much, but open to discussion here.

### Proposition

Make VLLM weight loading `RDMA` aware. This would be as easy as to replay the current full weight loading logic, but not reading local tensors, but remote ones.

### Disadvantages

- The tensors to load from have to be pre-registered on static memory addresses, which wouldn't be able to change without extra metadata exchange
- This would also lead to the requirement of having a scratchpad with weights on a trainer side or a parameter server, where the weights would have to be stored in checkpoint format
- This would also lock VLLM to a single `RDMA` framework

### Advantages
- easier on the trainer side

I'm strongly leaning towards `PUSH` based semantics and proposition 1, but open to discussion

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@robertgshaw2-redhat @kylesayrs 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Rust front-end
author: njhill
body: ### Motivation vLLM has always had a strong python bias to make it accessible to a wide range of contributors, and to exploit ML libraries including pytorch, triton, etc. Historically, we have managed the inherent performance downsides of python, which include garbage collection and restricted parallelism due to the GIL. The measures taken include resorting to multiprocessing for CPU parallelism, which includes the capability to scale out the API server process. As GPU latency continues to fall, request concurrency grows, and large-scale deployments become the norm, the CPU parts of the system have again become a bottleneck in many situations. This is often seen in the front-end process where the asyncio event loop can’t keep up. Further, our front-end python code has become increasingly complex and fragile as it has evolved organically. With the advent of coding agents, the python vs rust contributor accessibility issue is minimized. It seems the time is right to explore a rust-based alternative to the python front-end process: - It will allow us to eliminate the local api server process scale-out pattern which imposes some awkward limitations and is the source of significant complexity - It is an excuse to restructure the front-end code cleanly “from scratch” - It can be implemented as a “drop in” alternative to the existing front-end api server process transparently to users - It’s much better suited for maintainable production software: - It’s much harder to write bad code in rust - our current code has a seemingly endless number of edge case / latent bugs. Rust reduces the likelihood of these. - It’s much harder to write slow code in rust. We have experimented with an initial version of this, which is a drop-in alternative to the python api-server process and so can be used with the existing vllm serve entrypoint. The python launcher process will manage the various subprocesses as it currently does in the multi api-server case. It’s currently enabled via a `VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND` environment variable. Without this, the python path is used exactly as before. ## Performance Benchmarks All benchmarks: Qwen3-0.6B, DP=4 on 4x GB200 GPUs, vllm 0.19.0, request_rate=inf. Results shown at concurrency=1024. asc = `--api-server-count`. These is obviously not a realistic real-world configuration but chosen to emphasize the ceiling imposed by the current python implementation. We'll continue to benchmark with other models/workloads. **Benchmark 1 — Decode/streaming-sensitive** (`--backend vllm`, random completions, input_len=32, output_len=512, prefix caching disabled) | Frontend | Throughput (req/s) | P50 TTFT (ms) | P90 TTFT (ms) | P50 TPOT (ms) | P90 TPOT (ms) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Rust | 559.79 | 50.51 | 67.71 | 3.29 | 3.32 | | Python (default, asc=4) | 509.56 | 165.95 | 206.52 | 3.39 | 3.74 | | Python (asc=16) | 521.80 | 58.97 | 80.77 | 3.54 | 3.68 | Rust achieves 10% higher throughput than default Python and 3.3x lower P50 TTFT. Even with 16 api-server processes, Python can't match Rust throughput and has 4% higher TPOT. **Benchmark 2 — Preprocess-hot** (`--backend openai-chat`, speed-bench ~10K token chat prompts, output_len=16, prefix cache pre-warmed) | Frontend | Throughput (req/s) | P50 TTFT (ms) | P90 TTFT (ms) | P50 TPOT (ms) | P90 TPOT (ms) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Rust | 837.00 | 596.92 | 807.64 | 39.90 | 46.42 | | Python (default, asc=4) | 162.23 | 6076.09 | 7936.50 | 1.96 | 9.77 | | Python (asc=32) | 785.98 | 657.15 | 1211.37 | 38.89 | 46.66 | With prefix cache fully warm, the frontend becomes the bottleneck. A single Rust frontend matches or exceeds 32 Python api-server processes. Default Python saturates at only 19% of Rust throughput with 10x worse P50 TTFT. ## What’s implemented so far? Most core functionality for completions, chat completions and generate APIs, with the exception of a handful of parameters including n and beam_search. We are iterating quickly and it won’t take long to fill in additional functionality. ## Where would the rust code live? There are two options - either within the vllm repo, or a separate repo within the vllm org (e.g. vllm-rs). My current preference is that the code lives in a rust dir within the vllm repo because: - It can be built as a complete project - This is an internal component of vLLM, tightly coupled to other parts of the system. Changes to some internal interfaces/types will need to span the python and rust code. - It’s a common / well-established pattern, and we already have native C code / kernels within the repo. - In future we may want to implement some other internal components / libraries in rust ## How will it affect users/developers? For users it should be transparent, whether they are using the docker container or pip install. The (small) rust binary would be packaged as part of the wheel. For doing development pip install -e, there would be a choice of: - Excluding rust altogether (of course the env var then won’t work at runtime) - Use precompiled rust binary (`VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED_RUST=1`) - Build the rust crates too (needed of course for changes to rust code) - One line toolchain install: `curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh` ## Would this replace the python front-end? No, not for the time being. The hope is to include this as experimental/preview and see how things go. ### Proposed Change. Since there is a decision about whether the code should be part of the vLLM repo or not (see above), and to minimize the integration PR diff, we have created it in a separate repo for now: - https://github.com/Inferact/vllm-frontend-rs See also corresponding integration PR: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/40848
speedup_claims: Default Python saturates at only 19% of Rust throughput with 10x worse P50 TTFT

speedup_evidence.claim: Default Python saturates at only 19% of Rust throughput with 10x worse P50 TTFT
