This is heavily dependent on the chosen algorithm (both the watermarking scheme, and the PRF), we expect throughput degradation of O(0.3% for 1B models, 0.1% for 30B+ models) for Gumbel-max sampling and O(1% - 0.5%) for SynthID-Text (see Table 4 of [TextSeal](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12456)) - Watermarked sampling does not significantly distort the quality of an expected output of a model: this is mathematically proven theoretically but remains dependent on certain aspects of key generation and context handling, it will be empirically validated with evaluations - Watermarked generations are reliably detectable: we will provide TPR@FPR and detection power across lengths and generation entropies to accompany the baseline detection algorithm, but we expect downstream consumers to optimize their own algorithms as there is a large cost-quality tradeoff to explore that will differ by provider (as well as false-positive calibration) ### Note on diversity Note that while watermarked generation may induce a loss in diversity over a sequence (single-token non-distortion) or multiple sequences (single-sequence non-distortion), most methods that would be considered for production watermarking do not produce a _catastrophic_ loss of diversity (determinism, given a fixed key and input). The proposed Gumbel-max algorithm, given its simplicity, does exhibit this behaviour. If this RFC is accepted, we expect to add multiple other watermarking schemes. These schemes may employ techniques that restore diversity: - Repeated-context deduplication - Tournament sampling with randomly sampled candidates - Random-tape methods - Dual or multi-key methods - Gated watermarking (random, or conditional on entropy, or conditional on context) - Speculative decoding See Results section below for results. ### Additional points of discussion #### Choice of PRF Many watermarking schemes rely on a keyed PRF to guide generation, making the choice of such a function important to the behaviour of the algorithm. There are certain qualities we desire in our PRF: 1. Stability over time: a torch/triton update should not break a `(k, WM_k(output))` pair (see [Philox](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2063384.2063405), which otherwise would be an excellent candidate) 2. Fast on GPU: many PRFs are only available in CPU form (see [SipHash](https://www.aumasson.jp/siphash/siphash.pdf)), which would require us to maintain an internal GPU/triton implementation 3. Good statistical properties: the PRF must have good uniformity in its output, independence across inputs and no structure; most PRFs have this as a principal objective already 4. [optional] Cryptographically secure: it may be desirable for the `(context, key) -> pseudorandom value` mapping to be indistinguishable from a fresh random function, as it protect from attackers predicting keys from context, predicting values from unseen contexts, or generating strongly watermarked text without the key. We can also suppose that some deployments may require FIPS compliancy As we cannot ensure that every PRF is suitable to every use, we propose a modular PRF system to allow easy extension to new PRFs. This will allow us to implement a PRF that aligns with points 1, 2 and 3 while downstream consumers may extend the system to use PRFs with other qualities (such as FIPS compliance). Here are some candidates for a suitable PRF: | Candidate | 1. Stable | 2. Fast on GPU | 3. Statistical quality | |---|---:|---:|---:| | HMAC-SHA-256 | Yes | No | Yes | | Philox (PyTorch) | No, due to API | Yes | Yes | | SipHash-2-4 | Yes | No existing impl. | Yes | | TextSeal integer hash | Yes* | Yes* | Yes** | _* Assuming we maintain a frozen internal implementation_ _** Its statistical properties have no public analysis compared to the alternatives_ For an initial implementation, we propose an internal version of the Philox algorithm, that can be maintained as stable. It is high-performance and well-established for PRFs (supported by NumPy and used by PyTorch for CUDA RNG). [HMAC](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/224/ipd) is a potential contender, as it is also well-established, cryptographically secure and can be FIPS compliant (unlike Philox), but even an optimized GPU implementation may not be fast enough as the algorithm itself is much heavier. ```python def philox4x32-10-v1(key, context, token) -> uint32 -> uniform float ``` ## Results - Model: Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B - Dataset: GSM8K - top_p=1.0, max_tokens=256 - Watermark: Gumbel-max, Philox PRF, context width 4 ### Performance All ran on H100, median of 3 runs Config | Total output token/s/gpu | Delta v. baseline ---|---|--- Baseline | 11,056.947 | 0.000% Watermarked | 10,985.863 | -0.643% BSZ | p20 (ms) | Median (ms) | p80 (ms) | Peak temporary memory (MiB) ---|---|---|---|--- 1 | 0.037568 | 0.039088 | 0.040640 | 0.003906 8 | 0.038176 | 0.038800 | 0.039968 | 0.023926 32 | 0.042400 | 0.042544 | 0.042880 | 0.090332 256 | 0.254432 | 0.254960 | 0.256000 | 0.715820 ### Quality Evals were run and averaged over 8 watermark keys. Accuracy: Variant | T=0.7 | T=1.0 ---|---|--- Main | 42.88% | 27.63% PR, watermark off | 43.31% | 26.06% PR, watermark on | 44.00% | 27.63% Variance, min-max range and SD for each config: T | Main | PR (wm=off) | PR (wm=on) ---|---|---|--- 0.7 | 39.5–49.0%, 2.9 pp | 40.0–50.0%, 3.0 pp | 38.5–47.5%, 2.5 pp 1.0 | 23.5–31.0%, 2.2 pp | 23.5–31.0%, 2.4 pp | 25.5–30.0%, 1.8 pp Output length: Temperature | PR (wm=off) | PR (wm=on) | Difference | 95% CI ---|---|---|---|--- 0.7 | 117.70 | 121.59 | +3.89 tokens | [+0.93, +6.88] 1.0 | 137.37 | 155.60 | +18.23 tokens | [+13.98, +22.50] Fraction reaching `gen_length=256` limit: Temperature | PR (wm=off) | PR (wm=on) ---|---|--- 0.7 | 7.38% | 10.81% 1.0 | 16.25% | 32.94% This Gumbel-max implementation's single-token non-distortion does not guarantee non-distortion over a keyed sequence, we can see this here with a change in generation length. See "Note on diversity" above for solutions. ### Diversity _See "Note on diversity" section for notes on output diversity for this implementation of Gumbel-max._ This form of Gumbel-max watermarking exhibits a catastrophic collapse in diversity. ### Detectability All numbers use a threshold of `p<=0.01`, so a 1% FPR, and are averaged over 8 watermark keys. Watermarked GSM8K response detection: Temp. | Positive rate ---|--- 0.7 | 42.13% 1.0 | 84.17% Unwatermarked GSM8K response detection: Config | Temp. | Positive rate ---|---|--- Main | 0.7 | 1.154% Main | 1.0 | 1.139% PR | 0.7 | 1.172% PR | 1.0 | 1.135% TPR@FPR by sequence length (`Unknown Key` refers to having to evaluate the watermark score over 8 keys, and applying a Bonferroni correction to the p-value): ## References and ressources For key algorithms, definitions: - Gumbel-max: https://simons.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/2024-10/LLM24-2%20Slides%20-%20Scott%20Aaronson.pdf - Random tape Gumbel-max: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.15593 - SynthID-Text - Paper: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08025-4#MOESM1 - Appendix: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41586-024-08025-4/MediaObjects/41586_2024_8025_MOESM1_ESM.pdf - TextSeal: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12456 For the choice of PRF: - Philox's Random123 algorithm - Paper: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2063384.2063405 - Code: https://github.com/DEShawResearch/random123/blob/main/include/Random123/philox.h - HMAC: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/224/ipd For further reading: - Speculative decoding considerations: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.20418v1 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.01428

title: [RFC]: TreeWY: Tree Speculative Decoding for hybrid (GDN) models
author: sneha5gsm
body:
### Motivation.

Hello!
I recently explored speculative decoding for hybrid models (Qwen 3.5 model series) in vLLM and the recurrent-state memory bottleneck in the current implementation. With `mamba_cache_mode="all"`, a draft of `N` positions needs `N+1` full state snapshots per sequence per layer. On Qwen3.5-397B that is 90 MiB/seq i.e. 360 MiB for a depth-3 chain and ~1.2 GiB for a `[2,2,2]` tree (14 nodes), out of the same budget as the KV cache. To alleviate the recurrent-state memory bottleneck, my current implementation reconstructs the accepted state on commit rather than snapshotting it, using the WY/UT representation of the gated delta rule: one strictly-lower-triangular solve over the verify window gives every draft node's output, and any node's continuation state rebuilds from a small per-node stash. I extended it to support **tree** speculative decoding on GDN-based Qwen hybrids. Here's the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20961) related to the study. It has the memory analysis at both model scales, and the serving sweep.

I see that [ReplaySSM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47572) does something similar for part of this.
I benchmarked ReplaySSM against my implementation on Qwen3.5-35B, and ReplaySSM is the more performant one for chain speculative decoding in hybrid models. It also is broader in terms of model support. Kudos to the team!

Where the two designs diverge: ReplaySSM and my current implementation solve the same triangular system on the same corrected inputs. The two kernels differ in one predicate: an index comparison where mine loads an explicit ancestor mask, so a commit becomes an ancestor-masked reduction rather than a cursor move. That is what makes a tree reachable.

Here's the [current implementation](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/main...sneha5gsm:vllm:treewy-gdn-spec-decode), for reference.

Draft trees are not a throughput win yet: acceptance rises monotonically with width (from 3.23 to 3.44 on Spec-Bench) but throughput falls at every width. The cause is CUDA graph capture: a branching verify step cannot be fully captured today. Tree speculative decoding (width > 1) needs a non-causal ancestor mask on the softmax layers which leads to a fallback to PIECEWISE. 



 

### Proposed Change.

I would like to support tree speculative decoding for hybrid models in vLLM.

Since this relates to the ReplaySSM contribution, I am happy to collaborate with the ReplaySSM team to further support it for tree speculative decoding in hybrid models.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@Johnny-Liou 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Batch invariance for speculative decoding needs to cover the forward pass (M=1 vs M=k+1)
author: Leonccaa
body:
### Motivation.

At temperature 0, enabling speculative decoding can change the generated sequence relative to plain decoding. This is already reported for ngram spec decode in #41758, and #52522 proposes batch-invariant support for speculative decoding — but scoped to the sampling layer (RNG streams, request ordering, preemption recovery).

We ran a multi-day forensic campaign driving a 125B hybrid linear-attention/MoE model with a native MTP head (TP4, FP16) toward bitwise verify↔decode parity. Our finding: on our stack the dominant cause is **forward-pass arithmetic**, not sampling. The target model's verification pass computes rows with `M = k+1`, plain decode computes the same rows with `M = 1`, and **nothing in the current stack guarantees those two produce identical bits**. Real text contains decision points whose top-2 logit margin sits at ULP scale; one 1-ULP difference in one operator flips such a token, and greedy decoding turns that flip into a permanently divergent trajectory. Visible symptom on one of our workloads, purely from this effect: draft acceptance ~100% → 72%, decode ~110 → 89 tok/s.

**The invariant being violated:** given the same checkpoint, the same input and the same runtime/load configuration, the target model's verify pass over rows `[t..t+k]` must reproduce, bit for bit, what plain `M=1` decode would produce at each of those positions.

We are filing this because the mechanisms below are hardware- and method-generic, and because our experience says model-level point-mitigation does not converge. We deliberately do **not** propose a design.

#### Taxonomy of sources (each observed and isolated with bitwise evidence)

**Class A — kernel-level M-dependent reductions.** The same kernel produces different bits for the same logical row depending on how many rows were launched.
- Split-K GEMMs: partial-sum combination order follows launch geometry, which includes M.
- Explicit M-conditioned reduction configuration: we found a norm implementation selecting a 1024-wide reduction for M=1 and 512-wide for M>1 — a literal per-M topology branch.
- Hand-written F16 GEMM, M=5 vs 5×(M=1), random weights: ~92–114 of 20480 elements differ by 1–2 ULP.

**Class B — compiler/fusion topology.** `torch.compile`/Inductor generates reduction schedules **per shape specialization**.
- The native decomposition of an op (a gated RMSNorm, in our case) is fused differently inside an M=1 graph than inside an M=k+1 graph, producing sparse 1-ULP output differences from bitwise-identical inputs.
- **Opaque custom ops act as fusion barriers.** Registering an extra, numerically no-op custom op into only one engine's graph changed *neighbouring* arithmetic by 1 ULP; making both engines' graphs structurally identical restored bitwise equality. Graph structure — not just op semantics — is part of the numerical contract.
- Instrumentation participates in this: adding dump/trace ops changes fusion topology, so naive tracing perturbs the very difference under measurement.

**Class C — execution-form asymmetry between engines.** Spec-enabled engines route parts of the model through different execution forms than non-spec engines.
- An auto-gate keyed on "speculative config is present" moved a whole attention-block family to an opaque/eager path on the spec engine while the non-spec engine kept the compiled path → divergence at **prefill layer 0**, before any speculative token exists.
- The reverse leak also occurred: an opaque wrapper unconditionally instantiated in the non-spec engine moved the *non-spec* baseline trajectory. Which modules run compiled vs eager has to be treated as part of each engine's frozen contract.

**Class D — configuration-activated members.** Which of the above actually express depends on deployment configuration, so a fix validated in one configuration silently loses coverage in another.
- Quantization admission (a path accepted vs rejected) swaps whole kernel families in and out.
- **Load strategy is numerically non-neutral:** switching checkpoint loading between prefetch and mmap/lazy changed the greedy trajectory from token 0 with identical checkpoint bytes — not by corrupting data, but by shifting mapped addresses, allocation order and compile/capture timing, which re-rolls every Class A–C die.

#### Why model-level point-mitigation does not converge (empirical)

We closed a long series of individual members with pre/post bitwise evidence (top-k tie-break determinism, per-row replays of specific projections, norm dispatch admission, symmetric op placement, fixed-topology reduction reimplementations). Observed dynamics:

1. **The divergence point migrates instead of closing.** Across successive true fixes, the index of the first divergent token moved 14 → 2 → 14 → 10. Every real fix exposes the next member earlier or later, and each spec depth k, plus boundary prompt lengths (4/5/6 tokens), exercises *distinct* compile specializations with distinct expressing members.
2. **Gates lie in both directions when fed synthetic data.** Random-weight kernel probes over-predicted expression (kernel red, engine mute). Mild synthetic samples under-predicted it (operator gate green, real checkpoint red). Only per-instance gates on real checkpoint weights were trustworthy — and two layer instances sharing one kernel and one shape can still disagree, because expression is value-dependent.
3. **Replicating compiled arithmetic is a treadmill.** Matching Inductor's generated reduction means cloning exact codegen parameters (XBLOCK / R-block / warps / output tiling) per shape, it breaks on multi-output subgraphs with alias/buffer contracts, and any compiler upgrade invalidates it.

After closing every member that expressed at production shapes, we reached 16/16 greedy-token parity at 1K/4K contexts with acceptance restored to 81% and the expected spec speedup back — but residual 1-ULP members remained reachable at boundary shapes, each costing several full-model runs to localize. We stopped and documented those as known differences. That end state is operationally usable; it is a workaround, not a solution.

#### Gap relative to existing work

- #41758 is the symptom class, on a completely different model/method/hardware combination (Qwen3-0.6B, ngram, A100) — which is what convinced us this is systemic rather than a property of our stack.
- #52522's scope (sampling, RNG streams, preemption recovery) is necessary but not sufficient: none of Classes A–D live in the sampling layer.
- The `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` kernel work is the right neighbourhood, but its axis is batch composition across requests. Speculative decoding adds the `M=1 ↔ M=k+1` axis for the *same* logical row, which is the axis we found unguarded.

### Proposed Change.

What we are asking for is a **scope decision, not an implementation** — we have no design to offer here, and we think ours would be the wrong one: every mitigation we built lives at the model/site level, and the campaign above is our evidence that this level cannot hold the invariant durably.

The change we would like considered: treat **forward-pass batch invariance across M for a fixed logical row** as a first-class contract at the kernel and compilation layer, in the same way `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` treats batch composition today, and extend the batch-invariant spec-decode effort (#52522) to cover it rather than stopping at the sampling boundary.

Questions we think are worth settling before anyone writes code:

1. Is forward-pass M-invariance considered in scope for #52522, or is it a separate workstream?
2. Should verify↔decode bitwise parity be an explicitly documented guarantee under a batch-invariant mode (with the cost that implies), or an explicit non-guarantee — so that users stop treating greedy-output changes under spec decode as a bug in their own configuration?
3. If it becomes a guarantee, does it cover the compilation layer as well as kernels? Class B and Class C say that guaranteeing only kernels is not enough: fusion topology and per-engine execution form change results on their own.

We are happy to contribute evidence, reproduction methodology and measurements to whatever direction maintainers choose. Details in the appendices below.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

@SAKETH11111 (#41758), @andakai (#52522), and anyone working on `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` kernels or the spec-decode verification path.

### Any Other Things.

Everything below is offered as raw material for anyone continuing this investigation on their own stack. Each item exists because the naive version misled us first.

#### Appendix A — attribution methodology that survived

1. **Route-hit proof before interpretation.** Before trusting any A/B, prove the code under test actually executed (one-shot entry probes checked in logs). Note that logging inside compiled regions can be silenced by `torch.compiler.is_compiling()` guards — probe at admission time or outside the graph. Several of our early "fixes" were no-ops because the gate meant to admit them evaluated false on the spec engine; two others passed reduced gates and then regressed the full model. Arms without route-hit proof must be marked INVALID, never "no effect".
2. **Per-instance operator gates on real checkpoint weights.** Extract each layer instance's actual weights from the loaded engine and compare `op(k rows stacked)` against `k × op(1 row)` bitwise, per instance, for M = 1..8, plus padded-M variants. Per (1) above, do not substitute random weights. Our final inventory ran ~1,500 such comparisons across two operator families to certify zero expression at production shapes.
3. **Observation neutrality.** Under full CUDA graphs, naively saving intermediates returns capture-aliased garbage, and inserting dump ops changes fusion topology. The only neutral mechanism we found was copying from persistent, pre-registered graph buffers present identically in both arms, snapshotted after the step. Validate neutrality by checking that the instrumented run still reproduces the uninstrumented token sequence.
4. **Anchor gates.** Before comparing anything across arms: assert `input_ids` bitwise-identical, and pin both arms by full commit tuple. Every code snapshot silently spawns a new numerical baseline (Class B), so "matches the previously recorded golden output" is only meaningful when you name the build that produced that golden.
5. **Execution-form bisection.** Forcing both engines into the same form (both eager, or both compiled) is a cheap diagnostic: it collapses Class C entirely and leaves A/B isolated. In our case, unifying a single op's implementation across forms made all 48 layers' block outputs bitwise-equal over a 1024-token prefill — one op's fusion boundary accounted for the entire asymmetry.
6. **Fragile tokens are detectors, not evidence.** A token position with a ULP-scale top-2 margin is a sensitive tripwire, but different perturbations flip it to *different* tokens, so token-level observation cannot attribute cause. Attribution has to happen at the first divergent tensor, walked layer by layer.

#### Appendix B — measured signatures per class

- **Class A:** hand-written F16 GEMM, M=5 vs 5×(M=1), random weights: ~92–114 of 20480 elements at 1–2 ULP. The same kernel, gated per-instance on real checkpoint weights across 140+ instances × M=2..8: **zero** expression — fully latent on that checkpoint. This contrast is exactly why synthetic probes mislead.
- **Class B (fusion):** gated-RMSNorm decomposition under Inductor, M=1 vs M=2, bitwise-identical inputs: 1 FP16 element of 10240 differs, |Δ| = 7.63e-6, deterministic across reruns (a topology property, not a race). Generated reduction for the M=1 specialization: XBLOCK=1, R0_BLOCK=2048, 16 warps over a 128-element row — parameters that change per shape specialization.
- **Class B (barrier asymmetry):** one numerically no-op custom op registered into a single engine's graph → downstream layer outputs differ at 1 ULP across ~2.3M elements; symmetric registration → bitwise equal.
- **Class C:** spec-engine-only eager routing of an attention-block family → divergence present from prefill layer 0, before any speculative token exists.
- **Class D:** load-strategy flip (prefetch ↔ mmap/lazy) alone changed the greedy trajectory from token 0, with identical checkpoint bytes.
- **End-to-end:** first divergent token index migrated 14 → 2 → 14 → 10 across successive true fixes; acceptance ~100% → 72% and decode ~110 → 89 tok/s while members were expressing; after closing all members expressed at production shapes, 16/16 greedy-token parity at 1K and 4K with 81% acceptance and the expected speedup restored.

#### Appendix C — minimal reproduction recipe (any model, mainline vLLM)

1. **Symptom:** temperature 0, fixed prompt, spec decode on vs off, compare full token sequences (this is #41758's setup; any spec method works).
2. **First split:** compare the two configurations' **prefill** logits for the same prompt, bitwise. If they already differ, you have Class C/D — engine construction, execution form or configuration asymmetry — before speculation is even involved.
3. **Core check:** for an accepted prefix, compare the target model's verify-pass logits at position t (computed with M=k+1 rows) against plain decode logits at the same position (M=1). Any bit difference is Class A/B expressing. Walk layers to the first divergent tensor using pre-registered buffers (Appendix A.3).
4. **Shape axes that expose members:** tiny prompts (4/5/6 tokens — compile-specialization boundaries), prompts straddling block/graph-capture boundaries, and each spec depth k separately (each k is its own specialization).
5. **Configuration axes:** load format, quantization on/off, CUDA graph mode, `custom_ops` selection (native decomposition vs custom kernel), TP size. Each combination re-rolls which members express.

#### Environment

Observed on SM70/V100 ×4 (TP4), FP16 activations, a 125B hybrid linear-attention/MoE model with a native MTP head, full+piecewise CUDA graphs, `torch.compile`/Inductor. The SM70 software stack made expression *frequent*, but every mechanism above — split-K reductions, per-shape Inductor codegen, fusion barriers, spec-keyed execution-form gates, load-order sensitivity — exists on current hardware and mainline code paths.

Searched existing issues before filing; the closest are #41758 (symptom) and #52522 (adjacent scope), both linked above.

title: [RFC]: Per-KV-cache-group prefix-cache retention, with a hit-min exemption for hit-inert EAGLE sliding-window draft groups
author: nood-co1
body:
### Motivation.

**Summary.** On hybrid models that carry an EAGLE-style sliding-window draft group (DFlash/DSpark-shaped drafters), that group hashes `cdiv(sliding_window - 1, block_size) + 1` block ids at *every* prefix-cache boundary and frees them *cached* onto the protected tail of the one LRU that all groups share, while — once it is exempted from the hit `min` — contributing nothing to the reconciled hit length. On a GLM-5.3-Flash deployment this one group spends 87% of the prefix cache and caps coexisting conversations at ~50K tokens each. A per-group retention interval, combined with exempting such hit-inert groups from the hit `min`, restored ~4× the coexisting-conversation capacity with the fine hit grid kept for the target model's groups, and a third party reproduced 99.95% cached across alternating 120K conversations. All numbers below are **deployment evidence from a vLLM fork**, not upstream verification; the code reading is against upstream `main` @ `22df3a3`. This RFC asks for agreement on the policy before any code is posted as a PR.

**Where the cost comes from (upstream `main` @ `22df3a3`, verified).**

- `--prefix-cache-retention-interval` (`vllm/config/cache.py:156-158`, `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:530`) reaches the coordinator as one scalar, `KVCacheCoordinator.retention_interval` (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py:158`), and is handed unchanged to every manager at both `cache_blocks` sites (`:306-326` base, `:740-768` hybrid).
- Everything below the coordinator is already per group: `SingleTypeKVCacheManager.cache_blocks(..., retention_interval=None)` (`vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:432-436`), and each `reachable_block_mask` interprets it against its own block size and window (`:485-`, `:1010-`, `:1472-`).
- A sliding-window group needs `need = _contiguous_blocks_for_hit(window, block_size, use_eagle)` contiguous blocks at every retained boundary (`:898-908`, `:1028`); a full-attention group needs one block per boundary. Those SWA blocks are freed by `remove_skipped_blocks` -> `_remove_blocks_in_range` -> `BlockPool.free_blocks` (`:632`, `:605`), and because they are hashed they go to `blocks_to_evict_last` / `append_n`, the LRU *tail* (`vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:723-747`). Full-attention blocks stay allocated until request end; Mamba align-mode state blocks may also be freed mid-request (`single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:1529-1557`), but a 3584-token Mamba group frees one id per segment where the draft group frees 33. The group with the least reusable state gets the most eviction protection.
- `HybridKVCacheCoordinator.find_longest_cache_hit` folds every attention group, EAGLE draft group included, into the reconciled hit (`kv_cache_coordinator.py:770-903`, `curr_hit_length = _new_hit_length` at `:871`). So giving the draft group a sparser retention on `main` today would shorten everyone's hit — which is why the fork below carries a `min` exemption first.

**Measured (deployment evidence: GLM-5.3-Flash, 2× DGX Spark, TP=2, DFlash2 draft k=7; vLLM fork `0.1.dev20051+g487ecf187`; GLM-5.3-Flash support upstream is #53906).** Groups: MLA block 3584, four Mamba "align" groups at 3584, one EAGLE sliding-window draft group with window 2048 / block 64, scheduler block 3584; one `BlockPool` of 643 block ids (642 usable; derived from the logged `max_concurrency`, see *Any Other Things*).

| group | block ids per cached 3584-token segment (dense retention) |
|---|---:|
| full attention (MLA) | 1 |
| Mamba × 4 | 4 |
| **draft sliding window** | **33** (`cdiv(2047, 64) + 1`) |
| total | 38 |

Two conversations of `S` segments coexist only while `642 >= 43·S` (each of B's segments pops 38 ids while A's cached draft tail contributes 33 back), i.e. `S <= 14.9`. Measured on a clean server: 14 segments OK / 17 evicting; pair ladders at 45K / 56K / 66K tokens hit 99% / 0% / 0%.

Raising the single global `--prefix-cache-retention-interval` to 14336 restored the ladder to 99 / 98 / 97 / 96% at 45K / 56K / 66K / 80K — but it bought that capacity by coarsening *everyone's* retention grid: a diverging sub-agent prefix then hit only 45% of a ~29K prompt instead of landing on the 3584 grid.

With per-group retention — retention `0` (reachable-boundary tails only) on the draft group, dense for MLA/Mamba — and the draft group exempted from the hit `min`, the per-segment cost drops to 5 ids (+33 per turn boundary), projected `S <= 54` (~195K tokens per conversation) with the 3584 hit grid kept. Independent reproduction by a third-party tester on a different 2× DGX Spark deployment (`max_model_len=524288`, `max_num_seqs=4`), two distinct 120K-token conversations alternated A -> B -> A -> B:

```
A cold             cached      0 / 119,995   TTFT 174.522s
A warm             cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.581s
B cold             cached      0 / 119,995   TTFT 174.392s
B warm             cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.590s
A return after B   cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.567s
B return after A   cached 119,936 / 119,995   TTFT   0.567s
```

99.95% cached on every return, where the same shape previously evicted the parked conversation. Sources: https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks/pull/83 (per-group retention; the tester's receipt above is in its comments) and https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks/pull/84 (fine-grained hits, tested together). Those are recipe overlays on a fork; nothing there applies to `main` as-is.

### Proposed Change.

Three parts, in this order. The ask is agreement on 1 and 3 before any of the code is posted as a PR.

1. **Exempt hit-inert sliding-window groups from the reconciled hit `min`, with an explicit per-group lookup/consumption contract.** A sliding-window group is *hit-inert* when (a) it is EAGLE-annotated (`KVCacheGroupSpec.is_eagle_group`), so its hit length is not needed to bound the target's; (b) its window is shorter than `_cache_hit_alignment_tokens`, so its cached tail is only ever consultable at an alignment boundary; and (c) sparse retention is actually reachable for it: `need < alignment_tokens // block_size` (otherwise `reachable_block_mask` returns dense anyway, `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:1027-1053`), `block_size` divides the alignment, and `extra_retained_tokens == 0` (it separately affects admission/retention sizing, `vllm/v1/kv_cache_interface.py:694-730` / `single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:888-895`; nonzero values require separate handling or exclusion).

   The group is still looked up. If its own hit reaches the candidate boundary, its blocks are consumed as today — that is how the retained boundary tail keeps a conversation's own follow-up turn warm. If its hit is *shorter*, it must neither shorten `curr_hit_length` nor inflate `longest_hit_length`, and its per-group result must be an explicit "no reusable blocks; allocate a fresh window", not the empty list the current lookup would return: today `find_longest_cache_hit` initialises empty per-group results (`kv_cache_coordinator.py:795-800`), fills them only for `attention_groups` (`:815-874`), and `KVCacheManager.get_computed_blocks` passes them straight to allocation (`vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_manager.py:228-294`), so an empty draft result cannot reuse a retained tail. This is the same per-group-boundary concern #53786 raises for SWA fine-grained hits, and it is the part that needs design agreement.

   **Unproven risk, stated plainly:** final outputs are protected by target verification, but the drafter's *acceptance* depends on the window's KV being valid. Whether a newly allocated window block is zeroed depends on `needs_kv_cache_zeroing` (`single_type_kv_cache_manager.py:88-94`); the design must guarantee the window is recomputed during prefill of the uncached remainder rather than read stale, and the acceptance dip while it refills has only been measured on the fork (decode-rate control within noise), not upstream. It is free whenever the remainder is at least one window — the diverging-prefix / new-turn case. #50457 (all-sliding DFlash drafter with prefix caching, PR) is in this area and may be the right home.

2. **Resolve the retention interval per KV cache group.** `KVCacheCoordinator` gains `retention_interval_by_group: tuple[int | None, ...]`, resolved once in `__init__` and indexed at both `cache_blocks` sites. The manager API is untouched (already per call). With the identity resolution behaviour is byte-identical, which the accompanying tests pin. The seam patch is ready and rebased on `22df3a3` — `vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_coordinator.py` +37/−4, tests +72: https://github.com/nood-co1/vllm/tree/feat/per-group-prefix-cache-retention (commit https://github.com/nood-co1/vllm/commit/b9f82ae0f946039be1e96084ef15399e8cf2e07c). It is deliberately *not* opened as a PR: on its own it is plumbing with no user-visible effect, and it is only safe to use once part 1 exists.

3. **Policy:** resolve `retention_interval = 0` for groups that satisfy part 1's predicate, i.e. cache only the reachable-boundary tails (`SlidingWindowManager.reachable_block_mask`, `retention_interval == 0` branch), and the configured value for every other group. A genuine SWA target model (window spanning the alignment, or a group still inside the `min`) is unchanged. A user override can come later if wanted; the default should not need one.

Offered as a follow-up PR (parts 1–3 together, or 2 first if maintainers prefer the decomposition) once the policy is agreed.

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@rchalamala (#50457), @RichApple123 (#54397), @Suppressor72 (#53786 has the same DFlash2 all-sliding drafter shape), @woosebastian (#48532, eviction order in the shared pool).

### Any Other Things.

**Related work, and why this is not a duplicate** (`gh pr list` / `gh issue list --state open --search` for "per-group retention", "retention interval", "sliding window prefix cache eviction", "EAGLE draft prefix cache", 2026-09-01; titles verified with `gh` the same day):

- Issue [#48435](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48435) — hybrid-SWA prefix caching collapses under multi-session round-robin on Gemma-4 (eager-freed SWA tails recycled tail-first). Same LRU mechanism seen from the other side: there the SWA group *is* the target's own attention, its tails are needed for the hit, and losing them zeroes the hit. This RFC targets the case where the SWA group is a drafter whose hit is not needed; the eviction-order remedy for #48435 is different and the two compose.
- PR [#50457](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50457) — all-sliding DFlash drafter with prefix caching (open). Part 1 belongs near it.
- PR [#54397](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54397) — fine-grained SWA hits (draft). Orthogonal (lookup granularity, not retention or eviction).
- PR [#51886](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51886) — retention interval for `OffloadingConnector`; PR [#52747](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52747) — docs for the existing flag; PRs [#53803](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53803), [#53479](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53479), [#53945](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/53945) — which Mamba checkpoints are materialized. None make the coordinator's retention per group.
- Issues [#53670](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53670), [#53786](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/53786) — EAGLE last-block drop and SWA fine-grained hits on Qwen3.8/3.5 hybrids with DFlash2 drafters; same deployment shape, different costs.
- PR [#48532](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48532) — per-group eviction order in deferred block free (same pool, different path).

**Caveats.** All measurements are deployment evidence from a fork on GLM-5.3-Flash, which is not yet in `main` (#53906); the block-id arithmetic uses code paths that exist unchanged on `main` (`SlidingWindowManager.reachable_block_mask`, `BlockPool.free_blocks`). The pool size (643 ids) is derived from the logged `GPU KV cache size` / `max_concurrency` figure rather than logged directly — filed separately as a small observability request. The ~195K-per-conversation projection is from the capacity model (`642 >= 2C − D`), which predicted every measured row's sign and order but ran ~25% optimistic at retention 7168; the 120K × 2 reproduction above is the measured point.

Submitted by nood-co1 on behalf of Blockbrain Labs (https://x.com/blockbrain_labs, GitHub org blockbrain-ai); drafted with AI assistance (Claude, with an independent adversarial review pass by OpenAI Codex folded in) and reviewed by the submitter, who checked every `file:line` against `22df3a3`.

title: [RFC]: R3 support for prefill/decode disaggregation
author: ShuoleiWang
body:
### Motivation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with mixture-of-experts (MoE) models need a record of which experts actually ran for each token. Training can replay those routing choices. vLLM already captures and returns these R3 records. It can also reuse them with a local prefix cache.

Prefill/decode disaggregation adds a missing step. Prefill (P) and decode (D) run in separate instances. D loads key/value (KV) cache data from P and does not run every prompt token again. D therefore cannot produce all prompt routes from its own capture alone.

This RFC proposes native NIXL transfer of R3 records from P to D. It would build on the R3 storage code that the project accepts from [PR #45635](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45635), or a successor. Workers would transfer the route data directly and keep it alive together with the matching KV. The proxy would not carry or merge route arrays. This is a PD extension of the work discussed in [RFC #45221](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45221), not a second R3 store or a new design for a general Artifact Connector.

The key rule is that routes must match the KV that D actually uses, not just the same prompt text. Consider a 48-token prompt. D already has KV for the first 32 tokens and recomputes the last prompt token:

| Token range, start inclusive and end exclusive | KV source | Required R3 source |
|---|---|---|
| `[0, 32)` | D's existing local cache | The old routes that match this cached KV |
| `[32, 47)` | KV loaded from P for this request | P's routes that match the loaded KV |
| `[47, 48)` | Computed by D for this request | D's new capture |

Replacing all prefix routes with P's current trace would not preserve this link. The same prefix hash does not prove that two executions chose exactly the same routes. Block reuse, async output, partial blocks, and transfer failures also affect when records are valid and when their memory can be freed.

As of September 6, 2026, PR #45635 at `df09778c1f` replaces the old scheduler-side slot store with records that workers own and look up by block key. It still rejects R3 when a KV connector is enabled. This RFC would extend that storage design for PD instead of bringing back the old slot manager. See the [R3 worker code](https://github.com/xhx1022/vllm/blob/df09778c1f5ad65706fccf5bc9c0c82d2b650736/vllm/distributed/artifact_connector/worker.py#L65) and its [current configuration checks](https://github.com/xhx1022/vllm/blob/df09778c1f5ad65706fccf5bc9c0c82d2b650736/vllm/config/vllm.py#L1012).

Related work:

- [PR #39289](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/39289) addresses the same R3+PD use case. It carries route arrays in `kv_transfer_params` and merges them on D. This proposal instead uses NIXL for the route data and selects records based on the KV source.
- [PR #45419](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45419) relaxes the configuration check and relies on proxy-side merging. It has companion work in [vLLM Router #184](https://github.com/vllm-project/router/pull/184) and [llm-d Router #1627](https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-router/pull/1627). This proposal keeps the proxy's normal PD handoff role. The engine and connector would check that the KV and routes match and are complete.
- [PR #52902](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52902) reorganizes the R3 capture/replay tests. PD tests would extend that test setup and stay aligned with output-range work such as [PR #37094](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/37094).

This RFC asks for agreement on the native NIXL path and how it should fit with these efforts. It does not assume that it replaces an existing PR. The implementation would use the storage interfaces accepted by the project. Before that storage work merges, this RFC can define the smallest additions needed for PD.


### Proposed Change.


### 1. Goals and initial scope

The proposed first version would:

1. Transfer P's routes for the external KV that D actually reuses. Combine them with D's cached routes and new local capture to form the complete result.
2. Keep prefix caching, chunked prefill, CUDA graphs, and async output enabled. Correctness must not depend on turning these features off.
3. Require both KV and matching R3 to be ready before completing a load or exposing a cache hit. Keep transfer memory alive until no transfer can still access it.
4. Be disabled by default. When disabled, preserve the base version's NIXL compatibility checks, R3 output rules, and other serving behavior.

The first version would support:

- Model Runner V2, text-only MoE models, non-streaming completions, and `n=1`.
- One data-parallel replica per side (`DP=1`).
- Matching tensor-parallel (`TP`) layouts on P and D, plus compatible expert-parallel (`EP`) layouts that pass their own tests.
- Dedicated producer and consumer roles, NIXL pull, one full-attention KV cache group, and matching logical-block layouts, hash-block layouts, and R3 data formats.

The first version would not support MTP/speculative decoding, DBO/microbatching, LoRA, multimodal inputs, resumable requests, different TP layouts on P and D, multiple DP output workers, pipeline parallelism (PP), decode/prefill context parallelism (DCP/PCP), reverse transfer, or CPU KV offload. Passing tests with another EP backend does not prove DeepEP support. Unsupported combinations would be rejected at startup or during request preprocessing. These new limits apply only when this extension is enabled.

Weights would remain fixed while requests or transfers are active. To change weights, the deployment must first finish or safely stop those requests and transfers, then bring both sides to a consistent state. This RFC does not implement replay in the trainer or guarantee bit-exact training/inference logprobs.

### 2. Configuration and API behavior

Both sides would keep using `--enable-return-routed-experts`. They would also set the proposed `enable_routed_experts_transfer` field in `KVTransferConfig` to `true`. This new field would default to `false`. The P configuration would be:

```json
{
  "kv_connector": "NixlConnector",
  "kv_role": "kv_producer",
  "enable_routed_experts_transfer": true,
  "kv_load_failure_policy": "fail"
}
```

D would use `kv_consumer` with the same R3 transfer settings. The handshake would include an optional R3 transfer capability and data-format version. A transfer must fail if only one side enables the feature, or if versions or layouts do not match. It must not fall back to a warning or return an incomplete trace. With the extension disabled, the existing compatibility factors stay unchanged. This does not bypass vLLM's version checks or add a guarantee for mixed-version deployments.

The public R3 response format and token-range rules would stay the same. Normal requests to P would still return R3 as before. P requests used only for an internal PD handoff would not serialize a second copy of the full route array. D would return the complete route result. The last sampled token has no route row until it has run through a forward pass.

The proxy would keep forwarding the normal PD handoff. At most, it would pass along a small export ID. Workers would exchange the full route data, per-block transfer metadata, and memory descriptors directly. These would not travel as JSON arrays in `kv_transfer_params`.

### 3. Storage ownership and public interfaces

The base R3 code would still capture routes, store completed blocks, and build R3 output. It would also keep each request's unfinished block and decide when cached records can be removed. The unfinished part of a hash block is called a tail. Published records are immutable: their contents cannot be changed in place. NIXL would manage transfer snapshots, memory registration, transfer handles, and notifications.

The new PD control path would send small readiness and completion messages to the Scheduler through public interfaces. It would not add a second source-of-truth route cache or route-data transfer code to the Scheduler. It would not access the store's private memory or eviction tables, or NIXL's private handles. The base R3 output path through EngineCore and the API server would stay unchanged.

The first version would use CPU transfer snapshots with a fixed memory budget. It would copy the matching records from the R3 store into a stable export buffer. D would receive them into a separate staging buffer, validate them, and then commit them through the store's public API. Each snapshot belongs to one transfer. It is not used for prefix lookup and is not a second R3 cache. The first version would not borrow raw addresses from the store's private memory buffer or claim end-to-end zero-copy transfer.

A transfer lease keeps its data alive while a transfer may still access it. A manifest is the metadata that describes the transfer's source, format, and valid rows. The R3 worker layer would provide these public operations. Final method names can follow the accepted storage API, but the ownership and completion rules are part of this proposal:

| Operation | Input and result | Required behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Reserve a usable cached prefix | Candidate KV range and its R3 references → usable prefix and reservation | Check that the records exist and match the KV. Keep them alive so they cannot be evicted before use. |
| Prepare an export | Request, KV/R3 links, and token range → export lease and manifest | Include the needed full blocks and tails. Allow remote reads only after the snapshot is ready. |
| Prepare a receive | Manifest and target request → private staging buffer | Check size, format, ranges, and request identity. Reserve budget before allocating memory. |
| Commit received rows | Completed and validated staging data → local R3 references or tails | Commit through the store's API. Do not write private slots or change an existing immutable record. |
| Release export or receive data | Lease or staging reservation | Free it only after NIXL confirms that no transfer can still access the memory. |

With matching TP layouts, each rank would transfer its KV shards through the existing NIXL path. R3 uses logical token positions, layer IDs, and expert IDs. Only the output rank that holds the full route record would export it; other TP ranks would not send duplicate copies. Completion must cover all required KV ranks, not just the output rank.

### 4. Link KV to the exact route record

Each KV cache range used by an R3 request would carry a reference to its matching route record. The R3 store owns this reference. Callers pass it back to the store rather than build it themselves. A prefix hash finds a possible cache hit; the record reference identifies the routes that belong to that specific KV. NIXL must not select an arbitrary stored record based only on the prefix hash.

If KV moves to a new address without being recomputed, this link stays the same. If a new forward pass produces new KV, it must link to the matching new route record. An old record with the same prefix hash is not an automatic substitute. The R3 storage code would create and resolve record references and any needed version information. PD would not maintain a separate key-generation scheme.

The export manifest would bind:

- The source instance identity, a unique `transfer_id`, and the source cache epoch for this export.
- The deployed model/weight identity and R3 format: layer count, experts per token (top-k), expert-ID encoding, and numeric type (dtype).
- The matching KV/R3 record references, valid token ranges, and byte counts.
- The request and transfer identity that the receiver can check.

The deployment configuration or a coordinator supplies the model/weight identity. A local cache generation counter is not a weight version. The handshake checks that both sides declare compatible identities; it does not prove that checkpoint files contain the claimed weights. Instance identity after a restart, local cache epoch, and shared weight identity must remain separate. Equal generation counters do not prove equal weights. Different counters do not by themselves prove a mismatch.

A completion event must match the active request, `transfer_id`, and receive generation. An old notification cannot complete a new request. Data from an old epoch cannot be committed as valid data for a new epoch.

### 5. Normal transfer flow

1. **P keeps the records alive.** Before its handoff request ends, P retains the needed R3 records and tails for export. Request cleanup must not free them before the snapshot is ready.
2. **P prepares the export.** Once the async readout and snapshot are complete, NIXL gets stable export descriptors. A background `put()` that is only queued is not enough.
3. **D finds its usable prefix.** D reserves the longest local prefix with both valid KV and matching R3. It handles the rest as a normal cache miss: fetch both from P or recompute both.
4. **D receives the external range.** KV and R3 transfers may make progress separately. Until they are ready, other requests and prefix lookups cannot see the receive buffers.
5. **D resumes execution.** D leaves the load-wait state only after the external KV it will reuse and the matching R3 rows have arrived and passed validation. This does not wait for routes of tokens that D has not run yet.
6. **D commits the final records.** D runs the remaining tokens. It combines cached routes, received routes, and new capture based on their actual sources, then completes the final block and output through the R3 storage API.
7. **P releases the export lease.** Once all required KV/R3 reads have ended, NIXL notifies P to release its export snapshot. P does not wait for D to finish the whole generation. D manages its own staging and cache references through the local lifecycle.

If D needs no external range, it issues no R3 READ. It uses the existing notify-only path to release P's lease. Checking a cached prefix and retaining its records must form one reservation operation. There must be no gap where a record passes the check and is then evicted before use.

The first version would resume D only when both the reused external KV and its matching routes are ready. This keeps the normal output path from having to handle executed KV whose required routes are still in flight. Running D as soon as KV arrives while delaying route output is a possible later optimization, not part of this first version.

### 6. Tails and the final block

P's partial block would be copied into an immutable transfer snapshot with an explicit valid token range. Its export lease would keep it alive after the normal request tail is released. Transfers may use whole blocks, but D must use only the rows declared valid in the manifest.

If D recomputes the last prompt token, it must not use P's route row for that token in the final record. D first waits for the external range it will reuse, then runs its local tokens. The final immutable block, including D's new rows, is published after that forward pass. D must not publish P's full final block and modify it in place later. It must also not wait for its own new routes before allowing the forward pass that creates them.

### 7. Failures, cancellation, and limits

**Missing records before scheduling:** If KV has a cache hit but its R3 is missing, not ready, or from the wrong source, treat that range as a cache miss for this R3 request. Shorten the usable local prefix and fetch or recompute both KV and R3 for the missing range. The first version would not refill R3 alone, attach P's current routes to D's old KV, or disable prefix caching globally.

**Errors after a transfer starts:** Follow `kv_load_failure_policy="fail"`. End the affected request with an error. Do not retry without a bound or return a partly valid R3 result. If any required KV or R3 transfer fails, cancel or drain the others. Free receive buffers and source leases only after confirming that DMA can no longer access those addresses.

**Timeouts and unconfirmed cancellation:** A timeout does not prove that DMA has stopped. Memory must remain reserved and count against the in-flight budget until NIXL confirms that all access has ended, through completion or safe cancellation. It cannot be given to another request. If the connector cannot recover, use its failure or instance-isolation path rather than reuse memory that may still be accessed.

**Resource limits:** Each output worker would track export and receive snapshots separately from the R3 store. The first version's total snapshot-byte limit would equal that worker's effective R3 store capacity. The number of in-flight transfer windows would be limited to `2 * max_num_seqs`; a window is one tracked export or receive operation. A manifest could not contain more records than the full blocks and tails needed for the request's valid token range. This budget would not reduce or change the store's existing capacity. The deployment must account for snapshot memory as an extra cost. When the budget is full, reject new transfers with a request-level resource error, but keep completing and releasing transfers already in flight. Memory reports must separate the R3 store, snapshots, tail/capture buffers, and descriptors.

**Error handling:** Reject unsupported configurations at startup and invalid requests during preprocessing. Handle recoverable missing-data and transfer errors at request scope. Keep assertions for broken internal invariants. Do not hide code bugs with a broad exception catch. This follows the existing [review on error handling](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45635#discussion_r3908999090).

### 8. CUDA graphs, async scheduling, and pause

Route export would reuse the base R3 implementation's async GPU-to-CPU copy. It must not add CPU/GPU synchronization inside MoE layers or on each decode step. It must keep the device-buffer addresses used by CUDA graphs stable. Snapshot work, memory registration, and network work stay in the worker/connector lifecycle. See the [review on CPU/GPU overlap](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45635#discussion_r3909040668).

The Scheduler would receive public events for KV/R3 readiness and transfer completion. If the engine needs to track work that is only waiting on I/O, the KV connector would expose a small public progress interface. The implementation must not read NIXL's private state or add route-array handling to the Scheduler's main loop. See the [review on these module boundaries](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45635#pullrequestreview-4840148178).

Pause may stop model scheduling, but required transfers, heartbeats, cancellation, and cleanup must keep making progress. Before sleep or a change to registered KV memory, related transfers must finish or be cancelled safely. Waiting for a CUDA stream is not a substitute for draining NIXL DMA. Until these combinations pass validation, the extension must reject unsafe operations. It must not silently free memory or change the existing meaning of pause.

### 9. Implementation order and merge criteria

After the base storage changes merge and their public interfaces are settled, the PD feature would be submitted as one complete PR. It would include the small R3 transfer interface, NIXL support, shared KV/R3 lifecycle rules, and tests. Any new interface would ship with its actual caller, not as an unused general abstraction. Independent base-layer bug fixes can be submitted separately after checking for duplicate work.

The target implementation must pass the checks below before merge. Results from the old slot-based prototype do not count as passing these checks for the new design.

| Area | Required coverage |
|---|---|
| Correct record source | No local hit, partial hit, full hit, repeated requests, and different records with the same hash. Every KV range must use its matching R3. |
| Tails and block boundaries | Prompts that do not fill a block, chunked prefill, P tail lifetime, D recomputing the last prompt token, and delayed publication of the final block. |
| Cache lifetime | KV present but R3 missing, record eviction, block reuse, instance restart, and cache-epoch changes. Known incomplete pairs must not count as usable hits. |
| Transfer failures | Either KV or R3 finishing first, rank failure, abort, timeout, failed cancellation, and P finishing its request first. No early free or completion notification. |
| Common runtime settings | TP1, TP greater than one, the selected EP backends, async scheduling, actual CUDA graph replay, pause/resume, and sleep/wake. |
| Multiple hosts | At least one real two-host NIXL transfer test. A single-host P4/D4 test is not a substitute. |
| Extension disabled | The same base version's existing hashes, metadata, output, and normal serving behavior. No extra R3 transfer allocation or copy. |
| Performance and memory | Matched settings, repeated runs, and long-running tests. Report throughput, latency distributions, CPU use, memory, and cache hits. Separate capture, storage, transfer, and HTTP costs. |

This RFC asks the community to decide:

1. Should R3 PD use native NIXL transfer with these storage boundaries, rather than add more route-merging work to the proxy?
2. Should KV link to specific R3 record references, with bounded CPU snapshots for the first transfer implementation?
3. Is the proposed recovery rule acceptable: treat an incomplete pair as a miss before scheduling, and fail the request if transfer later fails?
4. Is the initial scope acceptable: matching layouts, DP=1, and no MTP/DBO? How should this work fit with #39289 and #45419?


### Feedback Period.

...

### CC List.

...

### Any Other Things.


### Prototype validation

A local prototype was tested on top of `1970f3ed4be7fa8620e4ddc4a12c36a8384cfc27`. It used the old slot-based store, not the new store in #45635. Tests ran on one host with eight H20 GPUs and Qwen3-30B-A3B in BF16. P and D each used TP4. These are local prototype results, not validation of the proposed worker-store design or results from upstream CI. The implementation PR would include code and reproducible test material.

| Test group | Result |
|---|---|
| Route capture, PD scheduler, NIXL, and configuration tests | 74 passed |
| Request preprocessing and error handling | 50 passed |
| R3-off hashes, old/new metadata decoding, and capability isolation | 5 passed |
| Async scheduler regression tests | 17 passed |
| Real P4/D4 requests | 16 correctness requests and 32 performance requests succeeded. Output tokens in the correctness run matched the no-R3 baseline. |
| Request failure isolation | An invalid P handoff returned HTTP 500 for that request. The service stayed healthy and later valid requests succeeded. |
| Prefix source test | Different P/D tags were used to warm, extend, and repeat a prefix. D's old cached routes were not replaced by P's current routes. |

This totals 146 unit and regression tests, plus real-model and separate tagged end-to-end tests. The tags test transfer and cache ownership. They do not prove that the model's actual top-k choices match those used by the trainer. Matching output tokens does not imply bit-exact logprobs. Prefix caching and normal CUDA graph settings stayed enabled; the tests did not use `--enforce-eager` to get a passing result.

### Initial performance data

One matched short test of the old-store prototype used 8,192 input tokens, 128 output tokens, concurrency 1 or 4, and cold or warm caches. Each case had eight requests, with warmup before timing. The numbers below are end-to-end output tokens per second and include transfer of the full HTTP response.

| Case | Baseline, R3 off | Prototype, R3 off | Prototype, R3 on |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Concurrency 1, cold cache | 178.00 | 178.95 | 158.72 |
| Concurrency 1, warm cache | 231.65 | 233.57 | 205.72 |
| Concurrency 4, cold cache | 468.15 | 475.34 | 437.65 |
| Concurrency 4, warm cache | 718.00 | 718.97 | 559.29 |

This short test showed no clear throughput loss with R3 off. Enabling the full R3 path reduced throughput by about 6.5%–22.1% relative to the baseline. That cost includes capture, readout, storage, transfer, and HTTP output. It cannot all be attributed to PD. Eight requests per case are not enough to establish serving capacity or p99 latency.

For this model, the prototype's wire format uses 48 layers × top-8 × 1 byte, or 384 bytes per token. The total NIXL counters showed 89,210,880 extra bytes for 232,320 externally loaded tokens. This exactly matches the route-data size and is 0.390625% of the original KV transfer bytes. This is a byte-count check, not a latency ratio. The proposed design's snapshot and store-commit costs must be measured again.

The base code does not support R3+PD without an extension. Future reports would therefore distinguish the base without R3, the base with R3, and the R3+PD extension. They must explain where a fully matched baseline is not available. Single-host results would not be presented as proof of multi-host network behavior.

### Known limits and coordination

The prototype still has an inherited DBO/microbatch route-overwrite issue. It has not completed validation of in-flight transfers with pause/sleep/wake, cross-host operation, or the full fault-injection test plan. The scope and merge criteria above reflect these gaps. These are not claimed as solved features.

This proposal does not ask to merge the prototype's scheduler-owned shared array or count its tests as tests of #45635. The implementation would use the accepted storage interfaces and coordinate ownership with the existing PD/R3 contributors. Reused code, design work, and tests would be credited, with their sources identified.


### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: RFC: per-M, per-shape kernel dispatch for blockwise-FP8 linear layers (W8A16 at decode, FP8xFP8 at prefill)
author: Zeuss5
body:
> **Scope caveat.** All measurements below come from a **single machine**: 4× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (GB202, sm_120), PCIe peer-to-peer, **no NVLink**, driver 580.126.09, CUDA 13.0, vLLM `0.28.1rc1.dev500+g51da0ca66`, model Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 at TP=4. The *enablement* work is general; the *conclusions about where a change pays* are specific to a latency-bound interconnect and should be re-measured on NVLink before being trusted there. Numbers were produced by a harness that enforces CUDA-graph-captured timing, two working-set regimes (this GPU has 134 MB of L2), clearing both the vLLM and torch-inductor caches between A/B configs, node-level trace assertions for any wiring claim, and an output-equivalence gate.

**Status: draft, not filed.** Measured on 4× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (GB202, sm120, PCIe).

## The claim

At decode batch sizes a blockwise-FP8 GEMM is **pure weight streaming**: it reads N×K weight
bytes regardless of how many tokens it serves, and the activation traffic (T×K) is two orders
of magnitude smaller. MMA throughput is therefore irrelevant there, so quantising activations
to FP8 buys nothing and costs a launch plus ~7× the numerical error. At prefill sizes the
tensor cores do bind and FP8×FP8 is the right kernel.

So the choice is a **regime** choice, and the regime boundary is per shape.

## Evidence

DRAM-resident (≥3× L2 rotating working set — the model's actual condition, since each weight
is touched once per step against ~6.75 GB/rank). Ratio is W8A16 ÷ (FP8×FP8 + activation quant):

| shape (per rank, TP=4) | T=1 | T=4 | T=32 | T=64 | T=128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `in_proj_z` 1536×5120 | **1.21×** | **1.22×** | 1.05× | 0.73× | 1.21× |
| `in_proj_qkv` 2560×5120 | 1.12× | 1.13× | 1.01× | 0.78× | 1.07× |
| `linear_attn.out_proj` 5120×1536 | 1.08× | 1.09× | 1.00× | 0.83× | 0.66× |
| `gate_up` 8704×5120 | 1.04× | 1.05× | 1.02× | 0.94× | 0.67× |
| `down_proj` 5120×4352 | 1.04× | 1.04× | 0.98× | 0.85× | 0.74× |
| **T=256 / T=1024** (down_proj) | — | — | — | — | 0.58× / **0.54×** |

Accuracy is the unambiguous part: **2.3e-03…4.5e-03 vs 2.3e-02…3.4e-02** against an fp32
reference, ~7× better, because activations never leave bf16.

End-to-end, decode isolated, equivalence PASS at every point:

| batch | FP8×FP8 | W8A16 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 112.0 | **117.9** | **+5.3%** |
| 8 | 654.0 | **700.6** | **+7.1%** |
| 32 | 1983.5 | 2014.3 | +1.6% (noise) |
| 128 | 4144.3 | 3878.3 | **−6.4%** |

And W8A16 removes the activation-quant stage outright: **234 standalone quant kernel launches
per step → 0** (`per_token_group_quant_8bit` 127.4/step, `silu_and_mul_per_block_quant` 42.5,
three others), confirmed by node-level trace assertion.

## What this asks for

`linear_backend` is currently selected once, globally. The proposal is to let a layer hold both
prepared weights and pick per call by M, with the threshold **per shape** rather than one
global constant — `down_proj` turns over by T=32 while `in_proj_z` is still winning 1.05×
there.

The honest cost: no FP8-weight kernel in vLLM streams with bf16 activations from the CUTLASS
layout. Marlin needs `gptq_marlin_repack`; Machete needs `machete_prepack_B`; `torch._scaled_mm`
rejects bf16×fp8 outright. So per-M dispatch means **both formats resident**, and since the
Marlin repack is int32 and the same size as the fp8 original, that is **≈ +6.75 GB/rank** at
TP=4 for this model — real KV-cache budget. A kernel that streams FP8 weights against bf16
activations *without* a repack would remove that cost entirely and is the more valuable change.

## GB202 note

Two things specific to this part that are worth recording for anyone tuning sm120:

1. **The N tile is pinned by the quantisation block size.** CUTLASS asserts
   `Scale Granularity M must evenly divide the tile shape M`, and in the sm120 `swap_ab` decode
   path the tile's M dimension *is* the original N, with `ScaleGranularityM = 128` because the
   weight's block scales are 128 wide. So `ceil(N/128)` CTAs is implied by
   `weight_block_size=[128,128]`, not chosen — a 64-wide N tile will not compile. Adding CTAs
   via a stream-K/split-K scheduler instead measures **0.80–0.93×** the default scheduler at
   DRAM-resident working sets.

2. **Measurement traps that produce wrong tuning decisions on this SKU.** L2 is 134 MB, so a
   benchmark looping over one 22–45 MB weight is L2-fed and can read *above* the 1792 GB/s DRAM
   peak — that regime reports W8A16 at 1.81× where the DRAM-resident number is 1.04×. And
   per-call timing charges CPU dispatch to the kernel (23.94 µs vs 14.45 µs back-to-back for
   the same GEMM), which also makes two GEMMs on two streams look like they serialise when
   under CUDA graphs they overlap. Byte-weighted, these GEMMs run at 1000 GB/s in microbench
   and 1125 GB/s in-model — 56% and 63% of peak — so the remaining headroom is ~1.6×, not the
   2–3× the narrow shapes alone suggest.

---

### Corrections history

This work published several wrong numbers before the harness caught them. They are listed
because they change how the remaining numbers should be read, and because two of them are
traps specific to this GPU that anyone repeating the measurements will hit.

| claim | corrected to | cause |
|---|---|---|
| W8A16 is 1.81× at T=1 | **1.04–1.22×** DRAM-resident | 1.81× was L2-fed; this GPU has 134 MB of L2, so a loop over one 22–45 MB weight reads above the 1792 GB/s DRAM peak |
| GEMM launches serialise, so split-K is dead | GEMMs **overlap** under CUDA graphs | per-call timing charges CPU dispatch to the kernel (23.94 µs vs 14.45 back-to-back) |
| micro-batching costs +18–28 µs/GEMM | **+1.2–3.9 µs** | measured eager, and never measured the shared-weight L2 case that the second micro-batch actually sees |
| 381 standalone quant launches/step | **234** | trace window included prefill |
| GEMMs run at 27–48% of roofline | **56–63%** byte-weighted | the 27–48% shapes carry 18% of the bytes |
| the 256 KB two-shot threshold is too high | it is **2.5× too low** (crossover 640 KB) | fitted `comm(T) = F + B·T` rather than assumed |
| stream priority gives ~0 protection | **1.83×** with a real prefill background | the original probe used a wall-clock spin kernel, which measures queuing, not contention |

Two further results are negative and worth stating so others do not repeat them: collapsing the
second barrier of a two-shot into per-peer flag waits changes F by 0.7% (the cost is PCIe flag
propagation, not wait-for-slowest), and a grid-wide doorbell that cuts F by 30% in isolation
measures **−24.7% end-to-end**, because a grid-wide flag is a full grid barrier and waits for
the slowest-*scheduled* block once other work is resident.

title: [RFC]: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash performance on ROCm
author: Fangzhou-Ai
body:
## Motivation

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash leaves a lot of the device on the table on AMD MI355X (gfx950). Measured on an 8x MI355X node, TP4, MXFP4 MoE + DSpark MTP:

| concurrency | out tok/s | out tok/s per GPU | TTFT p50 | ITL p50 | E2EL p50 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 35.89 | 8.97 | 0.898 | 0.0256 | 15.03 |
| 2 | 49.10 | 12.27 | 0.940 | 0.0267 | 17.22 |
| 4 | 86.99 | 21.75 | 0.634 | 0.0271 | 5.55 |
| 8 | 164.69 | 41.17 | 0.609 | 0.0307 | 12.10 |
| 16 | 292.60 | 73.15 | 0.684 | 0.0332 | 14.61 |
| 32 | 469.41 | 117.35 | 0.825 | 0.0477 | 17.57 |

The shape of that table is the telling part. Going from concurrency 1 to 32 costs only **1.9x** in ITL (0.0256 -> 0.0477) while delivering **13x** more output per GPU, so the device is nowhere near saturated: there is a large fixed cost per decode step that concurrency merely amortises. A captured decode trace says what that cost is. At a single-stream ITL of 25.6 ms, a decode step issues **14,020 kernel launches**, and 85% of each layer's 350 launches are attributable to the mHC block - bookkeeping on a 4x4 matrix.

| launches/layer | share | source |
|---:|---:|---|
| 162 | 48.6% | mHC sinkhorn loop |
| 122 | 36.6% | mHC pre/post mix + eager RMSNorm |
| 24 | 7.2% | MoE / FFN (already fused) |
| 12 | 3.6% | dtype casts/copies |
| 6 | 1.8% | attention + fused norm/quant |
| 4 | 1.2% | TP collective |
| 3 | 0.9% | other |

> **Trace methodology, since it affects what the numbers can support.** The trace had to be captured with `--enforce-eager`: with CUDA graphs on, roctracer's HSA queue interposition deadlocks against hipGraph replay on this ROCm build (the first step after `/start_profile` never completes and the workers spin in `queue_interposition.cpp` waiting on an HSA signal). So **only the launch counts and kernel composition should be read as load-bearing** - those are graph-invariant, since a graph replays the kernel sequence it captured rather than merging kernels. All wall-clock, occupancy and idle-gap figures from that trace are inflated by eager dispatch plus profiler overhead and are deliberately not used for any claim here. The throughput and ITL numbers above are from normal graph-enabled serving runs, not from the traced run.

This is purely a performance question - accuracy is already where it should be. Recording it here as the standard for the work below, since every item in this RFC is a performance change that has to hold accuracy. gsm8k 5-shot via lm-eval, same node and configuration:

| | strict-match | flexible-extract |
|---|---:|---:|
| baseline | 0.9704 ± 0.0047 | 0.9697 ± 0.0047 |
| with #56503 | 0.9727 ± 0.0045 | 0.9719 ± 0.0045 |
| with #56503 + #56513 | 0.9735 ± 0.0044 | 0.9727 ± 0.0045 |

Harness gate is 0.91. Anything landing against this RFC should be checked against the numbers above rather than just the gate, since a change can pass 0.91 while still having broken something.

What follows is grouped by optimization direction. Each item is verified against the code rather than assumed, and several turn out to be different from what they look like from the outside.

---

## 1. mHC seam fusion

The largest single direction, since 85% of per-layer launches live here.

### 1.1 mHC pre -> AITER

`vllm/models/deepseek_v4_1/amd/model.py` imports `mhc_pre_delayed_torch` / `mhc_post_torch` directly, so every sublayer seam spends ~141 launches Sinkhorn-normalizing a 4x4 matrix. V4 already dispatches through `MHCPreOp` / `MHCPostOp` and reaches AITER; V4.1 was never migrated, because it collapses each sublayer's input with the *previous* sublayer's pre-mix and AITER's `mhc_pre` neither returns its pre-mix nor accepts an incoming one.

Merged as #56503: 141 -> 4 launches per seam, worst relative error 1.2e-5, gsm8k unchanged.

At concurrency 1 that moved ITL p50 from 25.58 ms to 6.89 ms. Read that as directional only, not as a 3.7x per-token speedup: the agentic trace is time-driven, so the faster run sampled a different and longer segment (mean input 168,856 -> 206,458 tokens, mean output 954 -> 1,683). The confound runs against the result, but a clean figure needs a fixed-request-count replay. Details in the PR.

### 1.2 Fused mHC post+pre for V4.1

`deepseek_v4/amd/model.py` has 4 references to `MHCFusedPostPreOp` / `mhc_fused_post_pre`; `deepseek_v4_1/amd/model.py` has **zero**. `mhc_fused_post_pre_gemm_sqrsum` applies the post step and projects the resulting residual in one kernel, and has gfx950-specific tuning (`_mhc_fused_config_gfx950_256`). It needs the same `pre_mix` plumbing #56503 added, so it is a direct follow-on rather than separate work.

Sizing this honestly: because the delayed formulation still needs the pre-mix epilogue and the delayed collapse, folding in the post takes the seam from 6 launches to 5, not to 2. Measured on gfx950, all-reduce excluded: 5 -> 4.

Above 1024 tokens AITER's own heuristic prefers separate kernels, so this is a decode-path win by construction. The name misleads here: `mhc_fused_post_pre_large_m` is *not* a fused kernel, it is plain `mhc_post` + `mhc_pre` with a non-temporal store hint (`store_nt=0` above `8 * num_cu`) and `large_m_splitk=True`, neither of which the fused kernel can express. Once the residual stops fitting in cache there is nothing left for fusion to save.

Addressed by #56513 (draft). Measured at 1.28% lower mean ITL at concurrency 1, 95% CI [0.07%, 2.48%], as a two-way crossover over both halves of the node with a fixed 24-request replay -- the two GPU sets here differ by 0.96%, so a single-orientation A/B cannot resolve an effect this size. One loose end that change does not close: its fallback is the plain post plus delayed pre, so it asks for neither large-m tuning. Inert between 1024 and 2048 tokens, but a real miss at prefill, which reaches 16384 tokens here. Needs a `store_nt` argument on the shared `mhc_post` wrapper that V4 also uses.

Note `_AITER_MHC_FUSED_RMSNORM_SIZES = {1280, 2560, 4096, 7168}` excludes V4.1-Flash's `hidden_size=5120`, so the fused-RMSNorm variant does not apply here; extending that set, or the kernel's supported sizes, is a separate question.

**Parallel ROCm work on the same seam.** #56342 reaches 1.1/1.2 by a different route: instead of dispatching the AMD path through AITER, it fixes the TileLang `mhc_pre_big_fuse*` kernels on 64-wide wavefronts and moves V4.1's AMD path onto the fused TileLang kernels. Its own measurement is that the switch without the wavefront fix is a 91.1% -> 23.7% gsm8k regression, so both halves land together. That makes it and #56503/#56513 two answers to the same question -- which backend owns the V4.1 AMD mHC seam -- and they should be reconciled before either goes further.

### 1.3 Fused all-reduce + mHC post

Worth being explicit about why this, and not all-reduce + RMSNorm, which is the more obvious proposal. Three reasons, in increasing order of decisiveness:

1. **The ROCm AR+RMSNorm pass exists and auto-enables.** `RocmAiterAllReduceFusionPass` is selected when `fuse_allreduce_rms` is set and AITER is enabled (`vllm/compilation/passes/pass_manager.py:176-180`), and `enable_allreduce_rms_fusion` returns true on ROCm for TP>1 (`vllm/config/vllm.py:171-185`). Our server duly logs `Enabled custom fusions: ..., allreduce_rms, ...`.
2. **But it is an Inductor FX pattern matcher, and this model is invisible to it.** There is no `@support_torch_compile` anywhere under `vllm/models/deepseek_v4_1/` (verified: zero matches), so the pass never sees the model graph. "Enabled" in that log is misleading.
3. **And the pattern is not in the model anyway.** V4.1's decoder has no `all_reduce -> RMSNorm` seam. The TP all-reduce lives inside `_o_proj` / `_bpre_attn_gemm(..., reduce_tp=True)`, and what follows it is the **mHC post block**. Contrast `deepseek_v32/amd/model.py`, which does call `fused_allreduce_rms_norm` explicitly.

The fusion that does apply is already written and unused: `aiter/ops/custom_all_reduce.py` defines `fused_allreduce_mhc_post_only`, `_one_stage` and `_split` plus `launch_*` wrappers, backed by the prebuilt `aiter/jit/module_fused_ar_mhc.so`. vLLM has **zero** references to any of them. At 4 collective launches per layer, wiring this removes both the collective and the post kernel from each seam.

Proposal: add `rocm_aiter_ops.fused_allreduce_mhc_post` and call it from the V4.1 AMD seam. Separately, `docs/design/fusions.md:101-107` still documents AR+RMSNorm as NVIDIA Hopper/Blackwell + FlashInfer only and should be corrected now that the AITER path exists.

**Correction: 1.2 and 1.3 are alternatives, not additive.** Both consume the same post step -- 1.2 folds it forward into the pre projection, 1.3 folds it backward into the collective -- so whichever lands, the other has nothing left to fuse. Each is worth one launch out of six.
