`benchmarks/kernels/benchmark_*.py` script by hand and drop the result into `VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER`.  Furthermore, users need to maintain many config files for various architectures (including new ones) and would instead like an easy out of the box solution that just picks the right configurations for **all** the kernels being used in the serving model.

FlashInfer already solves the analogous problem with `--kernel-config.enable_flashinfer_autotune`, which tunes at kernel warmup for the model actually being served. There is no equivalent for Triton. This RFC proposes one.

### Proposed Change.

Add an opt-in flag, `--kernel-config.enable_triton_autotune` (default `False`), modeled on `enable_flashinfer_autotune`. When enabled, during kernel warmup — after the model is loaded and the KV cache is allocated, but **before** CUDA graph capture — vLLM tunes every Triton config-table kernel that the served model will actually use **but that has no config yet**, and persists the result to a local cache that later startups reuse without re-tuning. Scope is intentionally limited to category (2) above (kernels that read a JSON config table).

A "family" is one config table / lookup function, not one kernel. Each table implements a small interface:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TuningItem:
    table: str        # which table this belongs to
    shape: Hashable   # e.g. (headdim, dstate, dtype, nheads, ...)
    bucket: int       # the varying dimension, e.g. effective batch size

class TunableConfigTable(ABC):
    name: ClassVar[str]

    @abstractmethod
    def pending_items(self, worker) -> list[TuningItem]:
        """Items the served model will look up that have no config yet."""

    @abstractmethod
    def tune(self, item: TuningItem) -> dict | None:
        """Benchmark one item on scratch buffers; None if nothing valid."""

    @abstractmethod
    def commit(self, results: dict[TuningItem, dict]) -> None:
        """Persist results and clear the table's lookup caches. Runs on all ranks."""
```

Every rank must reach every collective and every rank must end up with identical configs (so captured CUDA graphs match across TP/PP ranks). The loop:

1. Each rank computes its own `pending_items` (shapes are per-rank, e.g. after TP sharding, but contain nothing rank-specific like a device index).
2. `all_gather_object` the union of pending items.
3. Deterministically sort the union and shard it `items[rank::world_size]` so each item is tuned exactly once.
4. Each rank tunes its slice; failures are caught so they never skip a collective.
5. `all_gather_object` the results; **every** rank calls `commit`, so all ranks write the same files and clear the same caches.

This runs from `kernel_warmup()` right after the `process_local_only` early return, so it always executes on the normal startup path on every rank and before `capture_model`.

### Persistence

- Results are stored under `VLLM_TRITON_AUTOTUNE_CACHE_DIR` (default `$VLLM_CACHE_ROOT/triton_autotune/triton=<version>/<table>/`), reusing each table's existing on-disk JSON schema (keyed by `shape/device/dtype`) so the same files are also usable via `VLLM_TUNED_CONFIG_FOLDER`.
- The config loader gains one extra lookup path (user folder → autotune cache → bundled default), so a second startup finds the tuned file and skips tuning.
- `VLLM_TRITON_AUTOTUNE_FORCE=1` re-tunes even when a config already exists.
- Curated bundled configs are respected by default; tuning only fills gaps.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@hongxiayang @vanshbhatia-amd @tdoublep 

### Any Other Things.

### AI assistance
This RFC was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed and revised by the author, who is responsible for the design.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Software-dequant fp8 KV cache for MLA on Ampere (sm80/sm86) — consolidate the existing pieces, a 1M-ctx field case, and a validation offer
author: ming616
body:
**Software-dequant fp8 KV cache for MLA on Ampere (sm80/sm86): the pieces exist, here is a consolidated path, a concrete field case, and a standing validation offer**

Three threads on this have stalled independently. This issue asks for a maintainer decision on a merge path and volunteers a production validation site.

**Problem**
MLA models (DeepSeek V4.x, Kimi-K3, GLM-5.3) on Ampere are bf16-KV-only today:

- `TritonMLAImpl` raises for any `--kv-cache-dtype fp8*` below SM89 ("native FP8 (fp8e4nv) requires SM89+") — even though the `fp8_ds_mla` layout is *storage-only*: queries stay bf16 and pages are dequantized on load, so no native fp8 arithmetic is required;
- `TRITON_MLA_SPARSE` lists only auto/fp16/bf16 (`triton_mla_sparse.py`);
- the fp8-capable sparse kernels (FlashMLA-sparse, FlashInfer-MLA-sparse) are sm90+ only.

Cost: **1152 B/token/layer instead of 656 B** (the fp8_ds_mla layout) — 1.76× KV capacity left on the table for every Ampere MLA deployment.

**The pieces already exist (all open, none merged)**
- #47629 — TRITON_MLA_SPARSE for sm80 (stated prerequisite in #48374's discussion)
- #48374 — sparse-path fp8 KV RFC; author verified end-to-end on sm_86, including an engine-level boot on a GLM MoE-DSA model (teacher-forced cosine 0.999996 vs bf16, 1.76× pool) and describes the implementation as working
- #52202 — dense TritonMLA decode RFC (~220-line software-dequant kernel sketch, storage-only fp8_ds_mla)
- #55173 — portable Triton fp8e4nv conversions (SM75 bitcode), A100-validated
- #55184 / #55177 — DSV4 pre-sm90 software-fp8 sparse-MLA omnibus, A100-validated (currently conflicted/unreviewed)

**Field case (why this matters beyond 24 GB cards)**
We run GLM-5.3-Flash (hybrid KDA + sparse-MLA indexer, AWQ W4A16) in production on 4× A800 (sm80) at max-model-len 1M — stock vLLM cannot serve this model on sm80 (no sparse-MLA backend), so a fork is required (wtdcode/vllm-backport v0.13.1). Baseline, verified this week on the bf16 path: 930K-context needle recall 5/5, decode 70 tok/s at 930K context, KV/token 11.6 KiB.

- KV budget 24.7 GiB/card → 2.25M tokens → max **2** concurrent full-length 1M requests (2.15×);
- with fp8 KV the same budget yields **~3.7×**, and 4× full-length becomes reachable within the existing headroom.

Ampere A800 remains the most widely deployed 80 GB datacenter GPU in China (per #57144); "more concurrent full-length contexts" is a measurable, recurring demand there.

**Proposed path (please advise or pick)**
1. Land #55173 (portable conversions) as the shared foundation.
2. Once #47629 lands, accept the sparse-path fp8 KV as a PR based on #48374's verified work.
3. For dense TritonMLA, evaluate #52202's sketch. Everything gated behind explicit `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3`/`fp8_ds_mla`; bf16 stays default; warmup/autotune must key on the cache dtype (the dtype-blind autotune behavior is documented in #48374).

**Standing offer**
We can validate candidate branches on our A800 sm80 fleet with a production-shape harness: teacher-forced parity vs bf16, needle-recall at 930K–1M contexts, throughput/concurrency sweeps, and a cross-session state-pollution canary (this hybrid model class is sensitive to cache interactions; our canary keeps the comparison isolated from speculation). We will report numbers publicly either way.

**Questions**
1) Is software-dequant fp8 KV for Ampere acceptable in principle?
2) Preferred sequencing among the pieces above?
3) For the dense TritonMLA decode kernel, is the #52202 sketch the shape you would accept?

title: [RFC]: Fast-Track Merging for Model Optimization PRs
author: benchislett
body:
# [RFC]: Fast-Track Merging for Model Optimization PRs

### Motivation.

Frontier coding models have become extremely proficient at inference model optimization and efficient GPU kernel development. The frequency of new vLLM PRs is rapidly increasing, and is outpacing reviewer bandwidth.
Powered by fully autonomous optimization loops (e.g. "autoresearch"), optimization development can be scaled horizontally across a wide range of models, hardware architectures, and deployment scenarios.

The potential speedups are extremely large, but careful steps must be taken to ensure that vLLM's code quality, usability, and reliability is not sacrificed in the process -- this is why we have a comprehensive review process. Striking a balance between contribution barriers and performance upside is critical.

The fundamental goal of the fast-track is to merge PRs faster, with the same standard of quality. The way to achieve this is by systematically verifying aspects that ordinarily require manual reviewer verification (correctness, performance, no risk of breaking other workloads, etc.). By focusing on a subset of PRs whose changes are strictly contained to an isolated module (namely, the "model forward pass") we can tailor guardrails to decrease reviewer involvement while maintaining a high bar for stability.

### 1. Proposed Change.

I propose a relaxation of the review and merge requirements, limited to cases where changes are contained, comprehensively validated, and provably limited to explicitly validated deployment scenarios.

The remainder of the RFC details the following:
1. Process changes we can make to more efficiently merge "safe" optimization PRs
2. How we can systematically ensure that an eligible PR is "safe to merge"

#### 1.1: One-Touch Merge ("LGTM")

Reviewers often need to revisit PRs multiple times throughout review: one pass to leave comments, another pass to approve and enable CI, additional passes to rerun/retry CI, and possibly a final force-merge request must be made.

For contained model optimizations, much of this can be prevented:
- If no comments are required, a single reviewer action approves the PR and starts an automated procedure to merge: CI runs and executes an automated procedure of rebase and retry until the PR goes in (up to 3 times) or a fallback force-merge is automatically requested. 
- If only trivial edits or conflict resolution are requested, a reviewer may submit a "conditional approval" on the requested changes. After the changes are made the automated merge procedure begins. The "conditional approval" persists through rebase, conflict resolution, acceptance of reviewer-suggested edits, and changes localized to tests/, provided the changes preserve the approved behavior. An amount of trust is delegated to the contributor in the event of a conditional approval.

The CI runs should hopefully not be an obstacle in these cases as changes should be contained to localized files/directories which will mitigate the range of detected test cases.

In cases when a maintainer decides nontrivial changes are needed, the maintainer closes or demotes the PR and the contributor is responsible for updating and re-opening or re-requesting review.

#### 1.2: Primary-Maintainer Merge

One common issue that blocks merge is when the primary maintainer of a feature makes a small PR to update an aspect of that feature which they themselves have the most expertise with. In such cases it can be difficult to find a dedicated second reviewer who can confidently approve the changes.

To resolve this I propose we permit core committers to merge their own PRs, provided they follow the validation and isolation requirements of the fast-track specification below.

#### 1.3: Priority Review

I propose that eligible fast-track PRs be automatically labelled as such, and that maintainer review is prioritized towards fast-track PRs. This will involve slack integration, an automated tracking dashboard, and escalation when fast-track-eligible PRs are "stale" for more than N=7 days.

Because fast-track model optimizations are targeted towards a specific model (or small family of models), there should be a small set of assigned reviewers who can be held more directly responsible for triaging fast-track PRs. This burden will be opt-in, but should not be too heavy as triaging fast-track PRs should be very easy by design.

#### 1.4: PR Template

Similar to the [PR-Checklist](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57084) change which updated the PR template, there will be a dedicated template for fast-track PRs which formalizes the requirements and streamlines review. PR will follow the RFC within a few days.

### 2. Validations and Confidence

#### 2.1: Isolation of Code Changes

The primary risk of merging code tailored to optimize one use-case is impact to other deployments. Performance regressions, breaking other features, or correctness violations are all common side-effects of a seemingly harmless change.

The first pillar of raising confidence in safety is _isolation_: limiting code changes to a specific deployment scenario.

I propose the initial prototype require that fast-track changes be limited to "flat model" subdirectories (e.g. all diff is within a folder such as `vllm/models/deepseek_v41/nvidia`). 

#### 2.2: Bounded Impact on Deployments

Optionally, changes can be further gated programmatically (e.g. a kernel fusion only enabled at small input sizes). The more isolated a change is, the smaller the potential impact. By placing rigid bounds on the changes, we can limit the impact to a very small set of deployment scenarios which can be tested explicitly.

Naturally, limiting the scope in this way also reduces the net improvement per PR: other excluded scenarios might benefit from the changes as well. This may also increase code duplication and redundancy. However, it creates a clear path toward improving stability and scalability as we accelerate the pace of optimizations with coding agents.

[TensorRT-LLM has merged a design](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/pull/19056) which isolates/replicates model code for each model, hardware, and parallelism triple (e.g. gpt-oss TP1 on SM103). This is a fairly extreme flavor of replication, but it highlights an architectural direction we can move towards for if the initial results from vLLM's flat-model design prove sufficiently maintainable.

#### 2.3: Explicit Validation of Affected Deployments

Once an isolated and bounded deployment is established for a contribution, what remains is to run sufficient validations against a representative set of configurations.

Since reviewers are still involved in the process, there is some flexibility in the extent of validation: some changes might warrant testing every parallelism configuration or testing on multiple hardwares, while others might be sufficient with only a single parallelism/HW configuration. If a contribution is not sufficiently validated, reviewers may request additional validation and approve conditionally (see 1.1) or they may demote the PR from the fast-track and/or close it as necessary. Submissions following the fast-track accept a higher evidence standard and a higher risk of reviewers closing low-quality PRs wholesale without discussion.

To codify expectations, I propose the following requirements:

- **E2E Correctness Evaluation:**
  - `GSM8k` and `GPQA-Diamond` be run for all proposed model optimizations
  - A long-context benchmark such as `MRCR v2 256K (8-needle)` and/or a long-generation benchmark such as `AIME25`/`AIME26` (pass@1 avg1) should be included when changes affect sensitive token-mixing operations such as FMHA or SSM.
  - A "hard" correctness benchmark such as `AIME25`/`AIME26` (pass@1 avg4+) or `HLE` or `TerminalBench (any)` should be included when changes include a "high correctness risk factor": low-level CUDA C++ or PTX/SASS or equivalent, or new communications kernels for which race conditions cannot be ruled out by formal verification.
  - All correctness evaluations should use at least "high" reasoning effort, where supported. All evaluations should compare against a known "good" baseline, either referencing official vendor reported numbers or those from a vLLM reference run. Running your own baseline on the vLLM main branch to compare against is acceptable. Measured scores should exceed or match the reference within one percentage point (absolute delta, after accounting for run-to-run variance).
  - Correctness validation runs should ensure that the deployment scenario is reproduced. For example, if adding a small-batch fusion, GSM8k should run at a correspondingly low batch size (to trigger the change and contribute coverage to the diff).
- **Kernel Correctness Evaluation:**
  - New kernels should be exhaustively validated for correctness on a broad range of inputs. This includes multiple possible input shapes as well as input distributions.
    - If bit-exactness is not maintained, it should be justified and validated with a strict tolerance.
    - If quantization or lossy optimizations are used, this is considered a "high correctness risk factor" and warrants additional E2E validation (see above).
  - For low-level CUDA kernels, include [compute-sanitizer](https://developer.nvidia.com/compute-sanitizer) tests such as `memcheck`, `racecheck`, and `synccheck` sanitization are required where applicable.
  - Note, committed tests should be a small subset of validation performed during development. These should exist strictly for regression checks, not for comprehensive reproduction. We do not want to run exhaustive correctness testing in CI every time we make a model change.
- **Performance Evaluation:**
  - PRs should include a "headline" speedup on a specified "target" workload. This is required but not sufficient for performance validation.
  - Performance change should also be swept across the range of bounded-affected-workloads: multiple concurrencies should be benchmarked almost always, as well as high/low sequence length when applicable. Any throughput or latency regression exceeding 1% for any measured configuration is unacceptable and disqualifies the PR from the fast-track.
    - For MoE models, ensure real prompts (such as speed-bench throughput_8k) are used so that expert balance is realistic. 

### Feedback Period.

Feedback period will continue for 12 days, ending on Oct 13. @benchislett will request maintainer review and open a candidate PR with a reference implementation of the proposed design. 

### CC List.

@njhill @LucasWilkinson @yewentao256 @WoosukKwon @mgoin @vllm-project/vllm-committers @xinli-sw 

### Discussion Areas

1. Do we want to further solidify the requirements from sec. 2.3 into a structured requirement matrix? Or do we want to leave it flexible for reviewers to decide on a per-PR basis if validation is sufficient?
2. How strict should we be about isolating code changes? Are minor one-liner integration patches in core files acceptable, or do we require rigid file-structure-based guarantees about isolation? Can we build static linting tooling (possibly AI powered) that can enforce or verify that changes are limited to the claimed workloads?
3. Is committer self-merge a good idea, or is it too permissive?
4. How much control are we comfortable delegating to automated verification systems, versus committer judgement? Should we be more/less aggressive in automating merge workflows?

title: [RFC]: A standard for Specialized (MonoKernels) Decodes in vllm/models
author: dllehr-amd
body:
### Motivation.

A **Specialized Decode** implementation is one where most/all operations in a model’s forward pass are manually implemented in a way that optimizes for the model’s specific shapes and execution patterns on certain hardware. Typically, these include heavy kernel fusions and overlap for low-latency execution, and custom kernels that tune exact grid sizes for certain batch sizes. These implementations can reach tens of thousands of lines of code, and present a major challenge in managing their complexity. This RFC proposes a standard way to modularize and integrate these runtimes into vLLM under `vllm/models/<model>/<vendor>/`.

#### Why Specialized Decodes like MonoKernels?

At low concurrency, decode is bound by launch overhead and weight reads, and a MonoKernel removes most of both. On 8× MI350X a graph-mode GLM-5.2 decode step issues ~2,459 kernels in vLLM. With the MonoKernel it issues ~210: 75 MonoKernel launches plus ~135 for dense layers 0–2, input prep and the head.
 
| GLM-5.2-MXFP4 (#60889), TP8, MI350X, ~3k-token context | vLLM | MonoKernel | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time per token, batch 1 / 8, defaults (BF16 attention) | 13.70 / 17.33 ms | 5.92 / 11.44 ms | 2.31× / 1.51× |
| Time per token, batch 1, FP8 attention opt-in | 13.70 ms | 4.80 ms | 2.85× |
| MoE layer w/o indexer (57 of 75), batch 4 / 8, FP8 | 178.8 / 189.6 µs | 69.1 / 100.6 µs | 2.59× / 1.88× |
| MoE layer with indexer (18 of 75), batch 4 / 8, FP8 | 214.9 / 227.6 µs | 88.5 / 123.4 µs | 2.43× / 1.84× |
| AgentX time between tokens, 1 / 8 users (3,600 s/point), FP8 | 15.0 / 20.4 ms | 6.5 / 12.7 ms | 2.28× / 1.68× |
| GSM8K strict, 1,319 questions, graphs, BF16 | 1228, 1234, 1235 (3 runs) | 1240 | parity: paired McNemar p = 0.22–0.63 |

Layer times are profiler-corrected, from one run. The gain shrinks with batch size, so the target is latency-bound serving: agents, chat and small-batch decode.

### Proposed Change.

#### Goals

1. **Opt-in:** off by default, enabled with one switch (`additional_config={"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}` today).
2. **Refuse at startup:** an unsupported deployment fails with one error listing every reason, never a silent fallback.
3. **The model owns it:** code lives under `vllm/models/<model>/<vendor>/specialized_decode/`, with no core changes.
4. **One `plan()` per step:** it picks the specialized kernels or vLLM's stock forward; prefill and mixed batches always run stock.
5. **One `step()` or `run()` per pass**  If specialized_decode exists, run the `step()` or `run()` function, else call stock
6. **Fixed batch sizes:** the decode kernel declares the batch sizes it serves; larger batches run stock.
7. **Avoid duplicating weights** where prudent, reading vLLM's loaded weights and caches in place.

#### Layout
Layout (shown for a monokernel; Kimi-K3 uses `nvidia/` and `cutedsl/`):

```
vllm/models/<model>/<vendor>/
    model.py                 # calls specialized_decode_config() in __init__, plan() in forward
    model_state.py           # MRV2 ModelState: builds the decode after load, binds KV caches
    specialized_decode/
        README.md            # supported checkpoints, refusals, options
        runtime/
            __init__.py      # DecodeConfig, batch sizes, specialized_decode_config(), unsupported()
            decode.py        # SpecializedDecode: plan(), run() or Step.layer()
            ...              # weight views, guards, model-specific helpers
        mono/                # the kernels, when the decode uses monokernels
tests/models/<model>/        # proposed: CPU tests for refusals and plan() routing
```

Instantiation of specialized decode happens at startup
```
self.specialized_decode_config = specialized_decode_config(vllm_config)
self.specialized_decode = SpecializedDecode(
            self.model, self.specialized_decode_config
        )
```
Two methods to Available. 

Replace the whole forward function with the specialized decode (and let it decide when to call the stock version)
```python
# Kimi-K3 (step mode, #61867): the whole step runs in the specialized decode
decode = self.specialized_decode
step = decode.plan(positions, intermediate_tensors)
if step is not None:
    return decode.run(step, input_ids, inputs_embeds)
return self.model(input_ids, positions, intermediate_tensors, inputs_embeds)
```

Replace the Decode Layer within the forward function with the specific kernel to run, and let the forward function decide.
```python
# GLM-5.2 (layer mode, #60889): a kernel per layer, or vLLM's layer
step = None if decode is None else decode.plan(positions, intermediate_tensors)
...
kernel = step.layer(idx) if step is not None else None
hidden_states, residual = (kernel or layer)(positions, hidden_states, residual)
```

**Not in Scope**

- Prefill and mixed steps. These always run vLLM's layers.
- Models compiled with `@support_torch_compile`.
- Launches that span more than two layer (some fusions may fuse end of one layer with beginning of another)
- No Runtime fallback. If a megakernel fails the engine should stop.

##### Enabling and refusal

- **Switch:** `--monokernel` (with `--no-monokernel`), the same for every model and off by default, like `--async-scheduling`. It sets `KernelConfig.monokernel`, so it also works from a config file or the Python API.
   - Additionally we can use `--additional_config={"decode_backend": "latency_specialized"}` As this will be used in the more generic case. 
  - It applies to the loaded model's spec. A model has at most one spec per vendor, so there is no name to pick.
  - There are no other user knobs. Tuning lives in the spec's `options`.
- **Refusal** happens in three stages: config (before load), model (after load) and caches (at every bind). Each stage reports every reason, not only the first. If the switch is on and the config is refused, startup raises.
- **Default-deny:** any feature in use that `supports` doesn't list is refused, then the spec's own checks run. The features are: PP, DP, EP, EPLB, DCP, PCP, LoRA, KV connectors, routed-expert capture, speculative decoding, sleep mode, CPU weight offload, weight updates, partitioned GPUs, and EAGLE3 aux layers among the kernel layers.
- MonoKernels run only under Model Runner V2.

title: [RFC]: Bring-Your-Own-GPU (BYOG) reproducible evals and benchmarks for PRs
author: LucasWilkinson
body:
### Motivation.

Reviewing performance- and accuracy-sensitive PRs is frequently bottlenecked on evidence and regression testing. Reviewers routinely ask "can you please provide e2e performance data?", "can you please provide eval results?", or "can you show 8k1k numbers on H100?". Not only are these requests often vague, leaving the submitter unsure exactly how to run the benchmark or eval, but the answers also arrive as screenshots, hand-run `vllm bench` output, or not at all. On the flip side, running a broad eval + benchmark matrix on vLLM-funded CI for PRs does not scale, especially as the volume of AI-generated PRs grows.

AI tools have made producing a PR nearly free, but reviewing one costs as much as or more than it ever did. Maintainer attention is now the scarce resource, and AI generation of PRs is skewing more of the cost of a PR onto the reviewer, who frequently has to validate the PR manually or validate it on other hardware. Asking for evidence that costs GPU time to produce moves some of that cost back to whoever wants the PR merged. It doesn't close the gap, and spending compute doesn't make a PR good, but it pushes in the right direction in two ways:

- the evidence gives the reviewer more confidence, making the PR easier to review;
- spending it signals that someone values the PR.

At the same time, the community has more datacenter hardware than vLLM CI, and more kinds of it (GB300, MI355X, older Hopper/Ampere fleets, and so on). Some of it may be free to help with evals for specific, important PRs, even if its owners aren't ready to commit it to vLLM CI full time by hooking it up as a CI agent.

This RFC proposes a standard, versioned **eval image**, built by vLLM CI when CI is run on a commit, which anyone can run on their own GPUs, coupled with a **public database of results**.

This could also help PRs under the [fast-track merging RFC (#59665)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/59665) by providing the extra evals and benchmarks it asks for.

### Proposed Change.

#### Goals

- Anyone with suitable GPUs can produce results for a commit with a single `docker run`: give the image a request or run spec, and it produces a result bundle.
- Results are reproducible: a bundle records everything needed to re-run it on the same GPU type and get the same result within stated tolerances.
- **Trust-based, with accountability.** Every upload is tied to the submitter's GitHub account.
- Reviewers can ask for a specific configuration, and any community member can donate GPU time to provide it, including hardware the author doesn't have.
- Reuse existing vLLM eval configs (`tests/evals/*`, `.buildkite/lm-eval-harness/configs`) and community benchmark recipes (SemiAnalysis InferenceX and AgentX) rather than inventing new ones.

#### Scope

- **Not in scope yet: hard merge gating.** For now results are informational, an informal gate: reviewers may expect them and may request specific runs, but nothing blocks merging automatically. Once the prototype has shown the results are reliable, we may make some results required for merging certain areas.
- **Non-goal:** replacing pre-merge CI or the existing post-merge performance dashboard.

#### Overview

1. **On the PR.** A maintainer triggers CI on a commit, and CI builds a signed eval image for it. A reviewer asks for results with `/byog request`, or the submitter simply runs the standard suites up front and uploads the results as extra evidence.
2. **On anyone's GPUs.** Anyone with suitable GPUs runs the request with a single `docker run`. The image runs the jobs that fit its GPUs, shows the bundle it produced, then uploads it after a GitHub login.
3. **On the results service.** The service records who uploaded the bundle, stores it, and updates the public dashboard and the PR via a comment.

#### Evals and benchmarks

##### Evals

Every eval costs GPU time, so we want the set that gives the **most signal per GPU-hour**.

**Proposed eval suites,** picked with `eval_suite:`. Listing `evals` in a request replaces the suite. Requesting community input on the contents and time budgets.

| Eval suite | When | Evals | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `smoke` | Quick check that nothing is badly broken | `gsm8k` | minutes |
| `standard` (default) | The general expectation for accuracy-sensitive PRs | `gsm8k`, `mmlu_pro` (300 per subject), `mrcr` (120 samples) | up to ~3 hours |
| `extended` | On reviewer request, for large or risky changes | `gsm8k`, full `mmlu_pro`, `mrcr` (240 samples) | hours |

Each eval in these suites covers a different kind of failure: `gsm8k` catches gross breakage quickly, `mmlu_pro` covers broad knowledge and isn't saturated on large models, and `mrcr` covers long context (attention, KV cache, prefix caching). All run against datasets pinned to a commit and baked into the image.

**Catalog.** Other evals a request can add. Costs are rough orders of magnitude for a typical config (for example a mid-size MoE on one node); reasoning mode and large models move evals up a bucket.

| Eval | What it catches | Existing harness | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Logprob / KL divergence vs reference logits | Numerical drift from kernels, quantization, attention backends, often before scores move | — (new) | minutes |
| `ifeval` | Chat template, instruction following, stop handling | lm-eval | minutes |
| `chartqa` / `mmmu` | Multimodal pipeline | `.buildkite/lm-eval-harness` | tens of minutes |
| `gpqa_diamond` (×N repeats) | Reasoning quality | `tests/evals/gpt_oss` | tens of minutes → hours |
| `bfcl` / tool-call subset | Tool calling, structured output, parsers | — | tens of minutes → hours |
| `aime25` (×N repeats) | Long-generation reasoning; high variance | lm-eval | hours |
| `livecodebench` | Code generation | — | hours |
| `ruler` / `longbench_v2` | Long context at 128k+ | — | hours |
| SWE-bench Verified / agentic benchmarks | End-to-end agentic quality | — (needs sandboxes) | hours → days |

Greedy decoding is not bit-reproducible across batch composition, so per-eval tolerances come from repeated runs on `main`. High-variance evals (AIME, GPQA) need `repeats` and report mean ± stderr.

##### Benchmarks

Modeled on SemiAnalysis InferenceX, so the results line up with numbers the community already reads.

**Proposed benchmark suites,** picked with `benchmark_suite:`. Listing `benchmarks` in a request replaces the suite. Requesting community input on these too.

| Benchmark suite | When | Benchmarks | Time |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `smoke` | Quick check that serving works and nothing is badly slower | 1k1k at concurrency 1, 64 | minutes |
| `standard` (default) | The general expectation for perf PRs | 8k1k at concurrency 1, 16, 64, 256, plus AgentX at 8, 32 | up to ~2 hours |
| `extended` | On reviewer request, for large or risky changes | 1k1k, 8k1k, 1k8k at concurrency 1–512, plus AgentX at 8, 32, 128 | hours to days |

| Benchmark | Workload | Client | Metrics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fixed_isl_osl` | `1k1k`, `8k1k`, `1k8k` random-token, `ignore_eos` | `vllm bench serve` | output tok/s/GPU, TTFT/TPOT/ITL p50/p90/p99, interactivity (tok/s/user) |
| `agentx` | AgentX trace replay: multi-turn Claude Code sessions with subagents and prefix reuse | `aiperf --scenario inferencex-agentx-mvp`, dataset pinned to a dated revision | throughput/GPU vs interactivity, TTFT percentiles, prefix-cache hit rate |

- **Concurrency sweeps.** Each concurrency point is a separate client run against the same server, with its own artifacts. For AgentX, concurrency counts live agent sessions, and each point runs for at least 900 s.
- **Speculative decoding.** InferenceX forces acceptance lengths for cross-framework comparability, which would hide the effect of PRs that change drafting, so BYOG reports natural acceptance by default.
- **Raw records are kept.** Every benchmark keeps its per-request records so results can be recomputed and re-aggregated.

##### Comparing against `main`

There should be a way to compare a PR's results against `main` results for the same spec on the same GPU type, when those exist. Sources include nightly `main` runs and `main` runs anyone submits. The image records the PR's merge-base, so the dashboard can find the closest `main` results. Results well below `main` on the same GPU type are flagged as suspicious, which also catches a misbehaving machine (throttling, misconfiguration) without collecting GPU telemetry; the submitter can then debug it.

#### Trust

The system is mostly trust-based, with accountability through GitHub accounts:

- **Uploads are authenticated with GitHub.** After a run, the image starts a GitHub device-flow login: it prints a code, and the submitter approves it in a browser. The token has no scopes, so it only proves who the submitter is.
- **The service records who uploaded each result.** It checks the token with GitHub and stores the submitter's GitHub user ID and username with the bundle's sha256 and the upload time. Results can't be submitted under someone else's name without access to their GitHub account.
- **Tampering is handled by flagging accounts.** If someone is found tampering with results, their GitHub account is flagged for result tampering and their results are removed. Anyone who doubts a result can re-run it with the bundle's `repro.sh`.
- **The token is kept away from the PR's code.** The job runs the PR's code, so the image only logs in once the job has finished, and refuses if any other process is still running in the container. In that case the bundle is kept, and a fresh `--upload-only` run uploads it.

#### Precedent: MLPerf

Results run on contributors' own hardware have worked elsewhere. MLPerf Inference has published vendor-run results for years. Submitters run the benchmarks on their own systems through a mandated harness (LoadGen). Trust comes from compliance tests, peer review by other submitters, random audits, and a rule that "results that cannot be replicated are not valid results".

BYOG starts from a stronger position. MLPerf submitters bring their own inference engine, so much of MLPerf's process exists to catch engine-level tricks. In BYOG, vLLM CI builds the entire image: the vLLM build under test, the eval and benchmark clients, the harness, and the hardware queries. The only thing a contributor brings is the hardware.

#### How it works

##### 1. The eval image

- **Built when CI is run on a commit**, the same way CI works today: PRs build only on commits where a maintainer triggers "run CI". That trigger doubles as the safety gate, since the image runs PR code on contributors' machines.
- **A thin layer on the CI image.** `docker/Dockerfile.byog` builds on the image CI already pushes for that commit (the `test-ci` target), adding the harness, the eval and benchmark catalog and suites, reference specs, pinned clients (`aiperf`; `lm-eval` is already in the test image), and pinned datasets. Registries deduplicate layers, and the large pieces that rarely change (clients and datasets) come from a separately versioned `byog-tools` image via `COPY --link`, so the per-commit addition is a few MB.
- **Signed and pinned.** Images are signed with cosign (keyless via CI's OIDC identity, or a vLLM-held KMS key) with SLSA provenance linking the digest to the commit. Images are pulled by digest, and the results service rejects bundles whose digest lacks a valid vLLM CI signature.
- **Retention (undecided).** Eval images could be ephemeral, for example expiring after 30 days, since they can be rebuilt from the commit. Rebuilt images get a new digest, though, so images referenced by results, or `main` images that PRs are compared against, may need to be kept longer.

##### 2. Run specs

A **run spec** is a YAML file that fully determines one run: the model, the exact `vllm serve` arguments and environment, the hardware, and the evals and benchmarks to run against that server.

<details>
<summary>Example run spec</summary>

```yaml
schema: byog.spec/v0
name: dsv3-fp8-tp8-8k1k
model:
  id: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2
  revision: 4f8c3b1...            # required, full HF commit sha
serve:
  args: --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 16384 --kv-cache-dtype fp8
  env:
    VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM: "1"
hardware:
  gpu: [H200, B200, B300]         # acceptable GPU types
  count: 8
eval_suite: standard              # smoke | standard (default) | extended
benchmarks:                       # replaces the benchmark suite
  - name: fixed_isl_osl
    scenarios: [8k1k]
    concurrency: [1, 8, 64, 256]
```

</details>

- **Reference specs** live in-tree under `tools/byog/specs/` and are reviewed like code. Their results are comparable across PRs and over time.
- **Custom specs** cover anything a reviewer asks for, such as "this PR with `--enable-expert-parallel` on 4×B200".
- **What actually ran is recorded too:** the server's real command line, the resolved non-default `VllmConfig`, the relevant environment variables, and the exact client commands. Any divergence from the spec is a validation error. Each bundle includes a `repro.sh` with the exact `docker run` command.

##### 3. Requests

Reviewers rarely want a single run. They want "these models × these parallelism schemes × these GPUs". A **request** describes that sweep: its `matrix` section lists the values to try for each setting (models, parallelism, GPUs, ...), and the request expands into one **job** per combination, like a GitHub Actions matrix. Each job is one server configuration. Starting a server is the expensive part, so every eval and benchmark in a job runs against that one server, and concurrency sweeps happen inside the job rather than in the matrix.

<details>
<summary>Example request</summary>

```yaml
schema: byog.request/v0
pr: 61234
title: "fused_moe: FP8 grouped GEMM rewrite"

matrix:                            # one job per combination of values
  model:
    - name: dsv3.2
      id: deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3.2
      revision: a7e62ac04ecb2c0a54d736dc46601c5606cf10a6
      serve: {args: --kv-cache-dtype fp8}
    - name: qwen3-30b-fp8
      id: Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8
      revision: 5a5a776300a41aaa681dd7ff0106608ef2bc90db
  parallel: [tp8, dp8-ep]          # shorthand for vllm serve parallel flags
  hardware: [H200x8, B200x8]
  variant:
    - name: default
    - name: no-deepgemm
      serve: {env: {VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM: "0"}}

exclude:
  - {model: qwen3-30b-fp8, variant: no-deepgemm}

include:                           # one-off jobs outside the matrix
  - model: dsv3.2
    parallel: tp4-dp2-ep
    hardware: B300x8
    variant: default
    evals: [{name: gpqa_diamond, repeats: 4}]
```

</details>

- **Matrix keys are free-form.** Each value sets part of the job: serve args, env, model, hardware, evals, or benchmarks. `exclude` drops combinations, and `include` adds one-off jobs.
- **Combining is strict.** Setting the same flag in two places is an error, as are conflicting env vars, models, or hardware.
- **Parallelism shorthand.** `tp4-dp2-ep` means `--tensor-parallel-size 4 --data-parallel-size 2 --enable-expert-parallel`; `pp`, `dcp`, and `pcp` work the same way.
- **Defaults.** A request only states what differs from the defaults. The smallest useful request is a model and the hardware. With no parallel flags, jobs use tensor parallelism across all their GPUs, and the `standard` eval and benchmark suites. Expansion writes these defaults into each job, so jobs stay reproducible if the defaults change later.
- **Validated before anyone spends GPU time.** Serve args are parsed with vLLM's own argument parser, the parallelism's GPU count must match the hardware, and unknown evals, benchmarks, suites, settings, and unpinned revisions are rejected.

**Running a request.** The image's entrypoint does everything, so the only host requirement is Docker (or Podman) with GPU support:

```bash
docker run --gpus all --ipc host -v $HF_HUB_CACHE:/weights/hub -v $PWD/out:/out -e HF_TOKEN \
    <image>@sha256:... --request /out/request.yaml   # or --job <job_id>, or --spec /out/spec.yaml
```

It expands the request, runs every job that fits the visible GPUs (on 2×B300, the request's B300x2 jobs), downloads any missing pinned weights, and writes one bundle per job. It then prints exactly what is in each bundle, every file with its size and sha256 plus the headline results, and uploads it after a GitHub login (see Trust). Large requests can be split by job across people with different hardware.

`tools/byog/request.py` previews a request without GPUs, listing its jobs and a rough GPU-hour estimate; the example above is 13 jobs and about 329 GPU-hours with the standard suites. On a PR, the request is posted as a `/byog request` comment and the bot replies with the job table.

##### 4. Environment logging

Collected before and after the run. This builds on `vllm/collect_env.py` (`get_env_info()`), adding:

- **GPU:** `nvidia-smi -q -x` (or `amd-smi`): GPU type, VBIOS, driver, CUDA, ECC, MIG, power limit, clocks, PCIe; `nvidia-smi topo -m`; NVLink status.
- **CPU, memory, OS:** `lscpu`, NUMA layout, `/proc/meminfo`, governor, kernel version and cmdline, `ulimit -l`.
- **Logs:** server and client logs.
- **Privacy:** the hostname, GPU UUIDs, and GPU serial numbers are redacted. Everything else is collected inside the container, where host usernames and paths don't appear.

##### 5. Result bundle

`bundle.tar.gz` contains:

<details>
<summary>Bundle layout</summary>

```text
manifest.json          # sha256 + size of every file below
result.json            # byog.result/v0 summary (see tools/byog/examples/result.example.json)
spec.yaml              # run spec, verbatim
spec.resolved.yaml     # with defaults filled in
env/                   # environment snapshots, before and after
server/                # actual command line, env, server log
evals/<name>/          # eval results
bench/<name>/<scenario>-c<N>/   # summary and per-request records
repro.sh
```

</details>

`result.json` is the summary the service indexes; raw artifacts are stored by content hash.

##### 6. PR comment

A bot comment on the PR keeps an up-to-date table: requested jobs, who ran them, PR vs `main` deltas, and links to bundles. Anyone with the hardware can run a request's jobs and submit results; nobody needs permission.

#### Rollout

1. **MVP:** `docker/Dockerfile.byog`, the `tools/byog` harness, suites and reference specs, plus a minimal results service, since uploads are authenticated: a GitHub OAuth app, an upload endpoint that records the submitter's GitHub account, bundle storage, and a simple public list of results.
2. **Service features:** the public dashboard with comparison against `main`, and the PR bot.
3. **Possible hard gating (future):** based on the prototype's track record, decide whether some results should become required for merging, and for which areas.

### Any Other Things.

#### Open questions

1. Which evals catch real regressions that `gsm8k` misses, and are they worth their cost? Examples of past regressions each would have caught are the most useful input.
2. Are smoke / standard / extended the right split for eval and benchmark suites, and is each one's content right for its time budget?
3. How many repeats do high-variance evals need, and should reasoning models be evaluated with thinking on, off, or both?
4. Is a logprob/KL-divergence check against stored reference logits a good cheap first gate for numerics-affecting PRs?
5. Retention for eval images and the CI images under them. Is the `test-ci` image acceptable for perf numbers, or do we need the leaner `vllm-openai` image?
6. Gated models: is it acceptable for reference specs to require contributors to accept licenses (Llama)?
7. Tolerances: who owns calibration per eval and GPU type, and how often is it redone?
8. AMD, TPU, and XPU support from day one, or NVIDIA first?

#### Prior art

- SemiAnalysis InferenceX / AgentX: scenario definitions and AIPerf trace replay.
- MLPerf Inference (see above).
- SLSA and Sigstore: build provenance and keyless signing for the eval image.

#### AI assistance

This RFC was drafted with AI assistance (Claude Code); the prototype harness referenced here was also written with AI assistance and tested on B300 GPUs.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: DFlash2 speculative decoding performance on ROCm (MI355X)
author: zhentaocc
body:
### Motivation.

DFlash2 on ROCm is slower than it should be, and at high concurrency on main it is slower than not speculating at all. Measured on one MI355X, Qwen3.8-27B with `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` and 7 draft tokens, using MRV2 and ShareGPT with 512 output tokens at temperature 0. Output tok/s:

| | c=1 | c=16 | c=64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main, no speculative decoding | 91.7 | 940.8 | 2855.4 |
| main, DFlash2 | 239.4 | 1829.9 | **2641.3** |
| DFlash2 + #61433 | 266.8 | 2392.4 | 4065.3 |
| DFlash2 + #61433 + #61434 (`--no-enable-prefix-caching`) | 262.2 | 2511.4 | 4456.2 |

The acceptance length is 4.0–4.3 in every DFlash2 row. The #61434 row is compared against #61433 with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`, which gives 262.9 / 2377.9 / 4027.9.

Since #61855 (merged), ROCm runs spec decode through a Triton port of the fused GDN MTP decode kernel by default, so #61434 now applies only with `VLLM_GDN_DECODE_KERNEL=triton`. #64325 adds the same deferred state to the fused kernel. On image `nightly-rocm100-5d35ce39` (includes #61855), default attention backends and `--no-enable-prefix-caching`, mean of 2 runs:

| | c=1 | c=16 | c=64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main, DFlash2 | 245.7 | 1835.3 | 2648.7 |
| + #64325 | 245.2 | 1948.1 (+6.1%) | 2865.8 (+8.2%) |

GPU time at c=64 with #61433 applied, from a rocprofv3 kernel trace of an offline run. The run uses 64 ShareGPT prompts, 256 output tokens each, and prefix caching on (the default), so the window includes prefill.

| | share |
|---|---|
| GEMM (hipBLASLt), including the split-K epilogue at 2.5% | ~61% |
| GDN recurrent update, `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update` | 18.3% |
| Inductor-fused norm, activation and RoPE | ~8% |
| Copies (elementwise, cat, `copyBuffer`) | ~4% |
| Full attention, target and drafter | 3.2% |
| GDN `causal_conv1d_update` | 1.5% |
| Vocab top-k (`torch.topk`) | 0.8% |
| DFlash2 grouped conv | 0.3% |

This issue tracks the plan: what is already up for review and what comes next. ATOM (ROCm/ATOM) and the aiter kernels were used as references.

### Proposed Change.

#### In review

| PR | Change | Result |
|---|---|---|
| #61433 | On ROCm, rank `ROCM_ATTN` below `TRITON_ATTN` / `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` when speculative decoding is on or the model is hybrid | +11% / +31% / +54% at c=1/16/64 |
| #61434 | Defer GDN spec-decode state stores: write one full state plus the raw per-token inputs, and replay the accepted tokens at the start of the next step | +5.6% at c=16, +10.6% at c=64 |
| #64325 | The same deferred state in the Triton fused GDN MTP decode kernel, the ROCm default since #61855 | +6.1% at c=16, +8.2% at c=64; kernel 382 → 213 µs at 64 sequences |
| ROCm/aiter#7069 | The same deferred state in aiter's Triton `fused_rearrange_sigmoid_gated_delta_rule` (opt-in `defer_spec_state`) | Kernel 86 → 61 µs at 16 sequences, 341 → 219 µs at 64 |
| #61760 | Triton `unified_attention`: split-K (3D) for non-causal speculative rows, and split a pruned sliding window across the segments | Drafter attention 4.7× faster at B=1 past the 2048 window, ≥ 1.0× at every drafter point measured; with #61433's default backends and 8k prompts, decode step −1.5% / −1.2% at c=1/4 (output +6.5% / +0.8%, mostly acceptance length). Outside DFlash: Gemma-4-26B-A4B (TRITON_ATTN forced on ROCm, 25/30 sliding layers) output +32% / +28% / +9% at 16k c=1/4/16 |
| #61429 | Exact Triton vocab top-k for `LogitsProcessor.get_top_k_tokens` when flashinfer is unavailable | Kernel 4–6× faster than `torch.topk`; end to end within noise |
| #62813 | Interim for #61433's accuracy dependency: on gfx950, rank `TRITON_ATTN` above `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` until the aiter pin has the #62606 fix | Accuracy fix (#62606), no speedup |
| #63069 | GLM-5.3-Flash + DFlash2: let `ROCM_ATTN` share the BLHNC KV cache layout | Startup fix; on main the server fails at startup |
| #63070 | GLM-5.3-Flash: default to breakable CUDA graphs on ROCm | +14–17% without spec decode; with DFlash2 +14% at c=1/16 (default capture sizes) |
| #63071 | GLM-5.3-Flash: deferred KDA spec decode state (the KDA version of #61434) | Step time −4.5% / −4.7% at c=16/64, +1.2% at c=1 |
| #63073 | GLM-5.3-Flash: Gluon KDA kernel for #63071's mode on gfx950 (stacked on #63071) | Step time a further −4.5% at c=64; removes the c=1 cost |
| #63072 | GLM-5.3-Flash: pass precomputed chunk indices to `chunk_kda` | Removes a host sync per prefill; throughput unchanged |

**#61433.**
- Draft, paused in review until vLLM's aiter pin includes ROCm/aiter#6661 (released in aiter v0.1.27; main pins v0.1.26). Before that, `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` gives wrong output on gfx950 for some KV cache sizes (#62606). #62813 is the interim change, and #61433 drops its gfx950 rule after the bump.
- `ROCM_ATTN` runs its prefix-prefill Triton kernel for every multi-token query, which here is 1 + 7 tokens per request.
- On hybrid models its block size (832 here) is not a power of two, so even single-token decode misses the HIP paged-attention path.
- After the change, the target picks `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN`. The non-causal DFlash drafter picks `TRITON_ATTN`.
- An explicit `--attention-backend` still wins, and dense models without speculative decoding keep the current order.

**#61434.**
- The GDN state is 48 heads × 128 × 128 fp32, about 3 MiB per layer per sequence.
- Today it is written once per draft position (8 times per step), and only one copy is used.
- The replay is exact for fp32 SSM state.
- It currently applies only when `mamba_cache_mode` is `none`, i.e. with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`.
- It changes `fused_sigmoid_gating_delta_rule_update`. Since #61855 that kernel runs spec decode on ROCm only with `VLLM_GDN_DECODE_KERNEL=triton`, or as the fallback when the fused MTP op does not support the model.

**#64325.**
- Same records and replay as #61434, in `fused_gdn_decode_post_conv_mtp_triton`, which is what ROCm runs by default after #61855.
- Enabled on ROCm with an fp32 state and `mamba_cache_mode` `none`. The CUDA op is unchanged.
- Spec rows of mixed batches (`_forward_core`) use the same update kernel, so every step of a request sees the same state layout.
- The two PRs are independent: each changes a different kernel, and the layer picks one of them at init.

**ROCm/aiter#7069.**
- vLLM calls this kernel only for non-speculative decode with `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, so the flag is for other users of aiter's GDN decode op.
- Opt-in flag, default off; requires fp32 state and 2D `ssm_state_indices`.

**#61760.**
- The DFlash2 drafter attends non-causally over its 8-token block with a 2048-token sliding window. Its rows were excluded from split-K, so at B=1 the 2D launch has 8 programs (one per KV head), and each walks the whole window.
- Separately, when split-K is used with a sliding window, the segments split `[0, seq_len)`. At long context only one or two of them overlap the window. This affects causal sliding-window decode and verify as well, which get 2–9.6× at B ≤ 8 and long context.
- ShareGPT is unchanged because its prompts mostly fit within the window.
- The larger beneficiary is a sliding-window target model. Gemma-4 is forced onto `TRITON_ATTN` on ROCm (head sizes 256/512), so its 25 sliding layers take this path by default: 16k random output +32% / +28% / +9% at c=1/4/16, 4k c=1 +11%, ShareGPT unchanged, GSM8K 0.708 → 0.711.
- The drafter regression at B=16, ctx 512 (0.86×) is fixed by a minimum segment size that scales with the batch: now 1.06×. Causal with ctx ≤ window at B=2–4 stays at 0.94–0.98×; it is codegen, not the tile bounds, which are identical to main's.
- The earlier +17% / +16% under `TRITON_ATTN` is superseded by the default-backend run.

**#61429.**
- At these batch sizes the top-k is a small part of the step.
- The PR is kept because it is exact, deterministic and much faster than `torch.topk` for larger draft batches.
- aiter's top-k APIs were compared and are not a better fit (see "Any Other Things").

#### Closed

- #62381 (skip the AITER packed GDN path under spec decode) was closed as superseded by #61855. Since #61855, `forward_hip` skips that path whenever the fused GDN spec decode kernel is enabled, which is the default on ROCm with speculative decoding. The remaining case (`VLLM_GDN_DECODE_KERNEL=triton`, or a model that the fused kernel does not support) was not measured.
- #62415 (zero out-of-window V in `ROCM_ATTN`'s sliding-window kernels) was closed. The NaN it fixed (#62828) no longer occurs on main since #60767.

#### Next

The first three items are planned in this order.

1. **GDN deferred state with prefix caching (`mamba_cache_mode=align`).**
   - With prefix caching on, which is the default, the GDN update is still 18% of GPU time, because neither #61434 nor #64325 applies there.
   - `align` reads per-token states at block boundaries in `preprocess_state`. The plan is to replay the records before that copy, so the deferred path also covers the default configuration.
2. **One GDN state slot per request.**
   - This follows the idea of ROCm/ATOM#1883 (ReplaySSM).
   - Speculative decoding currently keeps 1 + `num_speculative_tokens` state slots per request. For Qwen3.8-27B that is 48 GDN layers × 3 MiB ≈ 144 MiB per slot, or about 1.15 GiB per request with 7 draft tokens. This is an estimate from the config, not a measurement.
   - Building on #61434's records, a single checkpoint plus the per-token records would be enough, and the freed memory could go to the KV cache and larger batches. Measuring the memory and throughput gain comes first.
3. **Split-KV for `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` at small batch and long context.**
   - On gfx950, aiter's `unified_attention` defaults to its gluon backend. That backend always takes the 2D launch for query_len > 1, which has no split-KV.
   - With B=1, query_len=8 and 4 KV heads, that is about 20 programs on 256 CUs, so the time grows linearly with context.
   - aiter's `backend="triton"` path switches to 3D in that regime. It is 1.4–4.3× faster per call when B ≤ 4 and ctx ≥ 2k, or B ≤ 8 and ctx ≥ 3k; gluon is better at B ≥ 16.
   - At c=1 with an 8k context that is about 3.8 ms per step across the 16 attention layers.
   - Options: choose the aiter backend per batch size in `rocm_aiter_unified_attn.py`, or add split-KV to the gluon 2D path in aiter. The aiter fix addresses the root cause.
   - This is the target-side counterpart of #61760, which does the same for `TRITON_ATTN`.
4. **GEMM tuning for the verify step (tuned and measured; next is contributing the configs to aiter).**
   - The target sees M = 8 × num_seqs. GEMMs are about 61% of GPU time, and at M=8 they take about 11.4 ms per step, which is mostly weight streaming.
   - vLLM's default dispatch is within 1–4% of the best of `torch`, aiter `tgemm` (untuned) and aiter Triton at these M values. Untuned aiter therefore has nothing to offer.
   - aiter's bf16 tuner (`gemm_a16w16_tune`) was run on:
     - Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2 at every capture size;
     - >300B targets and their DFlash drafters at TP 1/4/8: Kimi-K2.5, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, GLM-5 and GLM-5.3-Flash.
   - The tuner times each candidate on its own, so a candidate within ±5–8% of hipBLASLt wins or loses by noise. The raw tuned CSV gave no end-to-end gain. Each tuned row was therefore re-timed against `F.linear`, alternating the two in one process over cold weight copies, and kept only if it is at least 1.03× faster.
   - **Qwen3.8-27B + DFlash2**, AITER linear env, all with #61433. Output tok/s, mean of 2–4 runs with GPUs swapped:

     | | c=1 | c=16 | c=64 |
     |---|---|---|---|
     | without AITER | 262.1 | 2418 | 3985 |
     | AITER, shipped configs + #62381 (closed, see above) | 264.3 | 2387 | 3958 |
     | AITER, verified configs + #62381 (closed, see above) | 273.0 (+4.2%) | 2407 (−0.5%) | 3991 (+0.2%) |

     The gain is at c=1. The biggest verified wins are `gate_up` (N=34816) with a Triton kernel at M=8/16 and `lm_head` at M=64 with FlyDSL.
   - **>300B shapes.** 338 of 442 tuned rows were kept; none of these shapes is in aiter's shipped gfx950 configs. Summed time of each distinct layer shape (not weighted by layer count), `F.linear` → verified configs, at M=8. These are GEMM microbenchmarks, not end-to-end numbers:

     | model | TP1 | TP4 | TP8 |
     |---|---|---|---|
     | Qwen3.5-397B-A17B | +30% | +33% | +17% |
     | GLM-5.3-Flash | +10% | +33% | +19% |
     | Kimi-K2.5 | +14% | +5% | +9% |
     | GLM-5 | +3% | +22% | +31% |

     The largest wins are small-K layers such as the shared-expert `down` and GLM-5.3-Flash's KDA `f_b_g_b` projection (1.5–1.9×), and the Qwen3.5-397B `lm_head` at TP1 (466 → 339 µs, 1.37×).
   - aiter issues found on the way:
     - A multi-path `AITER_CONFIG_GEMM_BF16` (and the default, which merges `model_configs/`) is merged into one fixed file, `/tmp/aiter_configs/bf16_tuned_gemm.csv`. Every process in the container shares it, so parallel processes with different configs read each other's. On duplicate shapes the merge also rewrites the source CSVs. Passing one pre-merged file avoids both.
     - The prebuilt opus module only contains the kernel ids used by the shipped configs. A tuned opus row with another id makes vLLM fail at startup ("kid N is not compiled"), so those rows were dropped.
     - The tuner's FlyDSL JIT caches keep one weight copy per compiled candidate, so tuner workers grew to about 285 GiB.
5. **QK-norm + RoPE + gate fusion on ROCm.**
   - `Qwen3NextAttention` only uses vLLM's `fused_qk_rmsnorm_rope_gate` on CUDA/XPU. #51406 (open, approved, needs a rebase) allows it on ROCm (`is_cuda_alike()`). The kernel test passes on MI355X.
   - Per layer it is 6.3× faster at 8 tokens (about 14 → 2.2 µs) and 2.1× at 512 tokens.
   - End to end on top of #61433, mean of 2 runs with GPUs swapped: 267.8 → 269.5, 2382.7 → 2400.3, 3956.3 → 3981.0 tok/s at c=1/16/64, i.e. +0.6–0.7%. That is below the 1–1.5% spread between runs. Acceptance length is unchanged. GSM8K (5-shot, 1319 questions) is 0.792 → 0.785 (8 questions).
   - aiter's `fused_qkv_split_qk_norm_rope_cache` additionally fuses the KV-cache write. It is 1.2–2.3× faster than vLLM's fused kernel + `reshape_and_cache_flash`, but that saves only about 25 µs per target step (16 attention layers, about 0.15%). Using it would also require the attention layer to skip its own cache write, and it has no mrope. So the plan is #51406, not aiter.

#### Not planned, with reasons

- **`ROCM_AITER_FA` for this model.** With aiter enabled it is 6–8% slower than `ROCM_AITER_UNIFIED_ATTN` + `TRITON_ATTN`. Its non-causal path (`mha_v3` kvcache) is 4–10× slower than `TRITON_ATTN` for the drafter.
- **aiter's ASM paged-attention fast paths.** The `pa_fwd_asm` MTP kernels and `pa_persistent_fwd` cover head 128 with GQA 8/16, or FP8 KV. Qwen3.8-27B uses head 256, GQA 6 and bf16 KV.
- **`pa_decode_gluon`.** It needs query_len ≤ 4, and DFlash2 here verifies 8 tokens.

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

**Environment.**
- Image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-rocm100-0cbac6cd1305f710e12193596b27488397bcb205`, which ships amd-aiter 0.1.23. main now pins v0.1.24.post1.
- The PRs above change only Python and Triton files. Each PR description has a Reproduction section with the serve command, the benchmark loop and a kernel microbenchmark.

**aiter top-k comparison.** V=248320, k=16, bf16, which is what the candidate head produces. Times in µs on MI355X:

| rows | `torch.topk` | #61429 Triton | `aiter.topk_plain` | `aiter.ops.topk_select.topk_select` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 82.3 | **17.2** | 49.3 | 84.3 |
| 112 | 197.2 | **44.8** | 72.9, duplicate indices | 135.1 |
| 448 | 575.6 | **112.6** | 114.9, duplicate indices | 276.0 |
| 1792 | 2072.6 | 383.6 | **175.1** | 888.5 |

- `topk_select` serves k > 1 in fp32 only, so bf16 must be cast first. It returns int32 indices.
- `aiter.ops.triton.topk.topk` raised a GPU memory-access fault at this shape.
- The `topk_plain` duplicates come from `topk_filter_kernel`.
  - It handles a whole row per block (`len_per_block = len`, marked `TODO: Consider multiple blocks`), yet it can still be launched with several blocks per row.
  - For bf16/fp16, the element-wise tail loop of an extra block re-reads the last `blockDim.x` columns of the row, and the merge then counts them twice.
  - Repro: set one column near the end of every row to the maximum. With 112 or 448 rows, every row returns that index twice. fp32 is unaffected.
  - The code is unchanged in v0.1.24.post1. The fix is ROCm/aiter#6586.

**aiter GDN decode kernels for spec decode.** Checked on aiter main for this model (H=16, HV=48, K=V=128, T=8, fp32 state):
- FlyDSL `flydsl_gdr_mtp` (chain mode) is the only one that follows vLLM's contract (roll back to slot `num_accepted - 1`, store every token) with vLLM's state layout. It does not fuse the conv or the norm and needs a uniform T. Recurrence only, µs at 1 / 16 / 64 / 128 sequences: FlyDSL 12.1 / 77.4 / 380.6 / 754.2, vLLM Triton per-token 15.2 / 92.2 / 393.1 / 745.2, vLLM Triton deferred (#64325) 13.1 / 55.8 / 205.3 / 411.3. FlyDSL is faster only at ≤ 4 sequences, so the plan stays with the Triton kernel.
- Gluon `fused_gdn_decode_qkvz` (gfx950) fuses split, conv, recurrence and norm, but handles one token per sequence only.
- HIP `fused_split_gdr_update` uses a swizzled state layout, and `gdr_decode_packed_bf16` is fixed to 8/32 heads with a bf16 state.
- The `fused_kda_decode*` kernels (including the ReplaySSM mode) are for KDA, not GDN.

title: [RFC]: Layerwise KV Pooling and P/D Disaggregation for High-Hit-Rate Agent Workloads
author: weijinqian0
body: # RFC: Layerwise KV Pooling and P/D Disaggregation for High-Hit-Rate Agent Workloads ## Summary This RFC proposes a coordinated layerwise design for KV-cache pooling and Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregation in Agent workloads with KV-cache hit rates above 90%. Pool reuse, P/D handoff, consumption acknowledgement, and block reclamation must follow matching layerwise lifecycle boundaries. This allows KV blocks to be reclaimed layer by layer while loading a later KV group is overlapped with computation on the current group. The core design is to reuse grouped KV blocks within a layerwise lifecycle and pipeline cache loading with model computation, with the goal of hiding as much loading time as possible. Supporting work includes reducing per-layer preparation overhead, avoiding redundant lookups, and addressing resource contention between H2D copies and AlltoAllV. ## Motivation In a test with 140K input tokens and a 95% cache hit rate, performance with 24 concurrent requests was reported to be about 50% worse than with a single request in token throughput. The result nevertheless indicates that cache hits do not automatically translate into better performance at higher concurrency. There are two related goals: 1. **Improve HBM utilization.** If cached blocks remain logically held after they are no longer needed, they cannot be reused for new requests, reducing effective concurrency. 2. **Hide cache-loading latency.** Pool loading should overlap with model computation. Any uncovered loading time remains on the critical path and can reduce throughput or increase latency. At high hit rates, Prefill is primarily constrained by HBM capacity: the more KV cache that remains resident, the fewer requests can run concurrently, making it harder to keep compute resources busy. Layerwise pooling can reclaim KV blocks as soon as their consumption at a layer is complete, reducing per-request HBM usage and increasing the number of runnable requests. Asynchronous scheduling can make block retention worse in non-layerwise execution. Because resources cannot be returned at each layer boundary, more blocks may remain held by requests while asynchronous loads and request execution progress. This reduces reusable HBM and limits concurrency. To realize layerwise reclamation, P/D handoff, consumption acknowledgement, and pool reclamation must use matching layerwise boundaries. Changing only pooling or only P/D disaggregation to layerwise is insufficient: without matching handoff granularity, Decode cannot confirm that a layer has finished consuming its data and release the corresponding block. **This RFC therefore proposes layerwise KV pooling and layerwise P/D disaggregation as a coordinated design, with later-group loading pipelined against current-group computation.** ## Goals and Non-Goals ### Goals - Improve effective HBM utilization and runnable-request capacity in high-hit-rate, long-context workloads. - Define matching layerwise data handoff, consumption acknowledgement, and block-reclamation lifecycles for pooling and P/D disaggregation. - Reduce exposed KV-loading time through grouped block reuse and loading-computation overlap. - Evaluate the end-to-end effects of hit rate, concurrency, and the coordinated layerwise design with reproducible metrics. ### Non-Goals - Change the KV-cache content format or model-computation semantics. The proposal does define lifecycle agreements needed for layerwise handoff, consumption acknowledgement, and block reclamation. - Treat performance results from one workload as guarantees for all models or hardware. ## Problem Analysis The current issues span two related areas: **the pooled-block lifecycle** and **the layerwise P/D data path**. The available analysis identifies the following problems: 1. Non-layerwise asynchronous scheduling can delay block reclamation, leaving more blocks held by requests and preventing timely HBM reuse. 2. Although layerwise execution provides the basis for per-layer processing, grouped KV reuse and HBM-block reclamation are still insufficient or delayed. 3. CPU-side preparation and redundant lookups add overhead to the per-layer path. 4. H2D operations may contend with AlltoAllV and reduce communication performance. ## Proposed Design ### Architecture Modules The proposal consists of two cooperating modules connected by a shared layerwise lifecycle. This RFC establishes their architectural boundaries and responsibilities; detailed APIs, state machines, and implementation mechanisms remain open for follow-up design. The current situation is as follows： Our plans about layerwise D2D is as follows: This plan can promptly release a large number of blocks. #### Layerwise Pooling Module - Organizes and manages grouped KV blocks at layerwise granularity. - Returns a group to the pool after consumption completes and makes its blocks available for subsequent groups. - Tracks group availability and lifecycle so a block is not reused while a transfer or computation still depends on it. - **To be specified:** group granularity, pool metadata, allocation and reclamation interfaces, concurrent access, and state synchronization. #### Layerwise P/D Disaggregation Module https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62504 - Coordinates the provision of KV groups by Prefill and their receipt and consumption by Decode at layerwise granularity. - Provides per-layer readiness and consumption-completion boundaries so the pooling module can safely reclaim the corresponding blocks. - Supports pipelined loading of later groups alongside computation on the current group, including waiting or backpressure when data is not ready. - **To be specified:** P/D handoff interface, ready/consumed signals, data-ownership boundaries, cancellation and error handling, and cross-process synchronization. #### Module Interaction 1. The P/D module requests or receives a KV group and advances the corresponding layer computation when the data is ready. 2. After Decode finishes consuming the group, the P/D module notifies the pooling module that the group has reached its reclamation boundary. 3. The pooling module reclaims and reuses the blocks. The P/D module can then continue with subsequent groups, forming a loading-computation pipeline. These steps describe the logical architecture and do not prescribe a specific transport backend, API, or synchronization primitive. Those details can be added during interface design. ### Design Principles 1. **Use a consistent layerwise granularity.** The pooling unit, P/D transfer unit, consumption acknowledgement, and reclamation unit must align. 2. **Define block ownership and lifecycle.** Specify when Prefill publishes a layer's KV, when Decode receives it, when consumption completes, and when the underlying block may be reused. 3. **Reuse grouped KV blocks.** Manage KV in groups suited to transfer, computation, and reclamation. Return consumed blocks promptly for reuse by later groups. The group size should balance management overhead, transfer efficiency, and reclamation opportunities. 4. **Pipeline loading and computation.** Prepare or load a later group while the current group is being computed. Use explicit ready/consumed dependencies to control visibility and reuse, keeping loading waits off the critical path where possible. 5. **Optimize for end-to-end results.** Group reuse, layerwise handoff, and synchronization can add scheduling or control overhead. Evaluate these costs together with HBM savings, loading coverage, and concurrency. ### Optimization Areas 1. **Grouped block reuse and timely reclamation:** Divide KV cache into independently managed groups. Reclaim a group's blocks after consumption and reuse them for later groups, lowering per-request HBM usage and increasing concurrency. 2. **Loading-computation overlap:** Pipeline prefetch/loading of KV groups with computation on the current group. When loading is not hidden, identify whether the cause is transfer bandwidth, CPU preparation, scheduling gaps, or resource contention. 3. **Reduce per-layer preparation time:** Find serial work and repeated operations in the layerwise preparation path and shorten CPU-side critical-path time. 4. **Avoid redundant lookups:** Reduce repeated cache-key lookups and overlap necessary lookup work with other stages where possible. 5. **Address H2D and AlltoAllV interference:** Measure contention and adjust execution timing or concurrency so H2D loading does not unnecessarily delay AlltoAllV. ## Reported Results For Agent workloads with cache hit rates above 90%, the final layerwise coordinated design was reported to outperform the non-layerwise design: | Metric | Workload and baseline | Reported improvement | |---|---|---:| | TTFT | Agent, >90% hit rate; layerwise coordinated design vs. non-layerwise | About 40% better | | Aggregate throughput | Agent, >90% hit rate; layerwise coordinated design vs. non-layerwise | About 20% higher | Earlier material also reported about a 3% performance regression for a layerwise workload at a 95% hit rate, with some optimizations not yet integrated. This is an intermediate result from a different stage; its metric and baseline were not specified, so it should not be compared directly with the final results above. Reproducing the reported gains requires the model, hardware, hit-rate definition, request set, concurrency, measurement methodology, and run count. ## Evaluation Plan Compare the coordinated design with the baseline using the same model, hardware, input lengths, and request-arrival pattern. Cover: - **Hit rates:** include low-hit, 90%, and 95% operating points. - **Concurrency:** single-request and 24-request cases, plus intermediate levels to identify saturation. - **Input length:** include the 140K-token case and record the actual token-length distribution. - **Metrics:** throughput, request-latency percentiles, TTFT, TPOT, peak and average HBM usage, runnable-request count, KV-loading time, the fraction of loading covered by computation, and pipeline gaps between groups. - **Resource contention:** record H2D and AlltoAllV timings and distinguish CPU preparation, P/D handoff, device copies, and model computation. - **Ablations:** compare no layerwise pooling, pooling only, layerwise P/D handoff only, the coordinated design, and per-layer preparation optimizations to isolate each contribution. Record software versions, model, hardware, parallel configuration, cache capacity, request set, warmup, run count, and metric definitions for each experiment. ## Risks and Trade-Offs - Synchronous reclamation can improve HBM reuse, but reclamation must wait until device-side asynchronous users have completed. - Grouped reuse can reduce cache capacity requirements, but may add management complexity and data movement; measure the end-to-end effect. - H2D/AlltoAllV scheduling may depend on hardware and communication topology and should be validated across target configurations. ## Open Questions 1. In the 140K-token, 95%-hit, 24-request result, does the reported ~50% performance drop refer to throughput or latency? How is the single-request baseline defined? 2. Does “about 40% TTFT improvement” mean TTFT latency is reduced by 40%? 3. What is the P/D handoff unit (a layer, layer group, or another unit), and where are the ready/consumed signals and block-ownership transition points? 4. After Decode consumes a layer, which resource is reclaimed: the local HBM block, a shared pooled resource, or both? Which asynchronous operations must complete first? 5. How should KV groups be formed (by layer, layer group, token/block count, or transfer batch), and what prefetch/buffering policy should be used? 6. Which profiler evidence shows H2D-induced AlltoAllV degradation, and which hardware configurations are in scope? 7. What metric, baseline, and set of changes correspond to the earlier ~3% regression result? ## References - Related discussion: [RFC: Improving MooncakeConnector](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/60523), which includes layerwise and pooling integration in its broader roadmap. This proposal focuses on the coordinated layerwise lifecycle and performance requirements for high-hit-rate Agent workloads.

title: [RFC]: PD disaggregation + RL lifecycle (pause, sleep, abort) tracking
author: aoshen02
body:
### Motivation.

RL training on PD disaggregation pauses, sleeps, aborts and resets the cache around every weight update. On main (`ce49c47`), only 8 of 27 lifecycle cases pass with MooncakeConnector on GB300. The rest block a pause for 480 s, wedge D, or return 500.

**Tracker:** https://claude.ai/artifact/5yU9HihNDSW86B1oZFL2mc


### Proposed Change.

Merge in this order:

- [x] #59625 Mooncake sleep mode
- [x] #60572 Drain async KV loads in a wait pause
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#86 Answer every pull and free dropped transfers promptly (R1–R3)
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#87 Release transfer-held KV before a cache reset (R4)
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#88 Stop the decode stream when its prefill fails (R5)
- [ ] aoshen02/vllm#104 Let P recompute KV that a cache reset dropped (optional, like SGLang's rebootstrap)

The fork PRs will be opened here one at a time. With all of them, the matrix passes 27 of 27.

Related: #59055 (sleep-mode memory).

title: [RFC]: Improve MTP configuration warning
author: nfm-corti
body:
### Motivation.

Hi,

currently, the MTP warning is rather aggressive:
```
(APIServer pid=1) WARNING 10-20 07:22:23 [speculative.py:1375] Enabling num_speculative_tokens > 1
will run multiple times of forward on same MTP layer,which may result in lower acceptance rate
```

Most production deployments will run with `MTP >= 3` and more typically `MTP = 5`. This is even more true considering that this is what many of the official vLLM recipes recommend. 

### Proposed Change.

Having a warning that highlights a risk without concrete recommendations on what to do, feels like an unnecessary papercut. I have a few ideas an would like to know what people think:
1. Reduce the level to `INFO`
1. Improve the message to point at `https://recipes.vllm.ai/` and to mention the draft acceptance rate metric with a target between 60 - 80%.
1. If we keep warning as the level, increase the threshold to `5`
