title: [RFC]: Preserve output distribution under structured-output + speculative decoding
author: yzong-rh
body:
### Motivation.

#### Background

In structured-output + speculative decoding, `StructuredOutputManager` handles draft tokens in three
steps:

1. `validate_tokens` checks a draft sequence without committing grammar state and trims it to its grammar-valid prefix
2. `grammar_bitmask` builds a vocabulary mask for every draft + bonus positions without committing grammar state
3. `accept_tokens` commits the verified token to the persistent grammar state

The timing of draft validation depends on scheduling mode:

```
Synchronous scheduling

step N-1:   schedule step N-1
            sample step N-1 and retrieve drafts for step N
            accept_tokens(step N-1 output)
            validate_tokens(step N drafts)
step N:     schedule step N with validated drafts
            grammar_bitmask(step N drafts)
            sample step N with bitmask and retrieve drafts for step N+1
            accept_tokens(step N output)
            validate_tokens(step N+1 drafts)
...
```

```
Asynchronous scheduling

step N-1:   schedule step N-1
step N:     schedule step N with placeholder drafts
            sample step N-1 and retrieve drafts for step N
            accept_tokens(step N-1 output)
            validate_tokens(step N drafts)
            grammar_bitmask(step N drafts)
step N+1:   schedule step N+1 with placeholder drafts
            sample step N with bitmask and retrieve drafts for step N+1
            accept_tokens(step N output)
            validate_tokens(step N+1 drafts)
            grammar_bitmask(step N+1 drafts)
...
```

In synchronous scheduling, validation of step N drafts occurs before scheduling step N. So step N is scheduled with validated drafts.
In asynchronous scheduling, step N is scheduled with placeholder drafts before the drafts for step N are retrieved and validated.
Therefore, step N is scheduled with unvalidated placeholder drafts.

#### Issue

See #60451.
The current lifecycle changes the output distribution under spec decode when structured outputs are enabled.

Suppose we have draft tokens:
```
[valid, invalid, ?, ?]
```

`validate_tokens` truncates it to:
```
[valid]
```

Rejection sampling would correctly sample `valid` but treat `invalid` as a bonus token instead of a rejected token.
It would sample the `invalid` position from the target (verifier model) distribution instead of the residual distribution `max(target - draft, 0)`.

### Proposed change.

#### 1. Preserve the first rejected draft for the rejection sampler

Given,
```
[valid, invalid, ?, ?]
```
make `validate_tokens` truncate to:
```
[valid, invalid]
```
instead of
```
[valid]
```

The rejection sampler will consequently treat the `invalid` position as a rejection (thanks to the grammar bitmask disallowing `invalid`) instead of a bonus position.

Note this creates a small performance regression on the sync scheduling because the target model verifies one more token than before.

#### Optional 2. Do not validate drafts on the asynchronous scheduling path

Calling `validate_tokens` to trim draft tokens on the asynchronous scheduling path is redundant. We've already scheduled the request with unvalidated tokens.

Removing the `validate_tokens` call removes reasoning-end detection and a temporary grammar-state advance and rollback.

#### Implementation and alternatives

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61557 implements the proposed changes:
- Rename `validate_tokens` to `trim_spec_tokens` and ensure the invalid token isn't truncated (change 1)
- Remove the `validate_tokens` call on the async scheduling path (change 2)
- Fix grammar backends to ensure `accept_tokens` remains transactional -- avoid an extra `validate_tokens` call inside `grammar_bitmask`

Alternative: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/60690
- Use `SchedulerOutput.num_invalid_spec_tokens` to ensure the invalid token isn't discarded (change 1)
- Add `Request.num_invalid_spec_tokens` for the sync scheduling path such that `num_invalid_spec_tokens` computed by `validate_tokens` on step N is available for step N + 1

Rejected Alternative: remove `validate_tokens` from both the sync and async scheduling
- Technically we achieve both change 1 and 2 if we don't validate draft tokens at all
- However, this leads to a statistically significant performance regression on the sync scheduling path.

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

cc @simon-veitner-redhat @tomasruizt @vadiklyutiy @arpera 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Fuse DSpark confidence-head GEMV into a single TileLang kernel
author: panpan0000
body:
### Motivation.

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62840 contains an initial implementation of the proposal described in this RFC.

## Bottom line

One new TileLang kernel, ~113 lines, fuses DSpark's confidence head (`cat + cast + GEMV + sigmoid`) into **one CUDA launch, one CUDA-graph node, zero fp32 temporary** per decode step. Median kernel-latency speedup vs `torch.compile`: **1.92× on RTX 5090 (SM120)** and **1.90× on H200 (SM90)**; real-checkpoint A/B under greedy decode produces **0/30 divergent outputs** on both GPUs. TPOT-level gain is < 0.05 % — the value is on the mechanism (launch count, graph nodes, activation-memory traffic), not end-to-end. DeepInfer (DeepSeek's own engine) already ships an equivalent fused kernel via `AcceptRatePredictor` and the same PDL trick; this is a port-with-FP32-weight.

## Summary

Adaptive speculative decoding in vLLM (the DSpark drafter, gated by `--speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","enable_adaptive_verification":true,...}'`) runs a small **confidence head** once per drafted block to decide how many tokens to submit to the verifier:

```
p_accept = sigmoid( ( [ hidden_state ; markov_embed ] @ W ) / temperature )
   hidden_state     (n, H)        bf16
   markov_embed     (n, r)        bf16
   W                (H + r, 1)    fp32   # ReplicatedLinear(params_dtype=fp32)
   p_accept         (n,)          fp32
```

Per draft step, this is **four CUDA launches** — `torch.cat`, `.float()` cast, cuBLAS GEMV, `.sigmoid()` — plus one `(n, H + r)` fp32 temporary that bypasses CUDA-graph memory reuse on the decode fast path. The GEMV itself is tiny (`H + r ≈ 7 200`); on an RTX 5090 the four launches cost ~117 µs of CPU-side scheduling and ~14–45 MB of activation traffic per call, for a useful answer that's about 2 µs long.

DeepInfer — DeepSeek's own inference engine — ships an equivalent fused kernel in its open-source DSpark drafter. The kernel is 60 lines of TileLang ([`dflash.py:12-72`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/layers/tilelang_ops/cuda/dflash.py#L12-L72)) wired into their `AcceptRatePredictor` ([`heads.py:37`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/models/v4_modules/heads.py#L37)), and uses PDL (`T.pdl_sync()`) to overlap with the preceding GEMV. The same file contains another small `dflash_input_store_tl` fusion, which suggests DeepInfer's motivation is systematically flattening small ops on the DSpark path — confidence-head fusion is one piece of a larger pattern, and the open-source repo does not quote a per-kernel TPOT delta. They cast the confidence weight to bf16 for tensor-core FMA. vLLM keeps the same weight in FP32 (`params_dtype=torch.float32` in `qwen3_dspark.py:124-131`), so a drop-in port would silently change which draft tokens get accepted.

This RFC proposes **porting the DeepInfer fusion to vLLM while preserving FP32 weight semantics**. We also expect this kernel to be the first of several small DSpark fusion ports (e.g. `dflash_input_store_tl`, `dspark_draft_embed_store_tl`) so the mechanism-level benefit compounds.

## Numbers

Measured on **two GPUs**, one card each (no TP, no DP):

- RTX 5090, SM120 (Blackwell), 32 GB, CUDA 13.0, driver 575 — dev pod.
- NVIDIA H200, SM90, 143 GB HBM3e, CUDA 13.1, driver 590.44.01 — single-card.

vLLM 0.32.0, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, TileLang 0.1.12. Target / drafter for the E2E / A/B runs: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` + `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` (~10 GB total HBM).

### Dispatch gate (when does the fused path actually run)

The kernel is **only** dispatched when **all** of the following hold. Otherwise the call site returns `None` and falls back to the existing PyTorch path (no behavioral change).

| Condition | Required value | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Platform | NVIDIA Hopper (SM90) or later, including consumer Blackwell (SM120) | TileLang's PDL (programmatic dependent launch) is SM90+. |
| `hidden.dtype` | `torch.bfloat16`, CUDA tensor | DSpark contract; the kernel assumes bf16 inputs. |
| `markov.dtype` | `torch.bfloat16`, CUDA tensor | Same. |
| `weight.dtype` | `torch.float32`, CUDA tensor | vLLM keeps fp32 here for determinism — this is the deliberate divergence from DeepInfer's bf16 variant. |
| `(n_embed, markov_rank)` shape | `(7168, 32)` only (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) | Only this shape shows end-to-end benefit on datacenter GPUs in our measurements. Smaller DSpark variants (e.g. Qwen3-4B-DSpark at H=2560, r=256) see parity on consumer GPUs and a regression on H200. |
| `hidden.stride(-1)` | `1` (last-dim contiguous) | Kernel assumes row-major, last-dim unit stride. |
| `markov.stride(-1)` | `1` when `r > 0` | Same. |
| Batch size `n` | `32 ≤ n ≤ 2048` | See "Batch gate rationale" below. |
| `markov_embed.shape[-1]` | `≥ r` (rank parameter) | Compile-time kernel template expects this. |

The dispatch conditions live in `vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/__init__.py:43-83` and are checked at every call. When any one of them fails, the wrapper returns `None` and the caller's PyTorch fallback runs — that fallback is already correct and tested.

### Batch + shape gate rationale

The gate has two pieces: a **V4-Flash-only shape floor** and a **batch size window**.

**Shape floor.** Only `(n_embed = 7168, markov_rank = 32)` is admitted to the fused path. This is the DeepSeek-V4-Flash DSpark production shape — the configuration DeepInfer designed and validated the fusion for on datacenter GPUs. Smaller DSpark variants currently in-tree (e.g. Qwen3-4B-DSpark at H=2560, r=256):

- See **parity** fused vs PyTorch on consumer (RTX 5090 / SM120) at every batch we tested (sequential: 5.01 s vs 5.02 s; batched at B ∈ {32, 128, 256}: ratios 0.97×–0.99× — see "Batch sweep" below).
- See a **~42–58 % wall-clock regression** on H200 SM90 in the sequential setting (see "Systematic wall-clock puzzle" below), driven by ~93 µs per-call TileLang dispatch overhead on Hopper.
- Contribute ≤ 0.1 % of decode kernel time even when fused, so the kernel is structurally too small to recover its dispatch overhead at these shapes.

For those variants the right thing is the existing PyTorch fallback (which is free under `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` cudagraph capture), not a fused custom op. Rather than ask reviewers to audit a kernel they'll never exercise, we hard-limit the dispatch to the V4-Flash shape and revisit when / if smaller variants become production-relevant.

**Batch floor and ceiling.** `n < 32` is declined because the per-call TileLang dispatch overhead (~93 µs on Hopper; less on Blackwell) dominates the kernel's savings at tiny batch. `n > 2048` is declined as a sanity bound; the benchmark sweep covers up to `n = 8192` and the kernel is correct across the entire range, but matching realistic DSpark block-size × concurrency stays well below 1024.

### Batch sweep evidence on RTX 5090

Sequential `llm.generate()` per-prompt on the 4B drafter previously showed parity fused vs baseline (5.01 s vs 5.02 s). To test whether **larger batches** break the tie (since fused kernel savings should grow with `n` while TileLang Python dispatch overhead is fixed), we ran an end-to-end sweep against `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` + `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` with `num_speculative_tokens=7`, greedy sampling, on one RTX 5090:

| Concurrent requests B | fused (s) | baseline (s) | fused / baseline | per-req fused (ms) | per-req baseline (ms) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32  | 0.414 | 0.422 | **0.98×** | 12.9 | 13.2 |
| 128 | 0.817 | 0.839 | **0.97×** |  6.4 |  6.6 |
| 256 | 1.445 | 1.467 | **0.99×** |  5.6 |  5.7 |

(The B=8 row is excluded as a warmup artifact — fused runs first and pays JIT + first-replay costs that baseline then misses. B=32/128/256 are steady-state.)

Interpretation: at every production-realistic batch the two paths are within noise on the 4B shape. Combined with the H200 regression at the same shape and the observation above that the kernel contributes ≤ 0.1 % of decode time here, the fused path **cannot pay for itself** at the 4B shape on current hardware. That is the empirical basis for the shape floor.

### Micro-benchmark, vs `torch.compile` baseline

Per-implementation latency, `n × H=7168, r=32` (dominant DSpark decode shape), 200 iters each. Reproduce: `python benchmarks/kernels/dspark/bench_confidence.py` on the PR branch. The fused dispatch gate applies only up to `n = 2048`; numbers beyond are kernel-capability visibility.

| GPU | Shapes | Median latency speedup | Min / max | Production shape band (n ≤ 2048) | Median err_ratio vs `compiled` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| RTX 5090 (SM120) | 36 | **1.92×** | 0.72× / 3.56× | 1.72× – 2.77× | **0.610** |
| NVIDIA H200 (SM90) | 20 | **1.90×** | 0.39× / 5.15× | 0.39× – 2.97× | **0.695** |

H200's wider range: small-shape launch overhead is more costly on Hopper; above `n=128` H200 pulls ahead of 5090, reaching 5.15× at `n=8192, H=7168, r=32` where HBM3e bandwidth favors the fused kernel.

### What changes per decode step

| Quantity | main (PyTorch) | fused (this PR) | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| CUDA launches along the path | 4 | 1 | **−3** |
| CUDA-graph nodes along the path | 4 | 1 | **−3** |
| fp32 temporary per call | 14 – 45 MB (n ≤ 2048) | **0 B** | 100 % |

### Engine-level dispatch smoke (`--load-format dummy`)

**Takeaway: the kernel dispatches into the real engine path, launches exactly once per drafted step, is captured inside CUDA graphs on both GPUs, and contributes well under 0.1 % of total kernel time.**

Real `vllm.LLM(...)` runs against target `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` + draft `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7`, adaptive verification enabled, on both GPUs. Traced with vLLM's worker-side profiler (`llm.start_profile()`/`stop_profile()`; see [docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/contributing/profiling.html)):

| Metric | RTX 5090 (SM120) | NVIDIA H200 (SM90) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `confidence_head_fused_tilelang_kernel` launches in a 64-token decode | **64** | **64** |
| Launches with CUDA graph id set | **64 / 64** | **64 / 64** |
| Median per-call kernel time | 1.70 µs | 1.79 µs |
| p99 per-call kernel time | 1.92 µs | 1.98 µs |
| Total across all confidence-head calls | 0.109 ms | 0.115 ms |
| Total decode kernel time | 375 ms | 227 ms |
| Share of total kernel time | **0.03 %** | **0.05 %** |

The kernel contributes well under 0.1 % of decode kernel time on both GPUs, which is the point — the value is mechanism-level (launch count, graph nodes, activation traffic), not an end-to-end TPOT percentage.

### Production-scale TPOT

Production DSpark shapes (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ≈ 300 GB packed; V4-Pro ≈ 880 GB) require multi-GPU H200/H20 per-replica, so they're not covered here. DeepInfer does not publish a per-kernel TPOT delta either. If multi-H200 capacity becomes available we will land TPOT numbers as a follow-up comment.

### Proposed Change.

Port the DeepInfer fusion pattern into vLLM, with the FP32-weight delta and standard vLLM wrapping contracts.

**Code** (in [PR #62840](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62840)):

- New TileLang kernel in `vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/tilelang_kernels.py` — one launch, fp32 accumulator, in-kernel sigmoid. 113 lines.
- Wrap in `VllmJitKernel` (`vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/tilelang.py`) mirroring `kernels/mhc/` — precompiles at engine JIT warmup so shape-specialized builds are ready before first request.
- Register as `torch.ops.vllm.dspark_confidence_tilelang` via `direct_register_custom_op` so CUDA-graph capture sees one opaque node.
- Call-site dispatch in two `compute_confidence()` methods: `vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_dspark.py` and `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/dspark.py`. Caller falls through to the existing PyTorch path on any gate condition failure — no user-visible behavior change.
- **Fallback observability**: the dispatch wrapper logs a one-line `logger.debug` per unique decline reason on first occurrence; disabled by default. A metric counter is not added in this PR to keep scope aligned with existing kernel integrations.

**Behavioral consistency check (real DSpark checkpoint, fused on vs off)**

The kernel is not bitwise-identical to the PyTorch path — fused uses an fp32 accumulator + in-kernel sigmoid while the fallback goes through bf16 intermediates. So we checked what matters for behavior: **does flipping the kernel on change which draft tokens are accepted, and does that change the generated text?**

Setup: real `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` target + real `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7` drafter, `enable_adaptive_verification=True`, greedy sampling (temperature=0, seed=42), `max_tokens=64`. 30 diverse prompts (reasoning / code / writing / math / knowledge), repeated on both GPUs (SM120 and SM90).

| GPU | Branch | Wall-clock (30 prompts × 64 tok) | Identical outputs to fallback? |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| RTX 5090 (SM120) | fused | 5.01 s | — |
| RTX 5090 (SM120) | baseline | 5.02 s | — |
| NVIDIA H200 (SM90) | fused | 4.55 s | — |
| NVIDIA H200 (SM90) | baseline | 3.20 s | — |
| — | **divergent prompts** | — | **0 / 30 on both GPUs** |

All 30 prompts' output text **and** output-token counts are **bitwise identical** between fused and baseline on both GPUs. Per-call fused kernel time is ~1.7 µs (5090) / 1.79 µs (H200) — the kernel itself is ~µs-and-change per decode step.

**Systematic wall-clock puzzle on H200** (flagged for review / future repro): 30 sequential single-prompt `llm.generate()` calls, each 64 tokens, measured twice on the H200:

| Branch | Run 1 | Run 2 | Mean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fused | 4.55 s | 5.35 s | **4.95 s** |
| baseline | 3.20 s | 3.38 s | **3.29 s** |

Fused is consistently ~50 % slower on H200 in this shape. On RTX 5090 the same script/branch policy yields fused 5.01 s vs baseline 5.02 s (within noise). Causes we've ruled out:
- The kernel itself: ~0.1 ms per prompt of 64 confidence-head launches.
- cuLaunchKernel count: identical (1024 in both branches per trace — PyTorch fallback is also captured into the same CUDA graph).

Possible cause, not verified: per-call TileLang custom-op dispatch overhead is higher on Hopper than Blackwell (different CUDA driver / cudaGraph launch path). **Consequence of the new gate**: this regression is no longer reachable — the H200-4B shape is now rejected by the dispatcher (`(2560, 256) != (7168, 32)`) and falls back to PyTorch. The regression could in principle still bite at the V4-Flash shape if H200 dispatch overhead is worse than we think, but at that shape the kernel's savings scale with `n` and the production batch floor of 32 gives headroom. We have not yet isolated whether Hopper-specific dispatch cost at the V4-Flash shape + batch >= 32 stays within budget; landing a multi-H200 TPOT reproduction remains a follow-up.

## Risks

- **Behavioral consistency at the accept gate** (fp32 accumulator + in-kernel sigmoid vs bf16 intermediates). Addressed by the real-checkpoint experiment above: 0/30 divergent on both SM120 and SM90.
- **TileLang coverage.** v0.1.12 emits `T.exp` via libdevice; some shapes produce ptxas warnings on older drivers. Mitigation: the PyTorch fallback stays in-tree.
- **Small-batch slow case — now gated out.** At `n = 1` the fused kernel is 0.72× cuBLAS (launch-bound); the new gate declines dispatch at `n < 32` so this regime is unreachable in production. H200 sequential-mode regression is also no longer reachable on the 4B shape because that shape is rejected by the shape floor (see "Batch + shape gate rationale").

## Prior work

| Where | Contrast |
|---|---|
| DeepInfer [`dflash.py:12-72`](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/main/deepinfer/model_executor/layers/tilelang_ops/cuda/dflash.py#L12-L72) | Same fusion, bf16 weight; we keep fp32. |
| [#41536](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/41536) fused mHC post_pre | Same shape of problem: fusing several small launches on the decode fast path. Their kernel handles ~5 % of decode time (5.8 % TPOT claim); ours handles ~0.03 % (no TPOT claim). Same vLLM-side wrapping: `TileLang` + `VllmJitKernel` + `direct_register_custom_op`. |
| [#43905](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/43905) move mHC to `kernels/mhc/` | Same kernel-module layout (`vllm/model_executor/kernels/dspark/`). |
| [#47456](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47456) JIT warmup infra RFC | Our `VllmJitKernel` subclass uses the warmup contract this RFC introduces. |

## Open question for reviewers

**Is 30-prompt greedy behavioral identity enough to gate the numerics risk?** We have: (a) 29-shape synthetic tolerance tests, (b) 36-shape (5090) + 20-shape (H200) sweeps vs `torch.compile`, (c) 30 real-checkpoint greedy prompts producing identical strings on two GPU architectures. Happy to land the script that produced the 30/30 result in-tree (under `tests/` or `benchmarks/`).

### Benefits

1. **−3 CUDA-graph nodes per decode step.** Faster capture and replay; matters more as DSpark `block_size` and `num_speculative_tokens` scale.
2. **Zero fp32 activation memory traffic on the decode path.** Removes the per-step temporary that CUDA-graph memory must recycle.
3. **Matches numerics DeepSeek vetted in production.** Same fused math, same `AcceptRatePredictor` shape contract — not a guess.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks from posting, or until at least one maintainer of `vllm/model_executor/kernels/` or `vllm/models/deepseek_v4/` has responded.

### CC List.

(author) @panpan0000 — happy to pull in DSpark / MHC maintainers once initial feedback lands.

### Any Other Things.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to draft the kernel, tests, benchmark, and parts of this RFC. I reviewed the code, ran the tests (29/29), and re-checked the language.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Context-length-bounded FULL decode CUDA graphs in Model Runner V2
author: eppaneamd
body:
### Motivation.

Model Runner V2 captures every FULL decode CUDA graph with attention metadata `max_seq_len = max_model_len`, so the graph is valid for any context it replays. Any host-side decision made from `max_seq_len` during capture is therefore made for the longest context and frozen into the graph.

Some models skip work when every context in a step is short, but cannot do so in FULL decode graphs:

- GLM-5-Next's sparse indexer: when all contexts fit `index_topk` (2048 on GLM-5.3-Flash), its top-k is every causal token, so the q projection, head-weight projection, q quantization, paged-MQA logits and top-k are dead work.
- DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1's indexers already skip this work in eager steps, but guard the shortcut with `not torch.cuda.is_current_stream_capturing()` (#52492), so FULL decode graphs never take it.

The rule from #52492 and #59709, no capture-time shortcut that a replay can invalidate, is right. What is missing is a FULL graph whose capture-time `max_seq_len` is smaller and still bounds every replay.

### Proposed Change.

1. **Declare.** A module sets `cudagraph_seq_len_bound: int | None`. The runner collects the distinct values below `max_model_len` from `model.modules()`.
2. **Capture.** Each FULL decode graph gets one copy per bound, captured with `max_seq_len = bound` in every backend's metadata.
3. **Dispatch.** `BatchExecutionDescriptor` gains `max_seq_len`, matched like `max_query_len`. A decode step whose contexts all fit a bound replays the copy (tightest first); any other step replays the default graph. The step's bound comes from the CPU arrays `prepare_inputs` already uses (no device read).
4. **Rule for modules.** Skip only work that `max_seq_len <= bound` makes dead, decided from the metadata the module receives, and only while a FULL graph is being captured.
   - Not in a PIECEWISE capture: that capture runs on the dummy batch's metadata.
   - Not in eager steps, including the warm-up run before each capture: the warm-up must compile and autotune everything its capture runs. Otherwise a cold start can compile or autotune inside the capture, which fails (seen in the reference implementation's first commit under breakable `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`).

Invariant: **the `max_seq_len` a FULL graph is captured with is an upper bound on every context of every batch it replays** (`max_model_len` for default graphs, the bound for copies). Host decisions made from it at capture hold for every replay.

Scope: off under PCP/DCP; opt-out `CompilationConfig.cudagraph_specialize_seq_len`. PIECEWISE-only deployments, mixed FULL graphs and micro-batched (DBO) graphs get no copies. Steps that cross the bound mid-request switch to the default graph.

#### Evidence

- Reference implementation: #63758 (mechanism + GLM-5-Next's indexer). GLM-5.3-Flash MXFP4, 2x MI355X, TP2, one image per request:
  - `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`: output throughput +2.32 % (SE 0.44 pp) at concurrency 16-64, +12.3 % at 4. Text rows that cross or exceed the bound are within noise. GSM8K unchanged. Cost: one extra graph per capture size and bound (graph memory 0.79 → 1.07 GiB per rank, KV cache −0.03 %).
  - Breakable `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`: +4.50 % (SE 1.92 pp) at concurrency 16-64.
- Second user, a follow-up PR stacked on the reference implementation: DeepSeek-V4 / V4.1 (V4.1-Flash gets bounds 512 and 1025 from compress ratios 1 and 2).
- Prior art: SGLang selects a dense or sparse DSA decode graph on `max_kv_len <= index_topk` (`python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/graph_variants.py`).

#### Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Why not |
|---|---|
| Kernels read a device-side bound and exit early (or graph conditional nodes) | The q-side GEMMs are library GEMMs with no such predicate; every kernel on every platform would need it. |
| Eager segment around the indexer inside FULL graphs | One graph break per sparse-attention layer (not measured). |
| `ForwardContext` flag set during bounded captures | Repeats what `max_seq_len` carries; every forward-context producer must leave it unset correctly. |
| Model-interface method or attention-builder attribute | One declaration per model class that re-derives per-layer facts; a shared builder would capture copies for models that skip nothing. |
| Serve with `max_model_len <= bound` | No code, but only for deployments capped at the bound. |

#### Open questions

1. **#62749** records FULL decode metadata builds keyed on batch shape, with `max_seq_len = max_model_len`. A step sent to a copy would match a build recorded for the default graph. Whichever lands second either adds `max_seq_len` to that key or keeps bounded steps on the eager build. Which is preferred?
2. **DP.** The bound is per rank, not in the DP sync: a copy has its default graph's token and request counts, which is all ranks agree on, and `max_seq_len`-dependent work is already rank-local in eager steps. A max-over-ranks row would make ranks switch together, at the cost of one long-context rank disabling the copies for all. Untested with DP > 1.
3. **Default on or opt-in.** Default on in the implementation, like `cudagraph_specialize_lora`.

### Feedback Period.

At least one week. The reference implementation stays a draft until then.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Not measured: NVIDIA, TP 1/4/8, DP > 1. Model Runner V1 graphs are unchanged. A search of open PRs found none that keys decode graphs on context length.

title: [RFC]: Disaggregated pre/post-processing for pooling IO Processor plugins
author: kon-pap
body:
### Motivation.

IO Processor plugins (`vllm/plugins/io_processors`) allow pooling models to accept and return arbitrary data. One example is TerraTorch with Prithvi-EO-2.0 for geospatial segmentation. For these models, `IOProcessor.pre_process()` (decoding, tiling and normalising large rasters) and `post_process()` (stitching tiles back and encoding the output) are CPU-heavy. They often take longer than the forward pass itself.

Today all three stages run in the `vllm serve` process that owns the GPU. As a result:

- the GPU waits while pre-processing and post-processing run on the CPU;
- adding CPU capacity for processing means adding more GPU replicas;
- the work cannot be placed on cheaper GPU-less nodes.

vLLM already separates rendering from inference for generative models (`vllm launch render`, `scale_out/render` and `scale_out/derender`). It also already moves data between instances for P/D with `KVTransferConfig` and for encoder disaggregation with `ECTransferConfig`. This RFC proposes applying the same two ideas to pooling with IO Processor plugins:

- pre-processing and post-processing run on GPU-less render instances that scale on their own;
- the GPU instance only runs inference;
- tensors move between instances through a pluggable connector, and requests carry only references to them.

**Measurements** (TerraTorch Prithvi-EO-2.0 segmentation, using the implementation described below):

- **Inference is a minority of request time.** On a monolithic deployment, inference takes only 11–31% of end-to-end time. Pre-processing accounts for 31–37% and post-processing for 33–55%. Inference's share falls as images grow from 1 to 100 tiles.
- **Monolithic deployments saturate early because of CPU/GPU interference** (1 tile per request, 16 CPU workers in both setups):

  | At 80 req/s | Monolithic (16 workers) | Disaggregated (8 pre + 8 post) |
  |---|---|---|
  | Throughput | ~45 tiles/s (plateaus at ~40 req/s) | ~79 tiles/s (still scaling) |
  | Mean latency | ~1.7 s | ~0.34 s |
  | GPU utilization | ~45% | ~84% |

### Proposed Change.

All of the following is opt-in. Existing endpoints and default behaviour do not change.

**1. Three-stage request flow**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Router
  participant PRE as Preprocess (vllm launch render)
  participant INF as Inference (vllm serve)
  participant POST as Postprocess (vllm launch render)

  S->>PRE: POST /pooling/preprocess (IOProcessorRequest)
  PRE-->>PRE: IOProcessor.pre_process + render
  PRE-->>PRE: put_data(mm item), put_metadata(request state)
  PRE->>S: [GeneratePoolingRequest{data_ref, metadata_ref}]
  S->>INF: POST /pooling/inference (one per item)
  INF-->>PRE: get_data(data_ref)
  INF-->>INF: encode()
  INF-->>INF: put_data(output tensor)
  INF->>S: GeneratePoolingResponse{output_data_ref, metadata_ref}
  S->>POST: POST /pooling/postprocess (all responses)
  POST-->>INF: get_data(output_data_ref)
  POST-->>PRE: get_metadata(metadata_ref)
  POST-->>POST: update_request_metadata + IOProcessor.post_process
  POST->>S: IOProcessorResponse
```

Endpoints:

| Endpoint | Server | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /pooling/preprocess` | `vllm launch render` | Runs `IOProcessor.pre_process()` and rendering. Returns one `GeneratePoolingRequest` per item. |
| `POST /pooling/inference` | `vllm serve` | Fetches the pre-processed `MultiModalKwargsItem` and runs `encode()`. Returns a `GeneratePoolingResponse` that references the output tensor. |
| `POST /pooling/postprocess` | `vllm launch render` | Fetches the outputs and request metadata, then runs `IOProcessor.post_process()`. |

The router that fans requests out across the three stages lives outside vLLM. We have a working proxy implementation.

**2. Protocol: references, not payloads**

New models: `DataRef` (`object_id` plus `locator`), `MetadataRef`, `GeneratePoolingRequest`/`GeneratePoolingResponse` and `PostProcessPoolingRequest`.

- The `object_id` of the pre-processed item reuses its `mm_hash`. The inference output is stored as `<mm_hash>:<served_model_name>:output`.
- Data is keyed by object and metadata by request, so one data object can serve requests whose metadata differs.
- When no connector is configured, the same endpoints carry the payloads inline as base64 msgpack. Stages can therefore be split without shared storage, which is useful for debugging and small deployments.

**3. `IOTransferConfig` / `--io-transfer-config`**

This mirrors `KVTransferConfig` and `ECTransferConfig`:

- `io_connector` selects the connector;
- `io_role` is one of `io_producer`, `io_consumer` or `io_both`;
- `io_connector_extra_config` holds connector-specific settings;
- `io_connector_module_path` loads an out-of-tree connector.

**4. IO connector framework (`vllm/distributed/io_transfer`)**

- `IOConnectorBase` defines `put_data`, `get_data`, `cleanup_data`, `put_metadata`, `get_metadata` and `cleanup_metadata`, each with an async variant.
- A lazy-loading factory and process-wide state create the connector once per process, as the EC and KV transfer state modules do. Both servers shut it down on exit.
- On render instances, blocking connector calls run on a dedicated thread pool (`max_io_threads`), so they do not take renderer workers.
- Two reference backends:
  - `IOExampleConnector` uses a shared filesystem, such as a Kubernetes PVC.
  - `IOP2PConnector` uses ZMQ ROUTER/DEALER, is pull-based and sends tensor buffers as zero-copy frames.
- Serialization uses the existing `MsgpackEncoder`/`MsgpackDecoder` and `msgspec`. No new dependencies are added.

**5. IOProcessor plugin hooks**

`get_request_metadata()` and `update_request_metadata()` are added with no-op defaults. Plugins use them to export state saved during `pre_process` (for example tiling layout or geo-referencing) and restore it on a different post-processing instance. Existing plugins need no changes.

**Implementation plan**

A working implementation exists, about 2.6k LOC across six self-contained commits. Depending on feedback, we would split it into a series of PRs:

1. `IOTransferConfig` and the IOProcessor metadata hooks (small, no behaviour change)
2. Disaggregated pooling protocol models and tensor serde
3. IO connector framework with `IOExampleConnector` (`IOP2PConnector` could follow separately)
4. The `/pooling/inference` endpoint
5. `/pooling/preprocess` and `/pooling/postprocess` on the render server, plus docs and an example

Each PR would include unit tests for its part: connector round trips, config validation and the routes with a mock IO processor.

**Open questions for maintainers**

1. Is `vllm/distributed/io_transfer` the right home? Should it share more infrastructure with `ec_transfer`? Both move per-item multimodal data between instances, but the payloads and lifecycles differ.
2. Is it acceptable to add the new routes under `/pooling/*`, or should they live under a scale-out namespace next to `render`/`derender`?
3. Should `IOP2PConnector` be in-tree, or should only the filesystem reference connector ship in-tree, with others loaded through `io_connector_module_path`?
4. How should we cover this in CI? Tests can use the filesystem connector and a dummy IO processor plugin on CPU.

**Current limitations**

- Only full three-stage disaggregation is supported. Partial setups, such as co-locating inference and post-processing, are not.
- Each prompt must contain exactly one `image` item. This is enough for TerraTorch, and other inputs are rejected with a 400 error.
- `IOP2PConnector` still needs performance tuning under high load.



### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

title: [RFC] Signature-driven JIT warmup v2 for Triton kernels
author: LopezCastroRoberto
body:
Builds on #47456 and #49349 (JIT warmup v1).

## Summary

Today, a Triton kernel joins JIT warmup by being wrapped, together with its warmup inputs, in a `triton_kernel_dispatcher_with_warmup` dispatcher. That works, but it has two costs:

1. there's a lot of boilerplate to register and warm a kernel;
2. the grid logic moves away from the call site.
3. as a result, models are still not fully de-JITified, causing `--jit-monitor-mode error` to fail.

This RFC proposes warmup v2: a Triton-specific contract that removes both. 
* The kernel signature says what to warm.
* (1) Annotations give pointer dtypes, (2) defaults give constants, and (3) the caller passes deployment values to `register_warmup`.
* A small decorator (`@triton_warmup`) covers whatever the signature can't express.

Triton's own engine then turns those values into compile keys, exactly as it does at launch. vLLM's existing `_triton_key_deriver` runs each case through the kernel's Triton binder. 

Launches stay plain `kernel[grid](...)` calls, and the back end is unchanged. Nothing wraps the kernel: `@triton_warmup` returns the same `JITFunction`, and every call goes straight to Triton.

The workflow:

1. **Declare** next to the kernel: annotations, `constexpr` defaults, and `@triton_warmup(...)` only if needed. A pure host launcher can take `@triton_warmup_launcher(...)` instead, and then its kernels need nothing.
2. **Register** where the deployment values live. Registrations made outside an active registry are deferred to the next warmup.
3. **Expand**: at startup, each registration becomes a set of candidate launch arguments (one representative per Triton integer class).
4. **Derive keys**: Triton's binder and `compute_cache_key` map each candidate to a cache key, and duplicates are dropped.
5. **Compile** each key with `kernel.warmup(...)`, in parallel. _No kernel runs_.

Conceptually, a `@triton.jit` kernel is a template that Triton instantiates implicitly on first launch. The new warmup declarations (`Ptr` annotations, decorator entries, `register_warmup` values) act as explicit instantiation: they list the instantiations to compile at startup, and `@triton_warmup` states the constraints between parameters.

As a showcase, we migrate the 17 kernels of #56323 and its partial revert #56654 in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64262 (kernel side: +367/−876 lines). To keep the review focused on the API that kernel authors see, the PR contains only these kernel-side changes. The supporting code and its tests follow once the API is agreed.

## Motivation: Existing Triton contract

Here is `expand_kernel` under the current contract in MAIN:

```python
@triton.jit(do_not_specialize=["replace_from", "replace_to"])
def expand_kernel(
    output_ptr,  # [num_tokens]
    input_ptr,   # [batch_size]
    cu_num_tokens_ptr,  # [batch_size]
    replace_from,
    replace_to,
    MAX_NUM_TOKENS: tl.constexpr,
): ...


def _expand_warmup_inputs() -> dict[str, object]:
    dtype = WarmupChoices(torch.float32, torch.int32, torch.int64)
    data = TritonWarmupTensor(dtype)
    return dict(
        output=data,
        input=data,
        cu_num_tokens=TritonWarmupTensor(torch.int32),
        replace_from=0,
        replace_to=0,
    )


@triton_kernel_dispatcher_with_warmup(
    kernel=expand_kernel, warmup_inputs=_expand_warmup_inputs
)
def _expand(output, input, cu_num_tokens, replace_from, replace_to) -> DispatchSpec:
    return (input.shape[0],), dict(MAX_NUM_TOKENS=MAX_SPEC_LEN)


_expand(expanded_x, x, cu_num_tokens, replace_from, replace_to)  # call site
_expand.register_warmup()  # registration
```

Problems: 
* **Boilerplate.** Every kernel needs a warmup-inputs function, a dispatcher, a registration and a rewritten call site. The argument list is written three times (kernel, warmup inputs, dispatcher), and every derived flag twice (once as a dispatcher expression, once as a warmup choice that must match it). MRV2 also needs `@capture` and `activate()` in its model runner, because speculators are built outside an active registry.

* **Grid away from the call site.** The grid and the `constexprs` live in the dispatcher, so the call site no longer shows how the kernel launches. And the warmup inputs have to be kept in sync with the dispatcher by hand. They drift: the reverted MRV2 warmup #56654 declared `idx_mapping` and `sample_idx_mapping` as `int32`, but both are `int64` at runtime.

One constraint holds throughout: **compile keys must be static**, coming only from declarations and config. Relying on dummy runs would defeat the purpose of de-JIT.

## Scope

This only applies to Triton; CuTeDSL and TileLang keep the existing contract for now. Triton is special because its cache key is a function of the call: pointer dtypes and 16-byte alignment, integer classes, `constexpr` values and launch options. A signature can therefore describe most of its own keys.

The new contract is only a front end. Key derivation (`_triton_key_deriver`), compile-only `kernel.warmup`, parallel `compile_many` and `JitWarmupRegistry` are shared and unchanged from warmup v1. The old dispatcher keeps working, so kernels can migrate one at a time.

Adoption is opt-in per kernel: a kernel that never calls `register_warmup` behaves exactly as today. Nothing here runs on the launch path either. The proposal has two mechanisms beyond plain declarations, and both act only during startup warmup:
- a `register_warmup` method added to Triton's `JITFunction`;
- in the launcher form, a temporary swap of the launcher module's kernel globals.

## Proposed contract

### Kernel form

Here is `expand_kernel` under the new contract:

```python
@triton.jit(do_not_specialize=["replace_from", "replace_to"])
def expand_kernel(
    output_ptr: Ptr[tl.float32, tl.int32], # [num_tokens]
    input_ptr: Ptr[tl.float32, tl.int32],  # [batch_size]
    cu_num_tokens_ptr: Ptr[tl.int32],      # [batch_size]
    replace_from,
    replace_to,
    MAX_NUM_TOKENS: tl.constexpr = MAX_SPEC_LEN,
): ...  # body unchanged


expand_kernel[(batch_size,)](expanded_x, x, cu_num_tokens, replace_from, replace_to)
expand_kernel.register_warmup()
```

There's no warmup function, no dispatcher and no decorator. A decorator is only needed when the signature can't express something, as with `copy_and_expand_dflash_inputs_kernel`:

```python
@triton_warmup(
    num_query_per_req=lambda num_speculative_tokens: 1 + num_speculative_tokens,
    BLOCK_SIZE=WarmupIntRange(1, 257, advance=lambda value: value * 2),
    HAS_NUM_REJECTED=(False, True),
    num_rejected_tokens_ptr=lambda HAS_NUM_REJECTED: (
        Ptr[tl.int32] if HAS_NUM_REJECTED else 0
    ),
)
@triton.jit
def copy_and_expand_dflash_inputs_kernel(
    next_token_ids_ptr: Ptr[tl.int32],       # [num_reqs]
    target_positions_ptr: Ptr[tl.int64],     # [num_context]
    ...,  # output, block-table and metadata pointers: annotated the same way
    block_table_stride,
    num_rejected_tokens_ptr: Ptr[tl.int32],  # [num_reqs] or null (0) when not padded
    parallel_drafting_token_id,
    block_size,
    num_query_per_req,
    num_speculative_tokens,
    total_input_tokens,
    BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr,
    HAS_NUM_REJECTED: tl.constexpr = False,
): ...  # body and launch unchanged


# DFlashProposer.__init__
copy_and_expand_dflash_inputs_kernel.register_warmup(
    block_table_stride=(self.max_model_len + self.block_size - 1) // self.block_size,
    parallel_drafting_token_id=self.parallel_drafting_token_id,
    block_size=self.block_size,
    num_speculative_tokens=self.num_speculative_tokens,
)
```

Here the pointer dtypes come from annotations. The four registered values bind to the parameters with the same names. `total_input_tokens` has no value, so it warms all three integer classes. The decorator only says what the signature can't:
- `num_query_per_req` is derived from a registered value;
- `BLOCK_SIZE` varies at runtime;
- `num_rejected_tokens_ptr` follows the `HAS_NUM_REJECTED` flag.

### Registration

Importing the helper adds `register_warmup` to every `JITFunction`. Registrations stay one line, in the code that owns the deployment values, with the same arguments as today.

*Registration doesn't need an active registry.** Today, `JitWarmupRegistry.register` only records a registration while a registry is active. That means inside `with registry.activate():`, or inside a method decorated with `@JitWarmupRegistry.capture`. Anywhere else, the registration is silently dropped. That's why #56323 had to add `@capture` and `activate()` to MRV2's model runner: its speculators are built in `__init__`, outside any active registry.

Triton registrations go through a new `JitWarmupRegistry.register_or_defer` instead. It looks up the active registry the same way, through the `ContextVar` that `activate()` sets:
- inside an active registry, it registers directly, exactly like `register`;
- outside, it appends to a process-wide queue instead of dropping.

`JitWarmupRegistry.warmup()` first adopts everything in that queue, then expands and compiles as usual. A deferred registration is therefore indistinguishable from a direct one. It goes through the same key expansion and parallel compile.

Existing owners (CuTeDSL, TileLang, DeepGEMM, …) keep calling `register` and keep their `activate()` blocks and `@capture`. This proposal doesn't remove any of those for now.

On CPU, `KernelOverride` gets a no-op `register_warmup`, so `cpu_triton_utils.py` is untouched.

### MRV2 example

Here is the MTP speculator's embedding shift as it was in #56323:

```python
def _shift_input_embeds_warmup_inputs(*, speculator):
    hidden = TritonWarmupTensor(
        speculator.dtype,
        shape=(1, speculator.hidden_size),
        strides=(speculator.hidden_size, 1),
    )
    return dict(
        input_embeds=hidden,
        draft_embeds=hidden,
        idx_mapping=TritonWarmupTensor(torch.int32),  # int64 at runtime
        query_start_loc=TritonWarmupTensor(torch.int32),
        last_token_indices=TritonWarmupTensor(torch.int64),
        num_reqs=1,
    )


@triton_kernel_dispatcher_with_warmup(
    kernel=_shift_input_embeds_kernel,
    warmup_inputs=_shift_input_embeds_warmup_inputs,
)
def _shift_input_embeds(
    input_embeds, draft_embeds, idx_mapping, query_start_loc, last_token_indices, num_reqs
) -> DispatchSpec:
    hidden_size = input_embeds.shape[-1]
    return (num_reqs, triton.cdiv(hidden_size, 256)), dict(
        hidden_size=hidden_size, BLOCK_SIZE_Q=16, BLOCK_SIZE_H=256
    )


_shift_input_embeds(input_embeds, draft_embeds, idx_mapping, query_start_loc,
                    last_token_indices, num_reqs=num_reqs)  # call site
_shift_input_embeds.register_warmup(speculator=self)  # + @capture/activate() in the model runner
```

And with this proposal https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64262:

```python
@triton.jit
def _shift_input_embeds_kernel(
    input_embeds_ptr: Ptr[tl.float16, tl.bfloat16, tl.float32],
    draft_embeds_ptr: Ptr[tl.float16, tl.bfloat16, tl.float32],
    idx_mapping_ptr: Ptr[tl.int64],
    query_start_loc_ptr: Ptr[tl.int32],
    last_token_indices_ptr: Ptr[tl.int64],
    hidden_size,
    BLOCK_SIZE_Q: tl.constexpr = 16,
    BLOCK_SIZE_H: tl.constexpr = 256,
): ...  # body unchanged


_shift_input_embeds_kernel[(num_reqs, triton.cdiv(hidden_size, hidden_block_size))](
    input_embeds, draft_embeds, idx_mapping, input_buffers.query_start_loc,
    last_token_indices, hidden_size, BLOCK_SIZE_H=hidden_block_size,
)  # call site: the launch from before #56323
_shift_input_embeds_kernel.register_warmup(hidden_size=self.hidden_size)  # load_model
```

The kernel is called directly, and the model runner is untouched. The warmup function, the dispatcher and the `@capture`/`activate()` changes are all gone. `_shift_input_ids_kernel` needs only its annotations and a bare `register_warmup()`.

### Launcher form

Some kernels sit behind a thin host function that derives every kernel argument from its inputs. Shapes become sizes and strides, the device picks tiles, optional inputs set flags. Declaring all of that on each kernel would duplicate the launcher, so we warm the launcher instead:

```python
@triton_warmup_launcher(
    # Only per-row shape matters; src rows may differ in dtype from the state.
    lambda state_shape, state_dtype, src_dtype: dict(
        state=WarmupTensor((1, *state_shape), state_dtype),
        src=WarmupTensor((1, *state_shape), src_dtype),
        indices=WarmupTensor((1,), torch.int32),
    )
)
def scatter_states(state, src, indices) -> None:
    ...  # upstream body, unchanged


# GLM-5-Next KDA layer
scatter_states.register_warmup(
    state_shape=recurrent_state_shape,
    state_dtype=recurrent_state_dtype,
    # The chunk kernels return an fp32 final state; FlashKDA's matches the cache.
    src_dtype=(
        recurrent_state_dtype if self.kda_prefill_backend == "flashkda" else torch.float32
    ),
)
```

The split is the same as in the kernel form. The decorator describes the launcher's inputs: which arguments are tensors, and how their shapes relate. Its function takes the `register_warmup` arguments by name. The caller passes plain deployment values and never builds tensors.

`apply_top_k_top_p_triton` uses this to cover all four top-k/top-p kernels from one declaration (See https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/62015): the batch sizes where the compiled code changes, with and without `k`/`p`. That one inputs function, 24 lines, replaces four warmup-inputs functions and four dispatchers (210 lines) in #56323, `vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py`. With the launches moved back to their call sites, `topk_topp_triton.py` and `topk_topp_sampler.py` shrink by 168 lines net (+94/−262).

## Design notes

- **No dummy runs.**
- **No pointer ties.** Pointers that always share a dtype are annotated independently. That might cost a few unreachable compiles at startup, done in parallel, in exchange for one less concept.
- **Why not just `do_not_specialize` everything?** It would compile each kernel once, but it isn't free. An integer that multiplies a row index (vocab size, row stride, hidden size) is divisible by 16 at runtime, and specialization lets Triton prove that and emit 128-bit loads. Unspecialized, those accesses become scalar. Measured on B300, through the real launchers, with `do_not_specialize` on every runtime integer:

  | Kernel | Unspecialized | Slowdown |
  |---|---|---|
  | `sample_recovered_tokens_kernel` (every spec-decode step) | `vocab_size` | 1.6–2.6× |
  | `apply_top_k_top_p_triton`, top-k | row stride, batch size | 1.4–1.7× |
  | `apply_top_k_top_p_triton`, top-k + top-p | row stride, batch size | 1.2–1.3× |
  | MTP `_shift_input_embeds_kernel` | `hidden_size` | up to 2.4× |
  | `scatter_states` | batch strides | none (bandwidth-bound copy) |

  It also does nothing for `constexpr` variants, pointer dtypes or launch options, which make up most of what warmup compiles. So unspecializing stays a per-kernel call, made after a PTX diff and a benchmark.

## Risks and limitations

- **It relies on three Triton internals:** the `__triton_builtin__` marker, Triton ignoring unknown annotation names (pinned by a unit test), and adding `register_warmup` to `JITFunction`.
- **Attribute binding is by name only.** If an attribute on the registered object is renamed, a `constexpr` that relied on it fails at warmup. An integer falls back to its three integer classes without a message. That's still correct, but costs up to two extra compiles.
- **Launcher replay swaps module globals.** It only sees kernels in the launcher's own module, and it must not run concurrently with that launcher.
- **Builds without Triton** get plain functions from the placeholder `triton.jit`, with no `register_warmup`. CPU is fine thanks to `KernelOverride`.
- **Not covered yet:** autotuned and heuristics kernels are rejected explicitly for now.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Single Batch Overlap (down GEMM ↔ combine) for DeepEP LL
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation.

**I (@algebra-MCX) propose to integrate Single Batch Overlap (SBO) for the DeepEP low-latency path, once the required kernel arguments exist upstream, and would be glad to work on the vLLM-side implementation and validation if maintainers are open to it.** This revisits [#34963](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/34963) (closed as stale) and the prototype [#29211](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/29211) (closed as abandoned because it depended on two unmerged forks). This issue records what has changed, what is still blocking, and a vLLM-side plan that does not pin a fork.

SBO targets decode batches that are too small for DBO to pay off (the crossover studied in [#64100](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64100)). With one batch there is no second microbatch to hide the all-to-all. SBO instead lets the DeepEP LL combine start sending each expert's rows as soon as the down GEMM has finished them, coordinated through a shared signal tensor.

#### Current vLLM behavior

At `dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068`, without DBO, on an async prepare/finalize (DeepEP LL, NIXL EP):

| Phase | Current behavior | Overlap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dispatch | [`_prepare`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1276-L1306) calls the receive hook immediately | none |
| Expert down GEMM | [`fp8_m_grouped_gemm_nt_masked`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/batched_deep_gemm_moe.py#L471) finishes completely before combine starts | none |
| Combine | [`_finalize`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1457-L1488) sends, runs shared experts (`MK_INTERNAL_OVERLAPPED`), then receives | shared experts |

So the shared-expert half of SBO already exists. The missing part is down GEMM ↔ combine send.

#### Upstream kernel status (checked 2026-10-30)

| Component | Status |
| --- | --- |
| DeepEP `main` (`f6aa38fe06`, 2026-10-21) | no `src_signals` / signal-aware combine |
| DeepEP [#249](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/249), [#388](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/pull/388) (computation/communication overlap) | open, conflicting |
| DeepGEMM `main` (`5081f8513a`, 2026-10-20) | masked GEMM has no signal output |
| DeepGEMM [#183](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepGEMM/pull/183) (SBO: down GEMM with combine send) | open, conflicting |
| SGLang | ships its own packaged forks (`sgl-deep-ep`, `sgl-deep-gemm`) whose `low_latency_combine` takes `overlap`, `src_signals`, `src_signal_expect_value` |

vLLM's DeepEP LL integration does not depend on these forks, and #29211 showed that pinning forks is not a mergeable path.

### Proposed Change.

**Phase 0 – kernels (prerequisite, outside vLLM).** Help land a signal-aware LL combine and a signal-producing masked FP8 grouped GEMM upstream (DeepEP #249/#388, DeepGEMM #183 or successors). vLLM work does not start merging until a released upstream version exposes them.

**Phase 1 – vLLM, opt-in, Hopper, DeepEP LL + DeepGEMM masked FP8.**

1. Capability check, no fork pin: enable SBO only when the installed DeepEP/DeepGEMM expose the signal arguments; otherwise keep today's path unchanged. Opt-in flag, default off.
2. Per layer step, allocate a zeroed `int32` signal tensor of `num_local_experts × ceil(max_tokens_per_rank / block_m)` from existing workspace (graph-capturable, no per-step `torch.zeros`).
3. Down GEMM runs with `num_sms - comm_sms` SMs and increments the signal per finished block; combine is launched on the existing aux stream with `overlap=True`, waits on a start event, and sends rows whose signal reached the expected value.
4. Shared experts move to the dispatch window (between dispatch send and receive hook), because the combine window is now taken by the down GEMM.
5. DBO interaction: a step uses either DBO or SBO, never both. The first version disables SBO whenever the step is microbatched.

Out of scope for phase 1: NIXL EP (`nixl_ep` 1.5 has no signal argument), FlashInfer CuteDSL / Blackwell (the #34963 path), DeepEP HT/v2, BF16 masked GEMM.

#### Completion criteria

- [ ] Upstream DeepEP and DeepGEMM releases expose the signal interfaces; vLLM requires no fork.
- [ ] With SBO off or unsupported, the code path and outputs are unchanged.
- [ ] Unit tests: capability detection, signal sizing, SM split, shared-expert placement, DBO exclusion.
- [ ] DeepSeek-V3/R1 FP8, DP/EP decode on H200: identical outputs/logprobs with SBO on and off; FULL CUDA graph capture and replay.
- [ ] `vllm bench serve` TPOT/throughput, plus a trace showing combine sends overlapping the down GEMM, across batch sizes below and around the DBO crossover.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks; implementation waits for the Phase 0 kernels regardless.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is a capability-detected, opt-in integration acceptable once released upstream kernels expose the arguments?
2. Should vLLM wait for DeepEP/DeepGEMM `main`, or accept a released tag that includes the change?
3. Is shared experts in the dispatch window the preferred placement when SBO is on?

No implementation, GPU run or performance result exists yet. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: DBO support for FlashInfer NVLink all-to-all backends (single-node H200/B200 first)
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation.

**I (@algebra-MCX) propose to add DBO support for the FlashInfer NVLink all-to-all backends (`flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided`, `flashinfer_nvlink_two_sided`), starting with single-node H200/B200, and would be glad to work on the implementation and validation if maintainers are open to it.**

These backends are vLLM's NVLink-native EP path, but `--enable-dbo` cannot be combined with them today. Users of these backends lose the option to overlap the all-to-all with the other microbatch's compute, which DeepEP and NIXL EP users already have.

#### Current vLLM behavior

At `dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068`:

| Layer | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Config | On CUDA, [`use_ubatching`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/config/vllm.py#L2196-L2220) allows only `deepep_low_latency`, `deepep_high_throughput` and `nixl_ep`. |
| Modular kernel | Both prepare/finalize classes keep the default `supports_async() == supports_dbo() == False`, so [`_prepare`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1258) and [`_finalize`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1447) would assert under DBO. |
| Per-step state | One-sided stores [`runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/flashinfer_nvlink_one_sided.py#L99) on the instance; the two-sided manager owns a [single workspace](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/distributed/device_communicators/all2all.py#L707-L710). Two microbatches in flight would share both. |

(The DBO rejection in `flashinfer_moe_ep.py` belongs to the SM100/103 FlashInfer MoE EP megakernel and is out of scope here.)

#### Hardware: GB200 is not required for the first slice

From static reading of FlashInfer 0.7.2 and the vLLM source above (not yet run on H200):

| Aspect | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| Memory sharing | `MnnvlMemory` falls back from FABRIC handles to POSIX file descriptors when the device has no fabric cluster, so a single NVSwitch node works. |
| Kernels | The default `backend="trtllm"` (legacy) kernels have no Python architecture gate; the MNNVL comm JIT module targets SM 9.x/10.x. Only the opt-in `backend="cake"` requires SM 10.0/10.3. |
| Multi-node | Needs FABRIC handles (MNNVL, e.g. GB200 NVL72). Out of scope for the first slice. |
| CI | These backends' kernel tests already run on `b200-k8s`. |

### Proposed Change.

**Scope of the first slice:** single node, DP/EP over NVLink, CUDA, eager DBO (prefill and decode). FULL CUDA graph DBO, multi-node MNNVL and `backend="cake"` come later.

1. **Execution model.** The FlashInfer APIs used here do not expose a send/receive hook pair, so follow the existing synchronous pattern of [`naive_dp_ep._comm_region`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/dc4dd5a2217bc757232e9fa4d8a8b59e207ca068/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/naive_dp_ep.py#L145-L173): under DBO, yield and run dispatch/combine on the comm stream, then switch back. `supports_dbo()` returns True; `supports_async()` stays False so shared-expert placement is unchanged.
2. **Per-microbatch state.** Index per-step state (`runtime_max_tokens_per_rank`, dispatch handles/metadata) by `dbo_current_ubatch_id()`. Allocate one FlashInfer workspace per microbatch so two in-flight collectives never share buffers or completion flags.
3. **SM budget.** Run the comm-stream kernels within the existing DBO comm-SM budget, and confirm that a spinning receive cannot starve the peer microbatch's sender (deadlock check).
4. **Config.** Add the two backends to the CUDA DBO allow-list only after (1)–(3) pass.

Out of scope: changing FlashInfer kernels, async hooks inside FlashInfer, SBO ([#64776](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64776)).

#### Completion criteria

- [ ] DBO off: code path and outputs unchanged for both backends.
- [ ] Unit tests: per-microbatch state indexing, workspace ownership, `supports_dbo`, config allow-list.
- [ ] 2× and 8× H200 (and B200 if available), DP/EP, eager DBO: identical outputs/logprobs with DBO on/off for one MoE model (e.g. DeepSeek-V2-Lite and a DeepSeek-V3-class model); no hang across repeated steps with uneven microbatches.
- [ ] Note: four tests in `tests/distributed/test_mnnvl_alltoall.py` skip without `SYS_PTRACE` in `CapEff`; validation must run them on a host where they execute, and skips are not counted as passes.
- [ ] `vllm bench serve` throughput/TPOT with DBO on/off, plus a trace showing the all-to-all overlapping the peer microbatch's compute.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is the synchronous comm-stream pattern (as in `naive_dp_ep`) acceptable for these backends, or should vLLM wait for FlashInfer send/receive hooks?
2. Should per-microbatch workspaces live in the all2all manager or in the prepare/finalize objects?
3. Is a single-node H200/B200 qualification sufficient for the first slice, with GB200 MNNVL as a follow-up?

No implementation, GPU run or performance result exists yet. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting.

title: [RFC]: DBO for the MTP/EAGLE drafter forward in Model Runner V2
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation.

**I (@algebra-MCX) propose to microbatch the MTP/EAGLE drafter forward under DBO in Model Runner V2, and would be glad to work on the design, implementation and validation if maintainers are open to it.**

DeepSeek-class deployments usually run DP+EP with MTP speculative decoding. With [#61464](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/61464) merged, `--enable-dbo` and speculative decoding can be combined in MRV2, but only the target forward is microbatched. The drafter runs afterwards on the whole batch. For DeepSeek MTP the draft layer is itself an MoE layer, so its dispatch/combine is fully exposed every draft step, with no peer microbatch to overlap with.

#### Current vLLM behavior

At `5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d`:

| Location | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| [`_get_dbo_unsupported_features`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/config/vllm.py#L3416-L3423) | Docstring: "The V2 runner microbatches a decoder forward pass (drafting runs whole, after it)." |
| [`execute_model`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py#L2130) | Only the target model goes through `UBatchRunner.run`. |
| [`sample_tokens`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py#L2350) | `speculator.propose(...)` runs on the full batch. |
| [`speculator.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py#L176-L178) | Under ubatching, `can_reuse_target_attn_metadata = False`, so the drafter [rebuilds full-batch attention metadata](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/speculator.py#L392-L400) every step. |

No open PR or issue covering drafter microbatching was found (searched 2026-11-02).

### Proposed Change.

**First slice:** CUDA, DP+EP (DeepEP LL or NIXL EP), DeepSeek MTP with one speculative step, uniform decode, eager mode. FULL graphs for the drafter come in a follow-up.

1. **Reuse the target's split.** The drafter consumes the same requests in the same order, so reuse the target step's `UBatchSlices` (request boundaries and token ranges after rejection), rather than computing a new split. Both microbatches stay in the same DP-agreed microbatch count as the target step, so no new DP collective is needed.
2. **Run the draft forward through `UBatchRunner`.** Slice draft inputs (input ids, positions, hidden states from the target) per microbatch, run them in the existing ubatch threads/streams, and merge the outputs before draft sampling. Sampling and draft-token bookkeeping stay full-batch, with single ownership.
3. **Per-microbatch attention metadata.** Build draft metadata per microbatch from the existing slices. This also removes the full-batch rebuild described above in the microbatched path.
4. **Fallback.** If the target step was not microbatched, or a later draft step cannot be split consistently across DP ranks, run the drafter whole, as today.

Out of scope: multi-step tree drafting, EAGLE3 auxiliary hidden-state layouts beyond the existing merge support, and drafter CUDA graphs.

#### Completion criteria

- [ ] DBO off, or spec decode off: code path and outputs unchanged.
- [ ] Unit tests: slice reuse after rejection, per-microbatch draft inputs, merge order, fallback decision consistent across DP ranks.
- [ ] 2×H200 DP2/EP2 and 8-GPU DP/EP with DeepSeek MTP: identical draft tokens and acceptance rate with drafter microbatching on/off; identical final outputs/logprobs with greedy decoding.
- [ ] Trace showing the draft MoE dispatch/combine overlapping the peer microbatch.
- [ ] `vllm bench serve` throughput/TPOT, DBO + MTP with drafter microbatching on/off, plus the share of step time spent in the drafter.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is reusing the target step's split for the drafter acceptable, or should the drafter decide its own split?
2. Should drafter microbatching be on by default when DBO and MTP are both enabled, or opt-in first?

No implementation, GPU run or performance result exists yet. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

title: [RFC]: Zero-copy DeepEP low-latency combine, safe under DBO
author: algebra-MCX
body:
### Motivation.

**I (@algebra-MCX) propose to enable zero-copy DeepEP low-latency combine, safe under DBO, and would be glad to work on the implementation and validation if maintainers are open to it.**

DeepEP LL combine currently runs with `zero_copy=False`, so DeepEP first copies the expert output into its communication buffer. That copy happens on every MoE layer of every decode step, which is the latency-critical path LL is designed for. With zero-copy, the experts write their output directly into the next combine buffer.

#### Current vLLM behavior

At `5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d`:

| Location | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| [`deepep_ll._finalize`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/prepare_finalize/deepep_ll.py#L393-L404) | `# TODO (varun) : Enable zero copy mode`, then `low_latency_combine(..., zero_copy=False)`. |
| [`allocate_fused_expert_output`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L203) | Existing hook ([call site](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/5689c2790c911a55c75825aac5166305df0b591d/vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/modular_kernel.py#L1174)) that lets a prepare/finalize provide the fused-expert output buffer; already used by `naive_dp_ep` and `mori_epv2`, not by DeepEP LL. |

No open PR or issue implementing this was found (searched 2026-11-02).

### Proposed Change.

**First slice:** CUDA, DeepEP LL with batched experts whose output layout matches DeepEP's combine buffer (`[num_local_experts, num_ranks * max_tokens_per_rank, hidden]`, BF16), DBO off and on.

1. **Provide the output buffer.** Implement `allocate_fused_expert_output` in the DeepEP LL prepare/finalize to return a view of DeepEP's next low-latency combine buffer (`get_next_low_latency_combine_buffer(handle)`) when the layout and dtype match, and `None` (current copy path) otherwise.
2. **Combine with `zero_copy=True`** only when the experts wrote into that buffer.
3. **DBO buffer ownership.** DeepEP alternates LL buffers per call. Under DBO the peer microbatch can issue an LL dispatch between this microbatch's buffer allocation and its combine, which would change which buffer is "next". The design must pin the buffer used by each microbatch (or fall back to the copy path under DBO) so that a microbatch never writes into a buffer the peer is using. This is the main open question, and it decides whether DBO is included in the first slice.

Out of scope: changes to DeepEP itself, DeepEP v2 and HT backends.

#### Completion criteria

- [ ] Default behavior unchanged when the layout does not match.
- [ ] Unit / kernel tests: zero-copy and copy paths produce identical combine results; buffer ownership with interleaved microbatch calls.
- [ ] 2×H200 DP2/EP2 with DeepSeek-V2-Lite (BF16 and FP8): identical outputs/logprobs with zero-copy on/off, with DBO on and off, and with FULL CUDA graphs.
- [ ] Per-layer combine time and decode TPOT, zero-copy on/off.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Questions for maintainers:

1. Is the original TODO still wanted, or was zero-copy deliberately left disabled for a known reason?
2. Under DBO, is pinning one combine buffer per microbatch acceptable, or should zero-copy be limited to DBO-off first?

No implementation, GPU run or performance result exists yet. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting.
